News.title: Labour should be securing our borders & restoring law and order on our streets – instead they’re obsessing about Israel
News.content:
A PRIME Minister’s first responsibility is the safety of the British people.

That should be the simplest principle in politics.



Yet Labour’s decision to impose new trade sanctions on Israel shows a government putting its own party-political ­interests ahead of our national interest.

These sanctions are performative politics, designed to appease Labour MPs and activists regardless of the consequences for Britain.



And those consequences could be ­serious.

Israel is an important security and intelligence partner for the United Kingdom.

We face common enemies. Iran and its proxies do not only threaten Israel.

MI5 has warned that the Iranian regime has plotted violence on British soil and targeted people living in this country.

At a time when we face a serious terrorist threat, deliberately damaging relations with a country whose intelligence helps save lives here is madness.

We can all see what is happening. The Labour Party is putting Britain’s national interests second in an attempt to win back support from Islamist and far-Left activists.



With Keir Starmer quitting Parliament, Labour is terrified of losing his old ­London constituency to the Green Party, as it did in the Gorton and Denton by-election earlier this year.

So now the Government is choosing to appease ideological fringe groups whose priorities are far removed from those of the majority of people in this country.

Britain faces serious and immediate challenges: Securing our borders, restoring law and order on our streets, strengthening the economy, easing the cost-of-living pressures facing ordinary families.



Instead, Labour is obsessed with Israel. But it doesn’t stop there.

Labour is also risking Britain’s relationship with our ­closest ally, the United States. The US Ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, has reportedly raised the ­possibility of trade retaliation against us over these sanctions.

Florida and other US states may do just that under their own laws, threatening jobs here in Britain.

Why would any British government ­voluntarily create a new dispute with Washington while simultaneously weakening relations with a vital Middle Eastern security partner?

Our relationship with Israel is not just some abstract diplomatic exercise. It touches the everyday lives of British ­people.



Israeli-linked pharmaceutical companies are major suppliers of medicines used by the NHS. Around one in every eight pills taken by British patients is produced by these companies.

People suffering from serious illnesses such as cancer and multiple sclerosis rely on these medicines.

Andy Burnham should explain to the British people why he is making it harder for NHS patients to access the medicines they need, to satisfy a left-wing, anti-Israel fringe of the Labour Party.



Criticism of the Israeli government is not antisemitic.

Israel is a democracy and its governments, like our own, can and should be challenged when they do the wrong things.

But the Labour Party’s obsession with Israel is entirely rooted in domestic ­politics. And let’s not forget who else is being thrown under the bus in Labour’s attempt to win back Islamist votes: British Jews.

Britain has witnessed a horrifying rise in antisemitic hatred since the October 7 attacks. British Jews have watched hatred of Israel repeatedly spill over into hatred directed at them.

Jewish schools and synagogues require round-the-clock security. Jewish families worry about the safety of their children.



The Government cannot claim to care about the poisonous atmosphere surrounding British Jews while it drives a relentless campaign to demonise Israel.

This has nothing to do with peace in the Middle East and a two-state solution.

Peace requires leverage and relationships with both sides.

Britain diminishes that influence when it substitutes gestures for diplomacy and alienates the countries whose cooperation we need.

If the Government was serious in its diplomacy, it would know that there is an upcoming election in Israel and there are limits on the Israeli government’s ability to change its policy on settlements until that election takes place.



This Labour Government has become far too comfortable sacrificing British interests for political gestures.

We cannot have a government whose first inclination is to surrender to pressure from activists.

Foreign policy should not be an ­instrument for managing Labour’s internal divisions.

It should defend our security, strengthen our alliances and advance the interests of the British people.

The Government should spend less time pandering to its activist base and more time fixing our broken economy and ­getting this country back on track.



Andy Burnham needs to decide which comes first — his party or his country.

For a Prime Minister, there should only ever be one answer.

News.title: Cambridge uni refugee expert called BA flier ‘a jihadist’ and told him to ‘blow himself up’ in racist rant on plane
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

BOFFIN'S RACIST RANT Cambridge uni refugee expert called BA flier ‘a jihadist’ and told him to ‘blow himself up’ in racist rant on plane

A LECTURER at Cambridge University branded a BA passenger “a jihadist” in a drunken racist rant at 30,000ft.

Refugee expert Dr Adam Coutts told Hammad Aziz he should “go to Birmingham to blow yourself up”.



He lashed out at Mr Aziz’s Middle-Eastern heritage and said he and wife Fatima Hashim’s marriage was a sham.

Coutts, 48, a doctor of philosophy, became “aggressive”, hitting a phone from Mr Aziz’s hand, when he “intervened” in a chat between Coutts and another passenger on the Cairo to Heathrow flight on July 15.



Married dad-of-two Coutts told him: “You should shave your beard. You look like a jihadist.”

Mr Aziz said in a statement: “I feared for the safety of me and my wife.

“He made several comments I felt were racist as we were both visibly Muslim.”

Ruaa Kamaran, defending, told Uxbridge JPs that Coutts, who has advised the UN on migration, was being treated for mental health conditions.

Coutts admitted racially aggravated harassment, assault, criminal damage and being drunk on a plane.

Judge Mohammed Bashir gave him a 16-month suspended sentence, telling him: “This was a very marked departure from your previous good character.”



Coutts must pay £2,204, including £700 in compensation.

Cambridge University, which sources say does not directly employ Coutts on staff, was approached for comment.

News.title: Comedian Dawn French handed six-month driving ban after racking up fourth speeding offence in three years
News.content:
DAWN French has been handed a six-month driving ban after racking up her fourth speeding offence in three years.

The comedian, 68, picked up 12 points on her licence after she was caught driving her £31,000 Mini Clubman Cooper S Sport at 36mph in a 30mph zone in Plymouth, Devon, on June 11 last year.



At the time of the offence French – famed for her role as Geraldine Granger in The Vicar of Dibley and her comedy double act with Jennifer Saunders – had already picked up nine points from speeding, Plymouth Magistrates’ court heard.

The TV star did not attend the hearing in person but her solicitor Chris Spencer said: “It’s a misjudgement on her part for which she has already pleaded guilty online.



“She expresses her remorse.”

Mr Spencer added that French accepted she would now receive a ban.

District Judge Stuart Smith told her she couldn’t get behind the wheel for six months following the hearing.

Judge Smith said: “It’s a matter which falls into the lowest subcategory of the speeding guidelines with a fine in Band A and three penalty points.

“Three penalty points added to the nine therefore triggers the disqualification provision.”

Ms French was also ordered to pay a £600 fine, £240 victim surcharge and £90 costs after the court heard her income was over £2,000 per week.



Judge Smith initially ordered the money be paid within 14 days but extended the deadline to 21 days after Mr Spencer requested she be given more time.

French – who recently revealed she has lost 7.5stone from walking more – was previously caught speeding in June 2025 – within days of the offence that led to her ban – July 2024 and June 2023.

The Plymouth-born star has previously claimed she is “the most excellent driver you will ever meet and that is a fact” but in a 2016 interview she also admitted she once racked up points in Devon and Somerset in the same night after speeding through roadworks on the county boundary in her Range Rover Sport.

News.title: Harry & Meghan’s soap opera is even worse in UK and huge problem for Royals – there’s more Palace rows to come
News.content:
IF the Sussexes thought their 5,000- mile move back to the UK might help mend family fractures, it appears the emotional distance has remained unchanged.

For it’s been less than a fortnight since the wheels of their PJ touched down at Birmingham airport, and already it’s kicked off.



On Monday, the King sent a letter to various senior officials making it clear that Harry and Meghan remain firmly outside the royal fold, should be treated as “private citizens”, are unable to use the title of HRH, and should not have any public money spent on them.

In a bid to perhaps try to soften the impact of this bluntly direct and highly public missive, a Palace source let it be known that the Sussex camp had been warned of its contents in advance.

Not so, the couple countered yesterday, making it clear they were “surprised” by it.



Their camp has also expressed concern about the timing because, yesterday, the Home Office committee responsible for whether Harry and his family will get royal security reportedly met.

All of which appears to suggest that any thoughts of there being a welcome in the hillsides of Balmoral etc are rather wide of the mark.

So where does that leave Harry and Meghan? On Monday, he was shown at his first official outing since arriving back here, described by some as a “pseudo-royal engagement”.

And therein lies the problem for Buckingham Palace.

For however many times they say that Harry isn’t a “working royal”, his status as a member of the Royal Family remains unchanged and certain charities/events/brands will want to tap into that.



Why else was he posing for cameras while signing a mural at Tower Bridge Studios on Monday?

Not because he’s Harry Windsor of OX7 or whatever Cotswolds postcode they’ve settled in, but because he’s still — and always will be — the King’s son.

And in commercial terms, that gives him a sprinkling of royal stardust that no amount of sternly worded letters from the King can remove.

So fasten your seatbelts folks, it’s going to be a bumpy ride.

Every appearance the Sussexes make will be viewed through a royal prism, every speech will be scrutinised for some coded reference to his family, and every disagreement with the Palace (trust me, there’ll be plenty more) will simply fuel publicity for whatever brand is paying them to turn up to an event.



It was the same when they lived in La La Land, but the distance and time difference slightly muted the jarring awkwardness of it all.

But now we have the curious spectacle of a prince doing things around the UK that look remarkably like the work of a prince, while the Palace reminds everyone that he isn’t there as a “working” prince on behalf of the King.

Harry and Meghan’s return to these shores was always going to test whether the wounds of the past six years had healed sufficiently for some sort of rapprochement.

Less than a fortnight in to this, er, brave new world, it appears that while the location of the soap opera may have changed, the script remains unchanged.

Beauty and brains…of a politician



FRANCE was considered one of the favourites to win this year’s Miss World contest.

But 21-year-old Indira Ampiot (I can’t tell you the number of times my auto-correct tried to write “Indian armpit”) didn’t even make the final six after she struggled with her English in the interview and speech round.

When Ms Ampiot, who is from the French-Caribbean island of Guadeloupe, was asked what she personally could contribute, she gave an answer about why her country was in the EU despite not being in Europe.

Consequently, commentators said her linguistic performance ruined her chances.



Still, every cloud.

Her skill at avoiding the question and saying something completely different means she’d make an excellent politician.

GEORGE CLOO’D UP NOW

GEORGE CLOONEY was all smiles after being honoured with the prestigious Golden Lion award at the Venice Film Festival.

He even joked around with photographers, handing one his trophy and grabbing their camera to take a snap.



Compare and contrast this jolliness with 29 years ago when, following the death of Princess Diana at the hands of a speeding drink driver, Clooney held a press conference and referred to the paparazzi as reckless “bounty hunters”.

The following month, he arrived at the premiere of his film The Peacemaker and all the photographers collectively dropped their cameras and booed him instead.

One explained: “We boycotted him to show that we have some restraint and that we’re not a bunch of idiots running around with cameras and causing accidents.”

A media boycott, of course, is career suicide for any celebrity wishing to publicise their new movie/record/product etc.

So nice to see that now he’s older, George has clearly wised up.



OWEN’S RIGHT

FORMER England striker Michael Owen has taken a lot of heat online (yawn) for saying that he “never, ever” tells his children he loves them.

“I just assume my actions would show them that I love them,” he mitigates.

If it’s a choice between the two, a child would much rather have a parent that shows their love by being present and engaged in their life than one who scatters “I love yous” to all and sundry like confetti but fails to show up to school events.

Michael’s 20-year-old son James is clinically blind, and his father once said: “If I could give him my eyes . . . I would.”



If that isn’t love, then I don’t know what is.

TESS ’N’ VERNON O-KAY

WHEN celebrity couples break up, it’s common for them to issue a statement about how they continue to respect each other and plan to remain friends.

Then, in some cases, the details of their extremely hostile divorce battle hits the headlines.

When they split up four months ago, Tess Daly and Vernon Kay also pledged to remain “great friends” and “fully committed to our roles as loving and supportive parents”.’



And judging by this happy photo of them on holiday with their two daughters, they mean it.

So congratulations to them for showing that, while a divorce is always sad, it doesn’t have to be toxically painful.

TV presenter Richard Hammond has bought a palatial pile in Wales set in 23 acres.

But the discovery of bats in his belfry (or wherever) has currently stalled his plans to upgrade it.

Still, as he paid £1.99million for it, there’s some good news too.



He won’t be stung for Labour’s rumoured “mansion tax” on any house worth over £2million, however large or (if you live in London) small.

SAFETY LAST . . .

IF at first you don’t succeed, skydiving’s not for you.

But luckily for experienced parachutist Holly Wiffen, she lived to tell the tale after being knocked unconscious on a 10,000ft jump and coming to in time to deploy her emergency chute.

It slowed her down enough that she sustained just a broken leg and fractured spine.



And now she can’t wait to get back up there again.

“Knitting or stamp collecting isn’t for me,” says the 35-year-old from Devon.

Maybe not, but they’re a hell of a lot safer.

THE SAS is struggling to recruit because soldiers fear being prosecuted.

With legal investigations ongoing over the elite squad’s actions in Northern Ireland and Afghanistan, who can blame them for feeling it’s a case of Who Dares Loses?



Why put your life on the line for your country in war when your country might throw you under a bus at a later date?

News.title: Wounded war heroes from Ukraine & Britain scale mountain together to show UK’s unwavering support in war against Putin
News.content:
WOUNDED war heroes from Ukraine and Britain have joined forces to climb the war-ravaged nation’s highest mountain in a defiant display of their unbreakable spirit.

Amputee Chay Coulbert, 37, and Rob Chell, 53, joined ten injured Ukrainian marines as they put two fingers up to Putin by summiting the 6,762ft Mount Hoverla.



The pair shared battle stories, helped each other up the climb and unfurled a marine flag at the top in a remarkable show of unity against Russia’s illegal war.

One veteran with an above-knee leg amputation had a flag with the face of his killed brother on.



When he couldn’t make it any further, the Brits carried it to the top and flew it in his honour.

And the pair are now helping a double-arm amputee who needs bionic prosthetic arms to overcome his injuries.



The Sun joined the wounded Ukrainian veterans who told us how they were prepared to die fighting for their freedom.

They also spoke about the moments they thought their life was over when they got injured, and how they have bounced back to show their brothers in arms that Putin won’t stop them living a courageous life.

When we reached the top with them, we signed a rock to add to scores of others supporting the war-torn country – letting them know “The Sun was here”.

The expedition was organised by rehab charity Vsesylni and Ukraine’s 39th Marine Brigade care service Sluzhba Turboty.



Ex Royal Marine Commando Chay, from Ashbourne, Derbys, who lost his leg to an IED fighting in Afghanistan in 2012, said of his fellow former soldiers on the trip: “We can talk to each other on a level that other people can’t.

“All the therapists that they’ll meet, unless they’ve actually been on the front line serving themselves, they won’t actually realise what it’s like to go through something like that.

Chay added: “The Ukrainian veterans are really inspiring guys.



“Our wars are, like, Iraq and Afghanistan, where we’ve gone to a foreign country, whereas here, they’re defending their homeland.

“They’re very committed. If it weren’t for the Ukrainians holding them back, the Russians would be walking straight through Europe until they’re knocking on our door.

“They’re not just fighting for their freedom, but our own too.”

Ex-combat Royal Engineer Rob, from Ashbourne, has multiple injuries in both his feet from fighting in Iraq in 2003.

He said of the Ukrainians: “They’re still taking the fight to the Russians. Outstanding determination and bravery.”



Among those climbing was hero Oleksii, 35, who defied the odds by reaching 6,000ft with a hugely debilitating above-knee leg amputation, supported by wife Elizabeth, 29.

The corporal, who got higher than his attempted climb last year, said: “I want to show my comrades and everyone with injuries that there is a life after. You can do everything.”

In September 2023, Oleksii was in Dnipro, throwing grenades away as they hurtled towards him — but approaching enemy soldiers moved back when they saw he was injured and starting to lose consciousness. Oleksii later realised that they were waiting for evacuation teams to come and save him so they could learn about Ukraine’s tactics and possibly target medics and hospital locations.



He crawled for more than an hour and a half towards safety so the evacuation teams would not need to give away his position.

The hero joked of how he got injured: “It was boring. It’s like in a movie. I thought it would be better.”

On the trek, Oleksii struggled behind most of the group because of his injury, but Brits Chay and Rob stayed with him the whole way.

He reached just below the summit but could not go on.

Chay, who now runs mountaineering support firm Vanguard Resilience Coaching, carried up a flag bearing Oleksii’s brother’s name and picture, who died during the war four days after his 32nd birthday. Chay told The Sun: “I went to war with my own brother and I was blown up one kilometre away from where he was on the ground.



“It could quite easily have been my brother carrying my flag. It was really meaningful for me to do that service for him in his honour.”

Oleksii added of Chay and Rob’s support: “It’s important that Royal Marines are coming with Ukrainian marines. We are going together until the end. It’s important and symbolic.”

A 31-year-old double arm amputee, given the military call sign Sour to protect his identity, was hit by mortar shelling while serving as a drone pilot near Pokrovsk in November.

He does not have prosthetics but still made it to the top of the mountain first.

And he misses the work so much that he has been training on a drone simulator using just his feet.

Recalling how he got injured, he said: “We were hit by mortar shelling on the most dangerous crossroad.



“My arms were on my head, so all the shrapnel went in my arms. My arms were like chopped beef.

“My brother in arms applied a tourniquet, but because the area was too dangerous we continued on foot.

“I knew my arms were going to be amputated. But I had to just survive.

“When you see this darkness after a shelling, it’s scary. You realise that you need to fight for life.”



“Russia was not ready for our spirit. They thought they could walk into Kyiv in three days. Four years later they can’t claim us.”

In April 2023, Vlad, 32, was in Kherson when a mine exploded, leaving him needing an arm amputation.

Vlad, who served in the 39th and other brigades, said: “My right hand was only one bone and the left hand was all blown off.

“I was trying to get up but I couldn’t. In front of me, I saw a guy without armour die when a small piece of shrapnel went into his heart.

“I thought my life was over, but I’ve changed my mind now. I climbed this mountain to show that I can do this, that Russia won’t stop us.”



He still has around 100 pieces of shrapnel in his legs and feet, and the two Brits are now helping him to source equipment that can help with his arm injuries.

Serghiy, 34, served as a sergeant major in the 39th brigade and had part of his left foot amputated in November 2023 after being blown up near a land mine on the left bank of the Dnipro river.

He spent a year and half healing before returning as a staff sergeant for a year, and now helps with military training.

He said: “I had half of my left foot blown up. When it happened I just thought, oh f***.

“I did everything I could to reach the evacuation point by myself. I was exhausted. My guys who were around helped me and carried me.



“A boat arrived and took me away. I was surprised that they didn’t cut the foot off totally.

“Now I am great. Mentally I don’t have too many problems.

“The trek gives people the understanding that they can do more than what people expect of us. It’s important for us to carry the memories of those we lost through this time and remind everyone around us that they had a name.

“This is somebody who gave their life for this country, and we should remember them.

“Russia had better stop. We are going to win.”



Drone pilot “Kasper”, 27, suffered two injuries in the hellish Donbas region. His first was in December 2024, and his second came in November 2025 when the location for a medal ceremony was leaked.

After rockets came, he needed his left arm below the elbow amputated.

He said of the Hoverla hike: “It is to prove to myself that I haven’t lost my power, my ability and my self confidence.”

Olga Pieskova, founder of the Odesa-based Vsesylni charity, said: “It’s also very important for the team of the 39th brigade to have this link between the marines in the UK and marines in Ukraine.

“For veterans and serving soldiers, it’s important to understand that the same guys with the same experience are supporting us.”



International relations lead Rosie Cecil added: “This has demonstrated the power of the brotherhood, and how they are a team whether they are still serving or not.

“I’ve never seen courage like that. People who’ve been wounded twice and are still getting up and trying to lead a normal life. It’s incredible.

“Their wives and girlfriends are extraordinary people. With these guys, it’s not just the physical support. It’s the mental strength and the feeling that they’re not alone.”

News.title: Another shooting in Brit holiday hotspot as victim shot in leg outside hotel weeks after man killed in same resort
News.content:
HOLS HORROR Another shooting in Brit holiday hotspot as victim shot in leg outside hotel weeks after man killed in same resort

A FRESH shooting has rocked a British holiday hotspot just a fortnight after a man was gunned down and killed in the same Costa del Sol resort.

A man was blasted in the leg near the four-star Aparthotel Monarque Sultan in Marbella at around 2.15pm today.



The broad-daylight attack sparked a dramatic police chase along the resort’s famous Golden Mile.

Two suspects were arrested after reportedly abandoning their vehicle and desperately trying to flee on foot.



One of the officers who intercepted the pair is understood to have suffered a head injury.

The nationalities of the alleged victim and suspects have not been confirmed, although at least one of those arrested is believed to be Dutch.



The victim’s condition was not known last night as Spain’s National Police launched an investigation.

A guest at the nearby aparthotel told local media: “We heard a load of shots and then from the window saw people running and the two gunmen fleeing.”

Police recovered spent cartridges from the scene, but the weapon used in the attack has not been found.

The gun is believed to have been ditched by the suspects as they fled from officers.



The latest bloodshed comes just two weeks after a 33-year-old man was shot dead in Marbella.

He was blasted twice in the stomach in the early hours of August 24, around a five-minute drive from today’s shooting.

The victim was found dead at around 2.20am in a public area on Calle Pintor Pacheco, close to Marbella’s seafront and fishing port.



Cops initially treated the incident as a possible hit-and-run before the grim truth emerged that he had been shot.

The National Police said: “The National Police have opened an investigation to clarify the homicide in Marbella of a 33-year-old man, found early on the morning of August 24 with two gunshot wounds to the abdominal area.

“The victim was found dead around 2.20am in a public area, with the corresponding judicial protocol being activated after medical personnel confirmed the person’s death.

“Officers assigned to the Specialized and Violent Crime Unit (UDEV) of the National Police Station in Marbella have taken charge of the investigation to fully clarify the facts.”

The earlier killing came after police were reportedly called to a fight in the same area, where several gunshots were heard.



A vehicle carrying at least two people was then reportedly seen tearing away from the scene.

Sources said at the time they did not believe the shooting was linked to organised crime.

Reports described the fatal attack as the fifth shooting recorded in Malaga province during August.

News.title: Shocking moment jet ski sends holidaymakers flying after slamming into sightseeing boat in popular tourist spot
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment a high speed jet ski sends holidaymakers flying after slamming into a packed sightseeing boat.

The speeding fiend swerved round one ship before ploughing straight into the stationary tourist vessel off the coast of Columbia.



Dramatic footage shows the jet ski crashing head-first into the tourist boat- launching one unsuspecting passenger over the edge.

The man in shorts had been standong on the deck before being abruptly plunged head first into the water.



The chaos unfolded on Sunday off the coast of Cholón – a bustling tourist hotspot in Columbia’s Rosario Islands.

Multiple boats and watercrafts can be seen bobbing in the peaceful blue waters – until the jet ski comes roaring into view.

The shock collision left the boat spinning in the water with a freshly splintered front.

The local port authority has launched a probe into the collision.

No injuries or deaths have been reported, confirmed officials.

A spokesperson for the Cartagena Port Authority said the facts still needed to be “verified”.



For now, they are “not drawing any conclusions about what happened for the time being”, officials added.

Hundreds of tourists swarm to Cholón during weekends and peak periods – clogging the waters with boats, jet skis and other watercrafts.

The bustling waters have led to some tragic accidents – with one many losing his life two years ago.



Italina national Nicholas Cudini, 26, was killed in December 2024 after two boats crashed together in Cholón .

Nicholas competed in the highest levels of US college football – playing for the Santa Clara University team.

His body was discovered by the coast guard after nearly 24 hours after the fatal collision.

Earlier this year a heroic Brit sailor saved the lives of an antire boatload of people after the vessel was sunk “titanic-style” off the coast of Columbia.

The boat had allegedly been slammed by “pirates” in the Caribbean.



Christian Powys-Keck, 33, immediately dashed below deck to alert passengers and crew as the holed yacht filled with water.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The bare-chested Brit and desperate survivors were left clinging to a holed life raft and debris for 20 minutes in darkness.

But all were rescued and were safe on land in Colombia last night as their hero was dubbed “Fletcher Christian” – after the crew’s saviour from Mutiny on the Bounty.

News.title: Ports denied request to land 120 migrants in RNLI boats
News.content:
Requests to accept the landing of RNLI boats carrying 120 migrants intercepted off the Isle of Wight were refused by both Portsmouth harbour and Southampton Port.

When the migrants were landed on Sunday at Eastney, in Langstone Harbour, anti-migrant protesters blocked the road.

Associated British Ports (ABP), which operates Southampton, said it was not the closest port and it "did not have suitable reception facilities available".

The BBC understands the King's Harbour Master (KHM) Portsmouth also declined a coastguard request, but it would not comment directly on operational matters.

The protest followed a separate demonstration at the Port of Dover on the previous day.

The Langstone Harbour Master said the migrants were "recovered" onto two RNLI vessels in the vicinity of the Nab Tower.

They said they would have travelled at "quite a slow speed" to Langstone because the vessels were so overloaded.

News.title: Trump shares misleading video of King and fainting worker
News.content:
US President Donald Trump has shared a misleading video on social media which appears to show King Charles shrugging and walking away from a man who fainted during a royal visit.

The footage, which has been edited, features in a video shared by Trump on his Truth Social platform which appears to show other world leaders being disrespectful. The video goes on to show a montage of clips where Trump is seen honouring fallen US troops, hugging veterans and shaking hands with law enforcement officers.

The clip of the King was taken from a longer video when, as Prince of Wales, he was visiting an Asda supermarket distribution centre in Bristol during the Covid pandemic in July 2020.

The full footage, which Trump did not use, showed Charles reaching out to the man as he fell before remaining close by as he received medical attention. The video posted by Trump edits out the King staying close to the worker.

Buckingham Palace said it was not something it would comment on. The White House has not responded to a request for comment.

News.title: Glastonbury confirms ticket sale dates - and highest ever price
News.content:
After taking a fallow year in 2026, the Glastonbury Festival has confirmed that tickets for next year's event will go on sale in October.

Tickets for the weekend will cost Â£408 including a Â£5 booking fee per ticket - an increase of Â£29.50 from 2025.

Headliners for the festival, which takes place from 23 to 27 June, have yet to be announced, but rumours are already swirling, with everyone from Harry Styles and Fontaines DC to Taylor Swift and Stevie Wonder said to be in the mix.

Tickets for the festival typically sell out in less than an hour, with thousands of fans joining online queues to fight for their place.

In a post on the official Glastonbury Instagram page, external, organisers said tickets with coach travel would go on sale at 18:00 BST on Thursday, 1 October.

General admission tickets go on sale a couple of days later, at 09:00 BST on Sunday 4 October.

As part of an ongoing campaign to stop touts, anyone wanting to attend Glastonbury had to be registered in advance. You can check your registration on its website. , external

In recent years, the festival has also introduced an automatic queuing system on the day of sale, with fans needing to be online before the start of the sale with a valid registration number.

News.title: Prince George attends first day at Eton College
News.content:
Prince George has officially started his first term at Eton College.

The 13-year-old, who is second in line for the British throne, was dropped off at the all-boys boarding school by his parents, the Prince of Wales and Catherine, Princess of Wales.

The future king follows in the footsteps of his father in attending the elite private school, which has taught 20 British prime ministers and where fees are around Â£65,000 a year.

The BBC's royal correspondent Daniela Relph explains what the prince is likely to expect at his new school.

News.title: Monty Don to leave Gardeners' World after more than 20 years
News.content:
Monty Don is to step down as the host of Gardeners' World after more than 20 years, the BBC has announced.

The 71-year-old, who is the programme's longest-serving head gardener, will leave at the end of the current series.

In a statement, Don said working on the show had been a "deeply rewarding experience," but added: "Now is the right time for a change."

The BBC said Don had "inspired and guided millions of viewers with his warmth, wisdom and passion for gardening" since joining the programme in 2003.

Don began presenting the programme at Berryfields, a rented garden in Stratford-upon-Avon, before it moved in 2011 to his own garden, Longmeadow in Herefordshire.

"Throughout that time - and around 700 programmes - I have had the privilege of sharing my own abiding passion for gardens and gardening with an equally passionate, and often equally knowledgeable audience," he said.

"That connection with millions, not just in Britain but across the world, who share a love of gardens, plants and the natural world is something I have always treasured and which I increasingly believe to be at the heart of a life well lived."

Don added he had "always relished the craft of programme making" and paid tribute to the "superlative BBC team" he worked with over the years.

"I look forward to continuing to work with and for the BBC on other projects, as well as following new avenues," he concluded. "And of course, I will still be gardening, dog by side, here at Longmeadow."

News.title: Iceland summons US ambassador over Trump's stars and stripes map
News.content:
Iceland has summoned the US ambassador after President Donald Trump posted a map on social media that appeared to show Iceland and several other countries covered by the American flag.

Trump posted the image on Truth Social on Monday, showing the US, Canada, Greenland, Iceland, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean covered in stars and stripes. The entire landmass was labelled "United States of America".

Iceland's foreign minister said the post was "completely inappropriate".

Trump's territorial ambitions have repeatedly strained relations with neighbouring countries, including his push to acquire Greenland and calls to make Canada the America's 51st state.

His post of the map did not include a caption and preceded a flurry of posts of maps renaming the US state of New Mexico as "New America".

Responding to Trump's post, Iceland's Foreign Minister ÃorgerÃ°ur KatrÃ­n GunnarsdÃ³ttir called in US ambassador to Iceland Billy Long, who formally took up the post last month, local media reported.

When an ambassador is summoned, it typically means they are being called for a formal meeting, where the host country will express displeasure over their government's actions.

The post also drew criticism from Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, who said on Monday that the position of Greenland's government and people had been made clear.

"The Greenlandic government and the Greenlandic people have said again and again that they do not want to be American," she told Danish news agency Ritzau in Nuuk.

"I hope no one is in any doubt about that, either in the United States or the rest of the world."

Trump's interest in Greenland has been a recurring theme on his social media accounts and in speeches since he took office again last year, claiming the island is necessary to the US to shore up its national security.

His post came shortly after the European Commission announced a â¬200m (Â£172m) investment in the Danish territory during a visit by Commission president Ursula von der Leyen and Frederiksen.

The European Commission said its investment would focus on education, internet connectivity, the use of raw materials in the country and hydropower energy.

Meanwhile, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said Mexico "is neither nor will be a colony or protectorate of any foreign country," after Trump's post.

"Proudly we are a free, independent, and sovereign nation," she wrote on social media.

News.title: Charli XCX says bye to Brat and Liam Gallagher's tambourine grin - Music Photography Awards 2026 shortlist
News.content:
Striking images of Oasis's reunion tour and Charli XCX bringing Brat to Glastonbury Festival are among the nominees at this year's Abbey Road Music Photography Awards.

The awards, which this year considered works by more than 24,500 submissions from 42 different countries, released a shortlist of 40 finalists across eight categories on Tuesday.

The likes of Kendrick Lamar, Fontaines DC, Tame Impala and Sombr also feature in the shots, while other images of stars including FKA Twigs have been selected - out of competition - for judges' awards.

All of the finalist photographs will go on display in the LED tunnel at entertainment complex Outernet London from 8 to 14 September.

These will include the five pieces picked out for consideration in the fan-voted music moment of the year award.

Voting is available online via the official website, external, and in person at the exhibition.

The winners will be announced at a ceremony at the London studios - made famous by the 1969 Beatles album of the same name - on 24 September.

News.title: Where is Israel's proposed West Bank settlement the UK opposes?
News.content:
The BBC's Middle East correspondent Lucy Williamson reports from Ma'ale Adumim - an existing Israeli settlement in the occupied West Bank, overlooking Israel's proposed E1 site.

UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, speaking to Parliament on Tuesday, announced sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank "to deter settlement expansion" and "prevent the development of E1".

Israel has opened up tenders for the construction of some 1,200 settlement homes at the proposed site.

Miliband said he would ban the import of goods from Israel's "illegal settlements" in the West Bank. He also said "ethnic cleansing" was being carried out by "settler terrorists" and accused the Israeli government of turning a "blind eye".

Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar responded to the move by saying that Israel will close the British consulate in Jerusalem and called the UK government "hostile".

News.title: New law to force tech firms to stop children taking or sharing nude images
News.content:
The government has said it will introduce a new law to force tech firms to prevent children from taking or sharing nude images on mobile devices.

Apple and Google, which develop the operating systems of most smartphones used in the UK, were given three months in June to block access to nude images on smartphones and other devices used by under-18s.

But culture secretary Lisa Nandy MP told MPs on Tuesday that despite "significant commitments" from both companies, current proposals "do not meet the scale of this crisis".

She said ministers would look to legislate "as soon as they can" - with the caveat it may reassess these if firms develop and implement solutions sooner.

Alongside making tech firms block nudity on devices used by children at device-level, the government said its draft legislation would also make providers of apps used by children introduce similar blocks on nude imagery.

"This will ensure that the whole ecosystem changes, tackling the means by which children are most often abused or groomed in the online world," Nandy said.

She told MPs that Apple and Google had already made "meaningful changes" to block nudity on smartphones used by children at the core of their systems, but more action was needed.

An Apple spokesperson said it launched its Communication Safety feature in 2021 to help stop children from seeing or sharing imagery containing nudity - and had since "continued to expand its capabilities".

"We share the UK's commitment to combating exploitation and abuse online, and have shared with UK officials future plans to strengthen Communication Safety and other tools even further to help keep kids safe," they said.

A Google spokesperson told the BBC it was an "industry leader in combating non-consensual intimate imagery and advancing child safety across our products".

They added Google was pleased to have "made progress" and remained committed to working on efforts to keep children safe online.

News.title: Harry and Meghan 'surprised' by King's letter making clear they remain non-working royals
News.content:
A spokesperson for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex says the couple were surprised to see a letter sent on behalf of King Charles clarifying that Prince Harry and Meghan remained non-working royals.

The spokesperson said the couple, who have recently moved back to the UK, "were a little surprised not to have been told about this in advance".

But royal sources say Prince Harry and Meghan were made aware of the letter, sent on Monday afternoon, before it was made public.

It is also understood a security committee, which includes Home Office representatives, is meeting this week to look at the level of taxpayer-funded security that should be given to the Sussexes who are now resident in the UK.

The Royal and VIP Executive Committee - known as Ravec - decides security for royals and public figures and Prince Harry has previously complained about a lack of adequate police protection in the UK.

The Home Office does not comment on such decision making - and would be unlikely to reveal the outcome of such a meeting.

"The UK government's protective security system is rigorous and proportionate. It is our long-standing policy not to provide detailed information on those arrangements, as doing so could compromise their integrity and affect individuals' security," said a Home Office spokesperson.

In terms of Prince Harry and Meghan being "surprised" by the King's message on Monday - it's understood that reflects the lack of time given to them to respond.

They were believed to have had only had sight of the letter about an hour before it was shared with the media. By the time his team had made contact with Prince Harry it's understood the letter was almost published.

News.title: Prince George begins first day at a rainy Eton College
News.content:
Prince George arrived on a rainy morning for his first day at Eton College, accompanied by his father and mother, the Prince and Princess of Wales.

Prince William and Catherine carried umbrellas as they brought George, wearing a jacket and tie, to be welcomed by the head teacher, Simon Henderson, and provost Sir Nicholas Coleridge.

"Welcome, good luck and enjoy," said the head teacher, shaking hands with Prince George.

They made small talk about the bad weather before the new pupil, parents and staff disappeared inside the historic school, where 13-year-old George will be a boarder.

George, who had travelled the short journey from his home at Forest Lodge in Windsor, was seen with his parents arriving at Eton's school yard, overlooked by the school's Tudor landmark of Lupton's Tower.

He was later photographed wearing the school's uniform, with black tailcoat, waistcoat and a stiff white collar.

The future king follows in the footsteps of his father in attending the elite private school, which has taught 20 British prime ministers and where fees are around Â£65,000 a year.

News.title: England up in reading, maths and science rankings as Scotland and Wales fall behind
News.content:
English pupils have pulled ahead of the rest of the UK in international reading, maths and science tests, new data suggests, with Scotland and Wales falling further behind.

The 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) saw reading and maths scores slump in each UK nation except England, while all four saw an uptick in science, with that rise again most notable in England.

The latest Pisa report, which is published every three years, also warned of a worldwide decline in teenagers' reading skills.

Teenagers were losing the skills that "matter most in the age of AI", such as being able to critically evaluate information from different sources, it said.

The share of "hasty readers", who rush through texts to give quick, incorrect answers, has almost doubled between 2018 and 2025. The report warned the fall was greatest in those from "relatively well off" families.

Run by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), the Pisa tests assess teenagers on their ability to solve problems, think critically and communicate, before asking them a wider range of questions about their education in a questionnaire.

Although the UK performed well overall, the rankings varied significantly again, with results showing England, where the curriculum is significantly different, pulling consistently ahead of Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales.

England's schools minister, Georgia Gould, said the government wanted to "build on" the positive results and "go further so all young people leave school with strong literacy and numeracy".

News.title: I was fired from The Voice - I didn't want to leave, says Sir Tom Jones
News.content:
Sir Tom Jones has said ITV "fired" him as a judge on The Voice, and he did not want to leave as he "loves the show".

The 86-year-old singer from Treforest in Pontypridd, Rhondda Cynon Taf, has appeared as an on-off coach on the singing competition since it premiered in 2012.

Following rumours that he may not return to the panel for the upcoming series, Sir Tom said the broadcaster decided a while ago, but he "was told recently".

He said on social media that he had been offered a reduced role - one he was "not thrilled" about.

The Voice confirmed Sir Tom would not be returning as a full-time coach for the new series.

A spokesperson for the show said: "We have loved working with Sir Tom Jones over the past nine years on The Voice UK.

"While he will no longer be a full-time coach on series 15, we continue to talk to Sir Tom and his team about his involvement in the next series."

In a social media post, Sir Tom said: "The reason given is because of a financial difficulty with insurance.

"They now say in the press they wanted to 'refresh' the show, and with a new coaching line-up there wouldn't be a chair for me.

"They are offering a much-reduced role where I would make an appearance but without being actually involved from the start, and I'm not thrilled about that.

"So the only thing I know right now is that there's never a good time to fire an 86-year-old who's still pretty good at his job."

The programme's 2027 series was due to begin production soon.

In the most recent series of The Voice UK, Sir Tom featured as a coach alongside McFly stars Tom Fletcher and Danny Jones, as well as US rapper Will.i.am and Destiny's Child singer Kelly Rowland.

Sir Tom has appeared alongside many famous coaches during his tenure on the show, including singers Jessie J, Olly Murs, Kylie Minogue and Rita Ora.

He has also mentored three winners on the programme, Leanne Mitchell in series one, Ruti Olajugbagbe in series seven and Anthonia Edwards in series 11.

News.title: Favourite Kane makes Ballon d'Or shortlist
News.content:
Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane is one of three England players nominated for the 2026 Ballon d'Or.

Real Madrid's Jude Bellingham and Arsenal's Declan Rice join Kane, the favourite for the award, on the 30-player shortlist.

Inter Miami forward Lionel Messi, who is looking to win his ninth Ballon d'Or, has been nominated.

The 39-year-old scored eight goals as Argentina lost the World Cup final to Spain in July, with Messi since retiring from international football.

Lamine Yamal is one of six Spain players that won the World Cup to be included.

Having scored the winning goal in the final, Paris St-Germain forward Ferran Torres, who joined the French club from Barcelona in the summer, makes the cut.

Back-to-back Champions League winners Paris St-Germain have nine players - excluding new signing Torres - nominated, including last year's winner Ousmane Dembele.

Real Madrid forwards Kylian Mbappe and Vinicius Jr also make the shortlist, as do Arsenal defenders Gabriel and William Saliba.

The award is celebrating its 70th anniversary, having been created by France Football in 1956, and the winner will be announced at an ceremony in London on 26 October.

The "symbolic choice of venue" is in tribute to former England player Sir Stanley Matthews, who won the first Ballon d'Or.

News.title: Blind man sentenced for 150-mile drive while drunk
News.content:
A blind motorist who took his partner's car and drove for 150 miles (240km) at night while drunk has been handed a suspended sentence.

Anthony Hall, 50, who does not have a driving licence, was stopped by police on the M6 near Carlisle at 01:45 BST on 29 June after he was seen swerving the Vauxhall Meriva between lanes and onto the hard shoulder, a court was told.

Hall told police he had driven from his home in Huddersfield after he and his partner had drunk four bottles of wine.

Kirklees Magistrates' Court heard Hall, of Lees Close, had admitted charges including dangerous driving at a previous hearing and was sentenced on Tuesday to 36 weeks in prison, suspended for 18 months.

Hall had also admitted drink-driving, driving without a licence or insurance and taking a car without consent.

News.title: Pensioner with 'largest hoard' of child abuse images found in Scotland jailed
News.content:
A pensioner who amassed what is thought to be the largest collection of child sexual abuse material ever seized by police in Scotland has been jailed for four years.

Alan MacPherson, 83, from Stenhousemuir, was found to have more than two million images on various electronic devices after his home was raided in 2025.

More than 805,000 were identified as depicting child sexual abuse - much of it in the most serious category - while the overwhelming scale of his collection meant much of material was not checked and categorised.

MacPherson was told by Sheriff Mayram Labaki that the scale of his crime was "exceptional".

The sheriff said: "The quantity [of images] was so great that a substantial proportion could not be examined and categorised by forensic examiners.

"Every image records the abuse or exploitation of a child. The possession and circulation of such material perpetuates that abuse."

MacPherson will also be supervised for three years following his release from jail and placed on the sex offenders register for life.

The former volunteer archivist with the Royal Scottish Country Dance Society previously admitted downloading the material over a 14-year period.

Sheriff Labaki added: "Your views towards your offending and your victims are unconscionable.

"I refer specifically to the passages in the [social work] report where you state that not only were the children consenting, but they were willing participants.

"Your attitude is unremorseful".

All five people who died when an Amazon cargo jet ran off the runway at Miami International Airport were inside a shuttle van used by an aircraft cleaning crew, authorities say.

The crash occurred during a landing attempt on Sunday when the aircraft hit the van on airport grounds, broke through a perimeter fence, and subsequently struck an SUV on a nearby city street.

Five other people were injured. Miami-Dade County Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said Tuesday that both the pilot and co-pilot have been released from the hospital, while two victims remain in critical condition and a third is in stable condition.

The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating the crash, with a primary focus expected to center on the absence of specialized systems designed to slow and stop overshooting aircraft at the end of runways.

open image in gallery The Prime Air cargo plane overran the runway and struck vehicles on September 6 at Miami International Airport in Miami, Florida ( AFP/Getty )

Miami International Airport is not among the 120 airfields across the US equipped with lightweight, crushable materials that the Federal Aviation Administration says have saved around 500 lives.

Even without an engineered deceleration system, the airport appears to comply with federal rules because it maintains a 1,000-foot (305-meter) safety buffer beyond the end of its runways, according to aviation experts.

NTSB Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy noted that while her agency aims to prevent such tragedies, runway overruns continue to occur despite previous safety recommendations.

"Our recommendations must be implemented or we’re going to be here again," she said during a news conference on Monday.

Investigators have recovered the flight data recorder and are reviewing its information. Official interviews with the pilot, co-pilot, air traffic controllers, and other witnesses are being scheduled, Homendy said.

Amazon released a statement expressing its full cooperation with the investigation, adding that its deepest sympathies are with the victims and their families.

Five people killed in a van used by plane cleaners

The five victims were traveling in a van owned by Professional Ocean Service Corp., a company contracted to clean planes. The vendor stated it would refrain from commenting on the crash out of respect for the families of the victims.

"Our employees are far more than the people who work beside us each day, they are family, and they are deeply loved. Our hearts and prayers are with every employee and every family whose lives have been forever changed," the company said in a statement Tuesday.

open image in gallery The five victims were traveling in a van owned by Professional Ocean Service Corp., a company contracted to clean planes ( AP )

The sheriff identified the deceased as Rolando Aleman Leon, 55; Yoel Rodriguez Naranjo, 53; Julio C. Pineda, 75; Carlos Acosta Fajardo, 53; and Javierkys Reyes Quevedo, 47.

The flight was finishing a two-hour journey from Puerto Rico as storms gathered near the Miami airport.

NTSB officials stated that the plane traveled approximately 1,300 feet (396 meters) past the end of the runway.

Homendy described the scene as "utter devastation," featuring scattered vehicle wreckage, deployed air bags, destroyed navigation equipment, and ruined fencing along the aircraft's path. She noted that safety precautions were necessary because jet fuel remained present 24 hours after the crash.

NTSB examining why pilots didn’t abort landing

Strong winds exceeding 25 knots were reported on Saturday afternoon. Experts reviewing footage of the landing suggested a powerful tailwind likely pushed the jet far down the runway past its intended touchdown point, with the aircraft remaining airborne without flaring its nose to force the wheels onto the ground.

It remains unclear why the flight crew did not abort the landing to make a second attempt.

Air traffic controllers had also not shifted the landing direction to allow the plane to approach into a headwind, an operational adjustment airports routinely make when winds change.

The flight was operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 originally flew as a passenger plane for several foreign airlines over more than two decades before being converted to carry freight in 2015, according to Flightradar24.

open image in gallery Miami International Airport is not among the 120 airfields across the US equipped with lightweight, crushable materials that the Federal Aviation Administration says have saved around 500 lives ( Reuters )

Two of the airport's four runways remained closed Tuesday. Homendy said they will not reopen until NTSB investigators gather all required evidence from the crash site.

More than 225 flights were canceled across Sunday and Monday, with hundreds more delayed, officials said.

Homendy said the NTSB will work to hand the runway back to airport management as quickly as possible after documenting the scene.

News.title: Porto v Man City LIVE: Haaland heads visitors in front in Champions League opener
News.content:
Copa Independent | The hard truth behind a CHAOTIC transfer deadline day

A new Champions League campaign launches into life with a meeting of two former winners as Porto host Manchester City in an intriguing opening-round clash.

For the first time in more than a decade, the visitors embark on a European adventure without Pep Guardiola at the helm, with Enzo Maresca stepping up for his first continental fixture in charge. A strong start to the Premier League season has come after another productive summer in the transfer market, and Manchester City are at just about full strength tonight.

Maresca will have another Italian for company on the touchline in Francesco Farioli, the highly-rated young manager who has restored Porto to champions of Portugal. Another storming start in the Primeira Liga will leave confidence high that the club can mix it with the European heavyweights as they return to the top tier for the first time in three years – and this early test will be a good gauge of their Champions League aspirations.

Follow all of the latest from the clash with our live blog below:

Ivanka Trump faced a wave of online criticism after sharing a horseback-riding video that many viewers dismissed as out of touch with everyday Americans.

The clip, posted Monday on X and Instagram, shows a woman galloping along a beach at sunset, set to Coldplay’s “Viva la Vida,” a song about a fallen king.

It was unclear whether Ivanka Trump was the rider, but the post quickly went viral, racking up more than 15 million views on X alone. Although comments were restricted, users across the political spectrum quoted the post to voice their displeasure.

Many pointed to rising living costs across the U.S., contrasting them with the carefree lifestyle on display in the clip.

“Americans: We can’t afford gas, food or tuition,” GOP podcaster Melissa Witte wrote. “Trump Family: here’s a video of Kai’s luxury dorm, Ivanka riding a horse and we’re also gonna rename both New Mexico and Lake Ontario ‘America.’”

open image in gallery The video, which has drawn more than 15 million views, shows a woman riding a horse on a beach as Coldplay’s 'Viva La Vida' plays in the background ( @IvankaTrump, X )

California Governor Gavin Newsom and MAGA journalist Eric Spracklen both highlighted that gasoline has surged in cost amid the ongoing Iran war.

“Real ‘Let them eat cake’ energy here,” wrote another user, while yet another questioned: “Is she racing to her nuclear bunker?”

“She turned off the replies. Of course she did. The corrupt Trump family is so out of touch with ordinary Americans,” the X account Republicans Against Trump added.

Trump has long faced accusations that he and his family have profited off the presidency. In his first year back in office, his personal income soared to $2.2 billion, according to The Wall Street Journal. “I'm profiting because the stock market is going up. Everybody is profiting,” the 80-year-old president told reporters in July.

Compared to her father’s first term, Ivanka Trump has largely shied away from politics. She and her husband, Jared Kushner, recently paid $1.4 billion for an island off Albania, which they plan to turn into a luxury resort. However, the island turned out to be a nature preserve and the announcement of the American couple’s plans to develop it into a commercial venture led to weeks of nationwide protests in Albania.

In response to the horse-riding video, other users pointed to an August investigation by The New York Times, which reported that, under the Trump administration, wild horses are being slaughtered.

open image in gallery Ivanka Trump faced online backlash over a horseback riding video she posted, with critics slamming her as out of touch ( Getty Images )

The outlet found that the Bureau of Land Management is “quietly” selling off thousands of horses to buyers for cheap, which can then be processed and sold overseas.

“Your dad is selling wild horses on federal land and shipping them off to be slaughtered,” wrote Headquarters, an X account formerly associated with former Vice President Kamala Harris.

Not all of the comments were negative, though.

“Why is this pissing off liberals?” wrote one user. Have they never been on vacation in the Caribbean?...I don't get it. Are we not supposed to enjoy life?”

Meta has introduced a new personal artificial intelligence tool called Muse that is designed to assist adults with everyday tasks like scheduling, shopping, and converting "long-term goals into action plans."

Currently restricted to users in the U.S., the technology is being rolled out by the parent company of Facebook and Instagram with an emphasis on privacy and safety. According to Meta, Muse operates inside a dedicated, secure virtual machine that stores both the agent and personal user data.

Users aged 18 and older can interact with the system through a standalone application named Muse or directly within WhatsApp. The software is built to manage quick actions such as sending emails or reserving travel, alongside broader ambitions like setting up a business or mapping out a full year of exercise.

"Once a person shares a goal with Muse, it helps them develop a personalized plan and coordinate their time and resources, then advances the work on its own. It can open a browser, fill out forms, and negotiate on their behalf," the company stated in a blog post.

Technology firms are positioning AI agents as the next evolution beyond standard chatbots, which offer answers and retrieve information but cannot perform tasks independently on a user's behalf.

At its core, an AI agent functions similarly to a standard software program designed to execute specific tasks, like opening an application. By pairing this capability with an AI large language model, the system can locate the information required to complete jobs without needing explicit, step-by-step guidance. Rather than merely drafting text for an email, it can theoretically oversee the entire workflow—reading an incoming message from a coworker, determining an appropriate response, and sending it out independently.

This release aligns with CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s broader strategy for accessible AI superintelligence for "everyone," an idea he detailed last month in a 6,500-word online essay.

Though panned by critics as overly fantastical, the document describes a future where individuals gain access to tools for launching companies, receiving Ph.D.-level tutoring, and obtaining tailored lifestyle advice.

"Everyone will have an exceptionally capable personal agent that understands you, your goals, and everything you care about. Your agent will work 24/7 on your behalf to improve your relationships, health, career, finances, home management, hobbies, and more," Zuckerberg wrote. "It will free up time for the things you enjoy, and help you accomplish more than you could otherwise."

Whether consumers will ultimately adopt the technology remains to be seen.

News.content:

Convicted shotgun killers Erik and Lyle Menendez are set to face a parole board more than a year earlier than expected, state officials confirmed.

The brothers, who were granted a tentatively scheduled March 2027 hearing, expressed gratitude through family members after learning the California Board of Parole Hearings had moved their August 2028 eligibility date up.

Officials cited provisions under Proposition 9, a 2008 state constitutional amendment, which allows early hearings if new information or changed circumstances suggest an inmate may be suitable for release.

The trials of Lyle and Erik Menendez and their conviction for killing their parents came at a time when televised trials captured national audiences in the 1990s ( California Department of Corrections )

Erik Menendez, 55, and Lyle Menendez, 58, were convicted in 1996 for the Aug. 20, 1989, slayings of their parents, Jose and Mary Louise "Kitty" Menendez, inside the family's Beverly Hills mansion.

The brothers maintained that they killed their parents out of fear after enduring years of emotional, physical and alleged sexual abuse by their father.

Originally handed life sentences without parole, the pair were resentenced in May 2025 to 50 years to life. The new sentence made them immediately eligible for parole consideration under California law because both were under age 26 at the time of the murders.

They were denied parole in August 2025, when the California Board of Parole ruled that Lyle Menendez still displayed “anti-social personality traits like deception” and that Erik Menendez broke jail rules by repeatedly using a cellphone.

Weeks after the board rejected their release a Los Angeles judge denied their petition that sought a review of their convictions based on new evidence supporting their claims of sexual abuse by their father.

In a statement released Monday, the family praised the board's decision, pointing to the brothers' prison rehabilitation work—including founding a hospice program and a beautification initiative called Green Space—and citing the declining health of aging relatives.

"We will always be profoundly grateful that they have been resentenced and that our family can now imagine a future in which they are once again part of our everyday lives," the family said.

Both men remain incarcerated at the Richard J. Donovan Correctional Facility in San Diego.

Star Trek actor Robert Picardo has claimed that spin-off series Starfleet Academy was canceled after being undermined by online comments from Elon Musk and Trump aide Stephen Miller.

The Paramount+ show starred Holly Hunter and saw Picardo, 72, reprise his role as the Emergency Medical Hologram (EMH), known as The Doctor.

The series debuted earlier this year and a second season is set to air next year. However, Paramount+ have already announced that the show will not return after that.

It was criticized as “woke” on social media, with Miller calling a clip from the show “tragic”.

Musk also passed judgement on a video showing Hunter’s character Captain Nahla Ake wearing glasses and speaking to first officer Lura Thok (Gina Yashere) and Lt. Rork (Tricia Black), writing on X: “Turns out they banned Ozempic and LASIK in the future lol.”

In a new interview with The Guardian, Picardo said: “Let’s face it: when someone that high up in the administration and also Elon Musk piled on the same day, do I think it’s a coincidence that the new owners of Paramount cancelled our show the first moment they could have? We did not get a fair shake. We were killed in the cradle.”

Robert Picardo reprised his role as The Doctor in ‘Starfleet Academy’ ( Getty )

Picardo went on to address suggestions that the series was “woke”, saying: “Yes, there was the fact that we had a gay Klingon. Did a lot of people get over-exercised about that? My feeling is, get over yourself! There seems to be a movement to drive us back to the 1950s. Star Trek is all about the future, not about returning.”

He continued: “In that climate the core values of Star Trek – science and also diversity and inclusion – are going to get lumped in with what is under attack. Some people say, do you feel that it was at all current politics that had to do with your cancellation? If we caught the same flu that Stephen Colbert and the editorial freedom of CBS 60 Minutes caught then we’re in excellent company.”

The Independent has approached Paramount+ for comment.

The streaming service did not give an official reason for the show's cancellation when it was announced in March, but Variety speculated at the time that it was due to low viewership. The trade publication noted that none of the first ten episodes ranked on the Nielsen Top 10 streaming viewership charts.

William Shatner, who made his name as Star Trek’s Captain Kirk, also responded to Miller’s criticisms of Starfleet Academy.

“Can you imagine they’re watching TV, criticizing TV,” said Shatner, 95. “I mean, it’s bizarre! I don’t understand it. I don’t know why they don’t – I don’t want to be political. I’m Canadian in America but it’s enthralling.”

Shatner went on to reject the idea that inclusiveness on Star Trek had gone “too far”, saying: “I don’t know what going too far is. Where’s the demarcation line? Who drew that line? ‘Now you’ve gone too far.’ Excuse me, I didn’t realize that. Where should I have stopped? And by the way, what is ‘woke’?”

Four family members traveling aboard a small airplane that vanished off the coast of the Bahamas were found dead Tuesday after relatives launched their own search effort.

Silvia Larrieu said that family members using private boats found and recovered the bodies. The family is now coordinating with the U.S. Coast Guard to bring their loved ones home.

"We are deeply grateful to everyone who supported us, searched alongside us, and kept our family in their prayers," the family said in a statement. "We respectfully ask for privacy as we mourn this unimaginable loss."

The plane, which was carrying Larrieu's uncle, his wife, and their two grandchildren, went missing Monday morning following its departure from Great Harbour Cay, a city located in the Berry Islands of the Bahamas. The flight was bound for Miami Executive Airport in Miami-Dade County, according to police in the Bahamas.

Larrieu noted that her uncle, 80-year-old Mario Lamar, possessed more than 40 years of aviation experience as a pilot and frequently traveled to the Bahamas, where he owned a second residence in Great Harbour Cay.

open image in gallery The plane had departed from Great Harbour Cay, a city located in the Berry Islands of the Bahamas ( Getty/iStock )

Also aboard the flight were his wife, Lili, 79, and their two grandchildren, Sofi Sosa, 28, and Christian Sosa, 22. They were traveling back home to Miami after spending the holiday weekend away.

Sofi Sosa had sent a text message to her parents in a family group chat stating they were taking off, and an official flight plan logged by her uncle detailed the aircraft's scheduled landing time, Larrieu said.

Relatives alerted authorities after noticing that subsequent text messages were not being delivered.

"This is awful," Larrieu said in a brief telephone interview with The Associated Press.

Police in the Bahamas identified the aircraft as a PA-34 Piper five-seater with the tail number N212ML. Air traffic control lost communication with the plane approximately 13 miles west of Andros Island, local police reported. The island lies roughly 150 miles (240 km) southeast of Miami.

Larrieu mentioned that her uncle maintained the plane in pristine condition and was always exceptionally careful.

U.S. Coast Guard Lt. Nicolina Converso said a Coast Guard aircraft was deployed to assist with search operations Tuesday. Officials in the Bahamas had sought the agency's help around 2 p.m. Monday following a report of a downed plane. However, initial search operations were postponed because of bad weather, the Royal Bahamas Police Force noted in a statement published on Facebook.

The four fatalities occurred less than two months after another plane crash in North Andros, Bahamas, resulted in 10 deaths.

News.title: Villa end goal drought to finally give Emery’s new era lift-off
News.content:
Unai Emery is building Aston Villa 2.0 and this was a night when his new kids on the block produced clear signs of lift-off for the next chapter.

Emery always springs into life on European nights and his reconstructed team secured their first win and goals of the season to leave Villa’s 1,700 fans singing in the rain.

Ten summer signings have arrived during a summer of upheaval which included plenty of high-profile departures after the club’s Europa League triumph in May.

Yet this was an evening that will have further energised Emery on his return to the Champions League.

Nicolas Jackson, Zion Suzuki and João Gomes embody this new Villa team and all stood out here in Bruges.

Record £65m signing Jackson’s fine individual goal proved to be the winner to settle a chaotic, absorbing contest with the Belgian Pro League champions.

News.title: Bird flu threatens French foie gras amid new duck cull
News.content:
The latest cull - like previous ones - was undertaken to protect both animal and human health.

Ducks are killed to stop the spread of the disease between farms, as well as to protect the health of farmers and minimise the risk of the virus mutating.

It is thought foie gras itself does not pose a risk to human health, even if it came from a bird-flu-infected duck, because it is almost always heat-treated before it is sold, which effectively destroys the virus, according to Public Health France.

“The consumption of meat, foie gras and eggs – and more generally of any food product based on poultry – presents no risk to humans,” said a spokesman for the Maine-et-Loire prefecture.

Veterinary experts say ducks are especially problematic regarding H5N1 because they can carry the virus without showing symptoms and have been described as the Chevaux de Troie or “Trojan horses” of bird flu.

It is unclear how the birds in the latest outbreak, located on a farm in Longué-Jumelles, contracted the virus, although it is typically spread by wild birds which shed the virus through their droppings.

It is for this reason that British poultry were forced into lockdown or “flockdown” from late October to April of this year.

This included so-called “free-range” birds, which, as the Telegraph reported in November continued to be described as free-range despite never seeing the light of day under a dispensation given by the Department for Environment, Food, and Rural Affairs (DEFRA).

Ducks reared for foie gras typically spend the first 90 days of their lives being reared in their tens of thousands in barns with very little access to natural light.

Animal rights campaigners say most never see water.

They then are put through a rigorous 12-16 day “fattening up” period where they are force-fed through a tube to significantly enlarge their livers, before being slaughtered.

While France introduced a vaccination programme to protect its duck population from bird flu in 2023, the jabs do not entirely stop the virus from getting into a flock.

Data collected by the French Agency for Food, Environmental and Occupational Health & Safety suggested that between 50 and 55 per cent of the country’s ducks are unvaccinated at any given time, due to a 20-day gap between the first and second dose of the vaccine and waning immunity over time.

The ducks subject to the latest bird-flu cull in Western France had received their first dose of the H5N1 vaccine, but not the second, meaning they were not fully protected, according to the disease monitoring firm Airfinity.

The threat to France’s £2 billion foie gras industry comes amid increasing global competition.

Once the dominant producer, it is now being challenged by China, which has rapidly scaled up its output of the delicacy and now accounts for 45 per cent of global production.

A tin of Chinese foie gras costs roughly £3.70, while a typical tin of French foie gras made from duck liver costs between £10 and £15. French foie gras produced from Geese costs anywhere between £70 and £150.

China is also said to operate a more rigorous poultry vaccination programme, according to an analysis by DEFRA.

It applies to all farmed birds in the country, which has managed to keep outbreaks of bird flu on farms relatively low compared with European levels.

The H5N1 avian flu pandemic has now been running for six years and has decimated flocks of farmed chickens and turkeys across the globe.

In the UK alone, more than five million farmed birds have been culled since 2021, costing an estimated £48 million in farmers’ compensation alone.

Last week, the virus was detected on a mink farm in the US state of Utah.

Minks in captivity have previously been described as pandemic “time bombs”. The size and density of fur farms – where thousands of the animals are crammed together in tight proximity – give invading viruses a perfect environment in which to mutate.

The virus has also done huge damage to wild birds and other animals. In South America alone, more than 600,000 wild seabirds have died since 2022.

Dozens of other mammals have been infected and died across the globe, including foxes, otters, sea lions, bears, and seals.

In June, the virus was found in Australia for the first time – the last continent on earth to record a case – and the government has since launched a vaccination programme to protect the country’s rare species, including birds like orange-bellied parrots and black cockatoos.

Scientists have long warned that if H5N1 gains the mutations necessary to spread between people, it could trigger a human-pandemic, something that would be of “enormous concern”, according to the World Health Organization (WHO), given the virus’s 50 per cent case fatality rate.

News.title: The Chancellor’s speech, as it happened
News.content:
John Healey failed to rule out tax rises at next month’s Budget in his first major speech as Chancellor.

Mr Healey also sought to blame Liz Truss and her mini-Budget in 2022 for the high borrowing costs being paid by the Treasury.

During a speech in Coventry, the Chancellor said he would be “honest” about the need to control public spending during his time in Number 11.

He was speaking days after the cost of government borrowing hit its highest level since 2007.

It was also overshadowed by Jaguar Land Rover announcing plans to cut 4,000 jobs in the face of “intense competition and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty”.
