World.title: Adamawa and APC’s emerging season of discontent, By Jibrin Musa
World.content:
More importantly, Haske’s anticipated defection could become a rallying point for politicians and supporters in other parties who are dissatisfied with their own political structures. His camp is already suggesting that the movement could attract supporters from the APC, African Democratic Congress (ADC), Labour Party and other parties.

One of the greatest albatrosses hanging on the neck of political parties in Nigeria is the poor manner in which internal democracy is being given expression to, which appears anything but anchored on popular choice. Thereafter, the emergent discontent is also hardly managed properly, leading to decouplings and political fragmentation. This is a concern transcending many of the political parties in the country, following the earlier congresses and primary elections many conducted.

A case in point now pertains to the All Progressives Congress (APC) in Adamawa State, which may be heading for one of its most consequential political unravelling ahead of the 2027 elections, with the possible defection of its frontline members and erstwhile governorship aspirant, Abdulrahman Bashir Haske, said to be on his way to the Allied Peoples Movement (APM).

If the move eventually happens, it appears to be more than the defection of a politician from one party to another, as it could expose the depth of dissatisfaction within the Adamawa APC and test the ability of the party to retain supporters who believe they have been sidelined by its internal political arrangements.

Haske’s political appeal seems to extend beyond his personal ambition, as over time he is considered to have built a network of supporters who see him as a viable alternative within the state’s political space. His supporters have consistently argued that he could have secured the APC governorship ticket if the party’s primary process had been allowed to operate freely.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

That perception is important because political defections rarely happen in isolation. When a politician moves with an established structure, loyalists, grassroots mobilisers and influential supporters, the impact can be considerably greater than the movement of an individual.

In the storm of discontent seemingly riddling that state, reports that some of Haske’s supporters have already moved to the APM could affect the momentum of the party, going into the 2027 general elections, particularly with the claim by his close associate, Alhaji Hussaini Ahmadu Har that the movement could become a “political tsunami.”

Of course, political rhetoric should always be treated with caution. Every politician preparing for an election believes his or her movement is bigger than it may actually be. The real test will come when the political structure is mobilised and the strength of the support base becomes measurable.

But the APC should not dismiss the development, especially with the similar pattern of discontent across many of the states in which it is the ruling party.

Adamawa is not a state where political victories can simply be assumed. The state has a history of competitive elections, shifting alliances and influential political personalities. A strong aspirant leaving the APC with a sizeable support base could certainly complicate the party’s calculations for 2027.

More importantly, Haske’s anticipated defection could become a rallying point for politicians and supporters in other parties who are dissatisfied with their own political structures. His camp is already suggesting that the movement could attract supporters from the APC, African Democratic Congress (ADC), Labour Party and other parties.

If that happens, the APM could suddenly become a platform worth watching in Adamawa.

The bigger question, however, as alluded to above, is why politicians such as Haske would feel compelled to look outside the APC in the first place.

Political parties survive not only by winning elections but also by managing ambition. Where multiple politicians aspire to the same position, the party’s ability to conduct a transparent and credible internal process becomes crucial. A process perceived as predetermined can create resentment that eventually becomes difficult to contain.

For the APC, therefore, Haske’s situation should be viewed as a warning rather than merely a defection story.

The party must ask itself whether its internal structures are sufficiently inclusive to accommodate ambitious politicians and their supporters. It must also consider whether pushing influential aspirants away could ultimately weaken its electoral prospects.

For Haske, meanwhile, moving to the APM will not automatically guarantee victory. Building a political structure outside a major party comes with its own challenges, including funding, organisation, visibility and the ability to translate personal popularity into votes.

His supporters may describe the movement as a “train of victory,” but elections are ultimately decided at the polling units, not on social media.

That is why the coming months will be particularly important.

If Haske succeeds in taking a substantial political structure from the APC to the APM, the move could reshape the opposition landscape in Adamawa and force the major parties to reconsider their strategies for 2027.

But if the anticipated mass defection fails to materialise, the episode could instead expose the limits of personality-driven political movements.

Either way, one thing is becoming increasingly clear: Haske’s political future is no longer merely an internal APC matter. His next move could have consequences for the wider contest for political power in Adamawa State.

And for the APC, the real danger may not be Haske’s departure itself, but the possibility that many of those who leave with him may not be coming back. This brings into bold relief the Achilles heel of the democratic culture in Nigeria, in which popular choice is increasingly being sacrificed to the inclinations of dominant and domineering tendencies within political parties, which also lack the capacity to manage difference or are simply unbothered.

Jibrin Musa writes from Yola, Adamawa State.

World.title: Police foil planned kidnap operation, recover arms in Akwa Ibom
World.content:
The Police Command in Akwa Ibom State says it has foiled a planned kidnap operation in Oron Local Government Area of the state.

Timfon John, the police spokesperson in Akwa Ibom, disclosed this in a statement to journalists in Uyo on Tuesday.

Ms John, a deputy superintendent of police, said the command received credible intelligence from members of the public who reported a suspected plan to carry out a kidnap operation around the Oron axis of the state.

She said that following the report, operatives of the command embarked on a joint intelligence-led operation to a suspected criminal camp along the Calabar-Oron channel.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Ms John said that during the operation, police operatives recovered one pump-action gun, two cartridges, and one white rope suspected to be intended for criminal use.

According to her, the police also recovered two speedboats, three 200HP outboard engines, and one 15HP outboard engine.

The police spokesperson said the recovered items had been properly documented and kept in safe custody for necessary investigation.

Ms John said that the operation was part of the command’s sustained intelligence-led and proactive policing strategy.

“The strategy is aimed at identifying, disrupting and dismantling criminal networks before they are able to implement their plans.”

She further said that the command was committed to denying criminals the opportunity of turning the waterways in Cross River to their operational corridors, hideouts or escape routes.

She said the marine police unit had continued to maintain heightened vigilance across strategic waterways and coastal communities in the state.

Ms John expressed the command’s commitment to the safety of residents of coastal communities, boat operators, fishers and other waterway users.

She said the Commissioner of Police in Akwa Ibom, Baba Azare, was delighted by the gallantry of police personnel in the state.

“The commissioner of police is happy, the men are working gallantly. He is happy at their display of professionalism, courage and actionable intelligence,” she said.

(NAN)
