World.title: Chrystia Freeland negotiated with Trump. Now she's watching a trade war unfold
World.content:
Chrystia Freeland negotiated with Trump. Now she's watching a trade war unfold

toggle caption Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

Canada's latest tariffs on American goods took effect Tuesday. It's another escalation in a trade war that is raising costs and testing a relationship that, until recently, was among the closest in the world.

Prime Minister Mark Carney's government imposed tariffs of up to 50% on about $20 billion worth of U.S. goods in response to U.S. tariffs on Canadian products. The latest measures match U.S. tariffs dollar for dollar, though not product for product.

But in Canada, the fight has become about more than tariffs. Many Canadians say they feel betrayed by a longtime ally. President Trump has repeatedly suggested Canada should become the 51st state and has said he would use economic pressure, rather than military force, to make that happen. Canadians have cut back on travel to the United States and boycotted American goods as tensions have grown.

Sponsor Message

And the economic ties are hard to untangle. U.S. auto exports to Canada have fallen 22% since the trade dispute began. Canada is the largest customer for 26 U.S. states and a top-three customer for 45.

Chrystia Freeland understands the relationship from her time at the negotiating table. The former Canadian deputy prime minister and finance minister helped negotiate the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement during Trump's first term. Trump once called it "the best trade deal ever."

Now, Freeland says, the U.S. risks pushing longtime allies away.

"If Americans are concerned about China in the world, which I am, the best way to act on China is with an alliance with America's traditional allies," Freeland told NPR's Morning Edition. "But it has to start with stopping punching your friends in the face, which is what Washington is doing right now."

Freeland also pushed back on the idea that Canada's much smaller economy means it ultimately has to give in.

She recalled a small meeting during an earlier round of North American trade negotiations when, she said, she was told the United States was 10 times bigger than Canada and therefore "should get our way 10 times more than you."

"That is not a way to have a partnership," Freeland said, "and Canadians simply won't stand for it."

Sponsor Message

Listen to the full interview by clicking the blue play button above. Peter Armstrong contributed reporting from Toronto.

World.title: Has the economy gone C-shaped?
World.content:
Has the economy gone C-shaped?

Nuthawut Somsuk/Getty Images

Today's economy is brought to you by… the letter K! Or is it C? Or … well, it depends on who you talk to about how the rich and poor are doing these days.

You've probably heard about " the K-shaped economy. " When people talk about it, they generally mean that inequality is widening (and the fortunes of the rich and poor are diverging, so it looks like the right side of the K). Recently, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he was "sick of hearing about this K-shaped economy." And, he said, he believed the better letter to describe it was a C, which is, shall we say, a more optimistic letter for how lower- and middle-class Americans are faring in today's economy.

Sponsor Message

This desire to Sesame Street the economy isn't a surprise: we're always looking for ways to shorthand or telegraph the essence of what's going on in the economy at any given time. But assigning something as basic as a letter to something as complicated as the economy seems way too reductive. Even for Planet Money! So how did we get here?

The Indicator from Planet Money C is for C-shaped economy Today's economy brought to you by the letter... Listen · 8:35 8:35

The story begins back during Covid.

Mike Strain of the American Enterprise Institute says people started talking about a K-shaped economy around 2020, when the effects of the pandemic — and the government's response — began to show through. It was pretty simple, really:

" The original usage of the term K-shape meant that the poor were getting poorer at the same time that the rich were getting richer."

Initially, the term didn't get much play. Temporary federal relief programs were pumping money into the economy, offsetting a lot of the damage being done by lockdowns and layoffs and business closures. All of which affected poorer Americans most. So while people at the bottom end of the economy were hit hard during Covid, it wasn't so obvious at first.

But as the government's stimulus programs began to end, those less wealthy Americans began to feel the pain. Poverty rates cranked up, from 7.8% in 2021 to 12.4% in 2022 . At the same time, the richest 10 percent of Americans were getting richer. Government stimulus and interest rate cuts juiced the stock market, which benefited the people who owned most of those stocks: the wealthy.

Sponsor Message

To a lot of econ watchers, this bifurcation in the fortunes of the haves and the haves-less looked like the letter K. It was appealingly simple. Rich up: poor down. And before long, we started to hear about the K-shaped economy everywhere. Including on NPR . A lot . But Mike Strain says almost as soon as 'K-shaped' became a relevant term to describe what was happening in the economy, people began abusing it.

"Over the last few years, different people are using the term in different ways, and some people are using it as just another way of describing inequality, which is different than its original usage," Strain says. "Inequality can be increasing even if both more affluent and less affluent Americans are seeing their outcomes improve in an absolute sense."

In other words, it's possible for poor people to acquire more wealth, and for the gap between rich and poor to widen at the same time. Which is what the trajectory of the wealth gap has been — for the most part —- since at least 1989, as tracked by the Federal Reserve .

U.S. Federal Reserve

Claudia Sahm, an economist at New Century Advisors, says if you focus on incremental movements at the top and bottom ends of a K or whatever you're missing the forest for the trees. The forest being the chasm between rich and poor that's clearly shown on that chart. Claudia points out that the top one percent of Americans own fully one third of all the wealth in the country. But the bottom half of all Americans own less than three percent of the wealth. It's a massive gap that doesn't change much from cycle to cycle.

But the K is here to stay, it seems. Or the Sesame Streeting of the economy is, at least. Recently Christopher Nassetta, the head of Hilton Hotels, said he sees a C-shaped economy now. Never mind that he was referring to the middle class, who are not at the bottom of the economy, but rather in the middle of it. Nonetheless, his letter was snapped up and repeated by none other than Treasury Secretary Bessent.

Sponsor Message

To be fair to Bessent, one recent measure does look a little C-shaped: after accounting for inflation, weekly earnings rose at the lower end of the wage scale but fell at the upper end. So maybe a C is appropriate — at least by that measure.

"You look at the average wage of a worker whose highest degree was a high school diploma and the average wage of a worker whose highest degree was a college degree, I think you do see their wage growth converging," Strain says. "And so you see wage inequality narrowing."

But there's a problem here, that you, dear reader, have probably already identified. In talking about the K and the C economies, even in this tiny space, we're getting our data all mixed up. Are we using wealth or income as the data point to measure the economy? Are we taking into account inflation? And what does that actually have to do with the entirety of the economy anyway? Claudia Sahm says this is a big problem with the alphabetization of the economy, and the question of whether we're in a K or a C or a whatever...

"Frankly we don't have very good data to answer this question. Because everybody's bringing their own data, and it gets really complicated really fast in terms of what's changing and how much."

The state of the wealth gap or income disparity is not the best indicator of the economy, Claudia says. There are many, much more relevant and accurate indicators out there. Indicators that are more granular and data-rich; indicators that paint a much clearer picture of where the economy is at today.

The only problem is that all that data and granularity tends to complicate a simple narrative. And that makes it hard to do something simplistic, like assign a letter to the economy. Take the jobs reports that came out last month: they say the unemployment rate is down to 4.1 percent. But they also say jobless claims are up, that businesses are shedding jobs, and hundreds of thousands of people are leaving the workforce.

Sponsor Message

But in the spirit of adventure, let's try and give this economy of ours a letter. Not K. Not C. Mike Strain says what he's seeing is an economy that's easing slowly; settling down after having been cranked up to a white heat by pandemic stimulus packages. To him, it's a return to normal.

So what's the letter for a normal economy? We say it's a W. Up and down like a yo-yo. Sometimes gentle, and sometimes sharp. Followed by another W. Short for What the hell is coming? And Who the hell knows!

World.title: Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia ignite fires at oil facilities and wound 73 people
World.content:
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia ignite fires at oil facilities and wound 73 people

toggle caption AP/AP

CAIRO — A wave of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia Tuesday wounded more than 70 people and ignited fires at several oil facilities and utilities in the kingdom's southern region, authorities said, a major escalation in the renewed conflict between an important U.S. ally and the Iranian-backed rebels in Yemen.

The attacks come after weeks of escalating clashes between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen, which shattered a four-year truce in the country's civil war.

The flare-up delivered a new jolt to a region already destabilized by nearly three years of wars and brings more uncertainty for the global economy. The fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis threatens to squeeze shipping through the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a critical route of the Arabian Peninsula for oil and global trade. It also comes at a time when the Iran war has nearly halted shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway that moved about one-fifth of the world's oil before the war.

Sponsor Message

Fighting has raged on multiple fronts including Yemen's west coast, with government forces saying they have made territorial gains in the provinces of Hodeida, Taiz and Baydah. The Houthis have also launched attacks on Saudi oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

Houthi attacks hit oil facilities in southern Saudi Arabia

The attacks early Tuesday hit "civilian and economic facilities" in the Saudi cities of Abha, Jazan, Najran and Khamis Mushait, said Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, a spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen.

Al-Malki said the attacks wounded 73 people, including women and children. He didn't provide further details.

The attacks ignited fires at several oil facilities and utilities in Saudi Arabia's southern region, the kingdom's Energy Ministry said in a statement. Operations at the oil facilities and utilities were temporarily suspended, it said.

The southern region houses major oil facilities, including a 400,000-barrel-per-day oil refinery in Jazan, which is one of Saudi Arabia's largest. The Houthis had previously attacked the Abha airport.

The ministry said firefighters were battling the fires Tuesday morning.

Al-Malki called the attacks a "serious escalation" and a "flagrant violation of the kingdom's sovereignty, and a direct threat to the security and safety of its citizens and residents."

Sponsor Message

He vowed retaliation, saying that the Saudi-led coalition "will take all necessary operational measures to deter the terrorist Houthi militia with utmost resolve."

The Houthis claimed responsibility for the attacks, saying they were in response to recent Saudi attacks on the rebels across Yemen.

In a prerecorded video statement, Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, the rebels' military spokesman, said they fired dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at oil and economic facilities, as well as an air base in southern Saudi Arabia.

He said they attacked Jazan City for Primary and Downstream Industries, a major industrial and logistics hub on Saudi Arabia's southwestern Red Sea coast. The rebels also attacked Aramco facilities in Najran and Abha, as well as King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait.

Saree blamed Saudi Arabia for the escalation, warning that "every aggression against our country and people will be met with a firm response."

Nasruddin Amer, deputy head of the Houthi media office overseeing the Saba news agency run by the rebels, took to social media to laud the attacks.

"The Saudi enemy has to understand that the time for committing crimes and massacres against the Yemeni people without response, deterrence or paying a price has ended," he said.

The attacks came hours after the rebels blamed Saudi Arabia for an airstrike that hit a prison in Yemen's northern province of Jawf. At least seven people, including a child, were killed and seven others were wounded in the strike in the Yemeni city of Hazem, the Houthis said.

Fighting forces about 18,500 people to flee their homes in Yemen

The latest escalation stemmed from a Houthi attempt to fly a plane from Tehran to Yemen's capital, Sanaa, challenging a decade-long air and naval blockade by the Saudi-led coalition. A coalition airstrike struck the runway of the Sanaa airport, preventing the landing of the flight.

Sponsor Message

The Houthis responded with missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, and a blockade of Saudi shipping in the Red Sea, ending a 2022 truce that had largely halted fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition.

The rebels also launched attacks on Saudi-allied forces inside Yemen, prompting government forces to respond with attacks on the Houthis across Yemen's west coast and elsewhere in the country.

Government forces reclaimed territory from the Houthis in the provinces of Hodeida and Taiz, and attacked the rebels in the northern province of Jawf as well as the central provinces of Marib and Bayda.

The flare-up displaced about 18,500 people in Taiz and Hodeida in southwestern Yemen, further pressuring communities in southern Taiz and the West Coast, according to the International Organization for Migration.

"Families are arriving with nothing: no shelter, no food, no way to know if it's safe to go back," said Abdusattor Esoev, IOM Yemen's Chief of Mission. "Many of these are people who have already been displaced once, twice, even four times before."

Yemen's civil war began in 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, and much of northern Yemen and forced the government into exile. A Saudi-led coalition intervened the following year to try to restore the government to power.

The civil war has killed at least 150,000 people, according to U.N. estimates, and at times pushed the country to the brink of famine.

World.title: The 2026 midterm general election season is upon us. Here's what to watch
World.content:
The 2026 midterm general election season is upon us. Here's what to watch

toggle caption Brandon Bell/Getty Images

Democratic enthusiasm and President Trump's unpopular second term agenda have drastically altered the political landscape of competitive races two months out from Election Day.

Republicans hold narrow majorities in the House and the Senate, and the party in power tends to lose ground in the midterms. But 2026 primary results and public opinion polling heading into Labor Day weekend, the unofficial kickoff of the general election season, paint potential pictures of Republicans losing control of both chambers of Congress and suffering defeats in traditionally conservative communities.

Sponsor Message

Voters have expressed concern over major priorities of the Trump administration, such as the war in Iran and immigration, tariffs and gas prices and the overall affordability of American life. The president's approval ratings have sunk to record lows as polls also show voters see a disconnect between their top issues and what Trump seems to be focused on, like the White House ballroom construction project.

Democrats, fresh off of stinging losses in the 2024 election up and down the ballot, have rebounded with their voting base and independents unhappy with the status quo.

The looming campaign for control of Congress saw states controlled by Democrats and Republicans enact mid-decade redistricting in hopes of maximizing the number of safe seats for their party.

Still, polling averages — which are a snapshot in time — suggest the likeliest outcome is that Democrats take control of the House, as more voters say they would prefer to have a Democrat represent them in Congress than a Republican.

At the start of the year, Democrats' path to winning a Senate majority looked tenuous, as states like Georgia and North Carolina were just a few of the expensive tossup races expected in what is a favorable set of contests on the map for Republicans.

Sponsor Message

But now, the costly contests that will decide the next two years of Congress run through Republican-friendly Iowa, Texas, Ohio and Alaska — and control of the chamber is no longer a given for either party.

The national environment being more friendly to Democrats is boosted in these states by strong Democratic nominees who are raising large sums of money, plus, in some cases, the presence of third-party candidates who could earn enough votes from people who don't like either party to sway the outcome.

For now, the two main drivers of how the midterms unfold will be money and messaging.

On the money front, Democratic candidates are outraising their opponents in key races, while Republican party committees and Trump's MAGA, Inc. super PAC have hundreds of millions of dollars more saved up in the bank to spend. Some Republicans have questioned if and when MAGA, Inc. in particular will spend to support vulnerable candidates like Texas Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton. Over the weekend, the super PAC announced a $10 million ad buy to boost his campaign.

Speaking of Texas, Republicans are holding an unprecedented midterm convention in Dallas this week featuring several battleground nominees and members of the Trump administration in an effort to rally a flagging base and send a message to independents that they deserve two more years of Congressional control to make things better.

Democrats are trying to solve their own messaging woes while also facing record unpopularity driven by their own base voters' dissatisfaction with party leadership. Since Trump's return to office, Democrats have seen drastic improvements in their margins with voters across the country and across demographic groups, including commanding victories in the Virginia and New Jersey governor races in 2025.

Primary voters have ousted several entrenched incumbents while others have voluntarily announced their retirement from Congress, and in several key House and Senate races this year, the Democratic nominee's message is built at least in part on acknowledging flaws with the party.

World.title: Canada, U.K., France to ban trade of goods from Israeli settlements in occupied West Bank
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In a packed British Parliament Tuesday, MPs gathered to listen to the government reset its relationship with Israel.

Nodding alongside his cabinet ministers, Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who came to power seven weeks ago, listened intently as his equally new Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, himself Jewish, announced a ban on settler trade from the occupied West Bank. He said Canada and France would take similar actions.

"Today, France and Canada are announcing alongside Britain that they will also ban the import of goods from illegal settlements," Miliband said.

Cheers echoed through the parliamentary chamber. Miliband noted the three countries are not alone in taking action against Israel’s continued expansion of settlements in the occupied West Bank.

"The Netherlands, Ireland, Belgium, Spain and Norway, which have either banned goods or are in the process of doing so, with many other countries, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Poland, Portugal and Sweden, [are] pledging today they will support further action."

U.K. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband arrives for a weekly government cabinet meeting at Downing Street on Tuesday in London, England. (Getty Images)

Miliband said the U.K. will also take action "against specific companies and individuals who provide services such as construction, infrastructure, financing or real estate for settlement expansion."

To another loud round of cheers, he said: "You will face the full force of U.K. sanctions."

Miliband said the U.K.'s action was coming now because Israel had crossed a "long-term red line," in reference to its recent announcement that it had opened tenders for construction of 1,200 settler homes in an area known as E1 in the occupied West Bank.

The United Nations and most countries deem the settlements illegal under Article 49 of the Fourth Geneva Convention pertaining to military occupations. Israel rejects this, viewing the area as disputed rather than occupied.

A drone view shows a factory belonging to Israeli company Libi Construction and Infrastructure in Shilo, an Israeli settlement in the occupied West Bank, on April 30. (Ammar Awad/Reuters)

It is nearly a year since Canada, the U.K. and France announced their governments would recognize the state of Palestine.

A sharp rise in reported violence in the occupied West Bank was another reason the U.K. had decided on sanctions, Miliband said.

"The British government," Miliband told parliamentarians, "agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, perpetrated by settler terrorists."

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar accused his British counterpart of "outrageous lies."

Sa'ar said Israel would undertake countermeasures, including expelling U.K. representatives from a joint military centre monitoring the Gaza ceasefire and ending U.K. training of the Palestinian Authority's security forces in the West Bank.

In addition, Israel will close Britain's consulate in East Jerusalem and prevent the entry into Israel of 12 elected U.K. officials, as well as other British citizens Sa'ar said were "involved in antisemitic and anti-Israel activity."

The British consulate in East Jerusalem is shown on Tuesday. Israel has ordered the closure of the consulate after London led Western sanctions over violence by Israeli settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. (Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty Images)

The seeds of change in the U.K.’s relationship with Israel were evident months ago.

In the days before Burnham became prime minister in July, he indicated a reset. He apologized for the governing Labour Party’s initial response to Israel’s military action in Gaza, saying the party "didn’t get it right" and under his leadership needs to "do better."

World.title: Separation making Alberta master of its destiny ‘a fiction,’ business leader says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

With fewer than 45 days to go until the Alberta referendum, few individual business leaders have spoken publicly on the prospect of separation from Canada.

But the leader of an Alberta business organization says that doesn’t mean they aren’t paying close attention.

“There is some hesitancy [to speak out],” Adam Legge, president of the Business Council of Alberta, told reporters Tuesday.

It’s likely that many Alberta companies have employees and customers who would support separation, Legge said.

But he added the majority of the group’s members have spoken “loud and clear” that they want him to speak in favour of remaining in Canada.

The organization’s membership includes more than 130 executives and presidents for top corporations across Alberta’s major sectors.

“They do recognize that if the referendum were to be positive in support of separation, that would create a massive amount of uncertainty,” Legge said.

On Tuesday, the council launched a new website , along with a series of videos and graphics, intended to make the case for Alberta to remain in Canada.

A significant number of members, particularly in the resource sector, have long been frustrated with federal policy, Legge said.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced the composition of her 'Alberta Next' panel at Heritage Park in Calgary last June. Adam Legge of the Business Council of Alberta watches at right. (Jason Markusoff/CBC)

While he said the status quo is not a path forward, sentiment has been changing in the wake of recent developments, like Alberta's proposed oil pipeline to the West Coast.

And factors that will determine if separation were to be positive or negative, like trade agreements, market access, currency and interest rates, are mostly outside Alberta’s control, Legge said.

“The notion that a separate Alberta would be a master of its own destiny is a fiction,” he said.

Legge sat on the provincial "Alberta Next" panel last summer, which held a series of in-person town halls across the province with the stated goal of devising ways to increase provincial autonomy.

The Business Council of Alberta said it isn’t registering as a third-party advertiser for the upcoming referendum, but will continue to produce content to post on its website and social media channels.

More groups expected to weigh in

The Business Council of Alberta isn’t the only major business organization to draw a line in the sand when it comes to separation.

In June, a report released by the Calgary Chamber of Commerce suggested separation could spur a business exodus and shrink the provincial economy by $62 billion a year.

Last week, the Canada West Foundation, a public policy think tank, said though Alberta’s grievances with Ottawa may be real, separation would be too costly and pose too many uncertainties.

Independence groups have suggested such projections assume “worst-case outcomes” and ignore Alberta’s leverage.

Keith Wilson, with the third-party advertiser Let Alberta Decide, sits behind a series of computer screens in his office. Wilson is also behind the Alberta Transition Council, which launched a ‘transition plan’ on Thursday. (Nathan Gross/CBC)

Last week, the pro-independence Alberta Transition Council, led by lawyer Keith Wilson, released a 214-page report laying out a “transition plan” should Alberta become its own country.

Wilson has said the nature of Alberta’s economy is immobile, meaning the province would be in a solid negotiating position in the event of a “yes” vote.

“They cannot relocate our natural resources, our expansive agricultural production, our oil and gas,” Wilson said last week. “We’re in a much stronger position, not only to negotiate with the rest of Canada, but also with the United States.”

World.title: Otto Jelinek, Canadian figure skating world champion and Olympian, dead at 86
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Otto Jelinek, a former world-champion figure skater and federal cabinet minister, has died at the age of 86.

"He was quite the ambitious guy," his younger brother Henry said Sunday, a day after Jelinek's death. "He was also sincerely and strongly a Canadian guy, who did everything he could to help this country."

Jelinek was born in Prague in 1940, and his family fled Czechoslovakia's communist government, arriving in Canada in 1952.

His father owned a successful cork factory in Prague and later rebuilt it in Oakville, Ont., a town between Toronto and Hamilton.

Jelinek and his sister Maria represented Canada in paired figure skating at the 1960 Winter Olympics in California.

In 1962, the pair won an emotional gold medal back in Prague, as champions of world figure skating. Henry said his siblings made the family proud by disproving the communist regime's propaganda of being the best system in the world.

The pair toured with the Ice Capades entertainment show while Jelinek became a sports commentator for CTV. He also started a company manufacturing hockey and figure skates.

In 1972, Jelinek entered federal politics, representing a Toronto riding before switching to the Oakville area. His 21 years in Parliament included a term as national revenue minister under then Prime Minister Brian Mulroney, as well as portfolios in sport and multiculturalism.

Jelinek described himself as politically right-of-centre, and he said he had been involved in backroom politics during the era of former Prime Minister John Diefenbaker.

WATCH | Jelinek tells athletes in 1987 to not expect much help from federal government: Otto Jelinek to Canadian athletes: The buck stops here | Duration 2:14 Otto Jelinek tells Harrington Telford and other Canadian athletes not to expect any government handouts.

Minister of amateur sport in 1984

As a young MP, buried deep in the Tory opposition benches during the 1970s, Jelinek baited Liberal Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau as a closet communist.

When the Tories swept to power in 1984, Jelinek became minister of amateur sport, later adding multiculturalism, public works, and supply and services to his resume.

In 1989 he became revenue minister, implementing and defending the GST while fighting an uphill battle against cross-border shopping.

Jelinek once remarked that he would make a poor diplomat because he speaks his mind too easily, such as in 1991 when he suggested the Tory government may have taxed Canadians too aggressively, earning him the wrath of some cabinet colleagues.

"I have a view on everything," he told Hill reporters in 1993, such as saying Canada's multiculturalism policy "has played its role" and should be shelved.

"I for one resent being referred to as a hyphenated Canadian. I believe we have to get rid of hyphenated Canadians," he told reporters in a scrum.

Jelinek also said it was unfair Ottawa spends so much on health care "just because every time a little kid has a runny nose the mother takes him to a doctor."

That year, Jelinek was shuffled out of cabinet and he said he would not seek election.

Jelinek announced his eventual retirement from politics to reporters, saying he had told his riding executive he would run for the party leadership only 24 hours prior.

"I was set to go until I ran into these guys -- my wife and my two boys, aged 10 and five years old. And suddenly life's reality hit home," Jelinek was quoted saying in a Canadian Press report, which noted his voice was cracking, with tears welling up in his eyes.

Refused to testify to Parliament

"It hit right where it counts, in the heart. Because these children have been growing up with a part-time father."

After politics, Jelinek took a job with a company that partnered with a firm that won the right to operate part of Pearson International Airport in Toronto, a move he said complied with conflict-of-interest rules.

The privatization of the airport was cancelled and became a major election issue. In 1994, Jelinek was among those who refused to testify to Parliament about the cancelled deal. The Bloc Quebecois at the time threatened to subpoena him and others.

Jelinek later moved to the Czech Republic and launched a consultancy in Prague, focused on helping Canadian and U.S. businesses get established in eastern Europe. He returned to Canada to retire.

In 2013, then-Prime Minister Stephen Harper appointed Jelinek as Canadian Ambassador to the Czech Republic. The role included overseeing the lifting of visa requirements for Czech nations, which had become a thorny issue that threatened to derail a free trade-agreement with the European Union.

Henry Jelinek said the family marveled that they went from fleeing communism to having Jelinek represent Canada as ambassador in the country of his birth.

Jelinek said his brother spent much of his retirement alongside Lake Ontario, where he loved gardening, golf, tennis, Frank Sinatra songs and parties.

"He loves to tell stories which he often exaggerates a little bit," Henry Jelinek said. "If somebody would need something, he would be there, always."

Jelinek died peacefully Saturday at the Trillium Health Centre in Mississauga, Ont., after living with Parkinson's disease for nearly 20 years, his brother said. "He took it with great heroism and dignity, to the very end."

World.title: Iceland summons U.S. ambassador over Trump's threat to take over Arctic nation
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump's latest map-making exercise has rattled the North Atlantic.

During a flurry of social media posts over the holiday long weekend, Trump posted a map coloured in the red, white and blue stars and stripes of the U.S. flag draped across all of North America — including Canada, Mexico, Greenland and Iceland, prompting Iceland to summon its ambassador.

The Truth Social post offered no explanation but recalled Trump's earlier talk of making Canada the 51st state and his repeated musings about taking over Greenland, Denmark's self-governing territory.

"It's disturbing and, in many ways, completely inappropriate," Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen told the national broadcaster DR on Tuesday. "It's obviously a sign that the U.S. president still harbours some kind of maximalist vision in his own mind. We need to rein that in."

Iceland's Foreign Secretary Thorgerdur Katrin Gunnarsdottir summoned U.S. Ambassador Billy Long to a meeting and said she made it clear that the post was unacceptable, national broadcaster RÚV said.

WATCH | Why the U.S. keeps threatening Canada: U.S. officials revive 51st state comments | Duration 4:18 U.S. Vice-President JD Vance was among the officials to refer to Canada as the 51st state following the collapse of trade talks, but some Republicans tried to distance themselves from the tariff brawl ahead of midterm elections.

Arctic on edge

The Arctic region has been on edge since Trump ramped up his rhetoric at the start of the year about U.S. control of Greenland.

His post came Monday as the European Union sought to reassure Greenland with the promise of a stronger partnership and hundreds of millions of euros in investment following Trump's repeated threats.

Iceland — just 290 kilometres away — became alarmed when Trump mistakenly named their country four times while speaking about his designs on Greenland.

Iceland is a NATO member, but the gaffe led its left-leaning coalition government to move up a referendum, originally planned for next year, on whether the country should resume long-stalled negotiations to become a member of the EU.

Voters rejected the measure Aug. 30 that was promoted, in part, as an effort to strengthen ties with Europe to better insulate the country from geopolitical instability.

Thousands of Icelanders also signed a petition urging the prime minister to reject Long as ambassador after he made a crack earlier this year about Iceland becoming the 52nd U.S. state and making him governor. Long apologized and took up his post in Reykjavik last month.

Canadians react to Trump's threats

Trump has riled up Canada with frequent talk of it becoming a U.S. state, launching the ongoing trade war between the two countries and recently renaming Lake Ontario as "Lake America."

More than 225,000 Canadians have signed a petition calling on the government to expel the U.S. Ambassador to Canada, Pete Hoekstra, over the threats.

Canada's former ambassador to the UN Bob Rae says it wouldn't do much good, as Hoekstra is "a direct affiliate of the Trump enterprise."

"Look, we know what we're up against," he said in an interview with CBC's Andrew Nichols. "Yes, Trump has ambitions that go way beyond trade."

He says the administration's threats make it difficult to get the U.S. to refocus on the trade agreement.

"It is a sign of the profound disrespect in this administration for the Canadian people, for the Canadian government, and for our future as a country," Rae said. "We are dealing with people who don't believe we should exist."

Over the Labour Day weekend, the global map was not the only thing on Trump's mind, as he also suggested renaming the state of New Mexico "New America."

World.title: Prince George starts Eton College as Harry and Meghan grapple with 'brutal put-down'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It was a day of ups and downs for the Royal Family as, on the one hand, Prince George started his first day at prestigious Eton College and, on the other, Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, grappled with their status as non-working members of the Royal Family.

The Prince and Princess of Wales were all smiles as Prince George started his first day at the 600-year-old school Tuesday morning, following in his father's footsteps. The trio appeared relaxed as they dropped off George, King Charles's 13-year-old grandson and second in line to the throne.

"Welcome, good luck and enjoy," said headteacher Simon Henderson, shaking hands with George before ushering everyone inside to the school where George will be boarding.

Later, George was photographed grinning in his new school uniform: a black tailcoat, waistcoat and a white collar.

Prince George begins his first day at Eton College in Windsor, Berkshire, in this photo taken Tuesday and provided by Kensington Palace. (Matt Porteous/Kensington Palace)

Eton is the alma mater for many of ​the ⁠country's elite, including Prince William and Prince Harry, and has educated 20 British prime ministers, including Boris Johnson and David Cameron, as well as actors Hugh Laurie, Damian ⁠Lewis ​and Tom Hiddleston.

As BBC reports, George's time at Eton will likely see him somewhat shielded from media and public attention. Prince William has previously spoken about much he enjoyed being "just another student" at the school.

The late Diana, Princess of Wales, left, Eton housemaster Dr. Andrew Gailey, Prince Harry, Prince William and Prince Charles are pictured on Prince William's first day at Eton College on Sept. 6, 1995. (Princess Diana Archive/Hulton Archive/Getty Images)

Harry and Meghan 'surprised' by letter

On the other hand, Prince Harry and his wife, Meghan, experienced what some observers are calling a rude awakening back in the U.K. after Charles confirmed Monday they will remain non-working royals.

The news, which came in the form of a letter from Buckingham Palace sent to senior British officials, said that after ​Harry and Meghan stepped down from official royal duties in 2020, they "are no longer working members ​of the Royal Family."

"In short, their position is akin to ​private citizens with commercial and charitable interests," the letter stated.

On Tuesday, T he Associated Press reported that the Duke and Duchess of Sussex were surprised by the way Buckingham Palace released the letter. It caught the couple off guard when it was released to the media on Monday in part because they were given little time to review or comment on its contents, a person familiar with the discussions told AP.

They were "a little surprised not to have been told about this in advance," their representative said in a statement on Tuesday, as reported by BBC.

The couple’s representatives received a copy of the letter just one hour and 12 minutes before it was released to news outlets, the person said. That left them with little time to respond because they were unable to reach Harry, who was in a meeting, until just two minutes before the letter was released, the person added.

The letter reiterates the palace's previous stance.

Harry and Meghan stepped back from royal duties in 2020 when they moved to North America to make their own living, turning to ventures such as deals with Netflix and Spotify. At the time, Queen Elizabeth made clear that the couple could not be part-time royals. Charles reiterated that position after he became King in 2022.

WATCH | Harry and Meghan move back to the U.K.: Harry and Meghan moving back to the U.K. | Duration 2:06 Prince Harry and his wife Meghan are moving back to the United Kingdom with their children, Buckingham Palace has confirmed. The couple will remain non-working royals and live as private citizens.

'Warning shot'

In an interview with GB News, royal historian Alexander Larman called Charles' move a "brutal put-down."

"I would call it a right royal knees-up, actually, because Harry's just been back a couple of weeks now and we're seeing how it's all going for him," Larman said.

"This is basically the King saying: 'You're back, I'm delighted on a paternal level that you're back. But, as head of a firm, I'm making it very, very clear that you are not back in the Royal Family."

As CBC's The Royal Fascinator reported over the weekend, Harry and Meghan's return to the U.K. set off shockwaves because it seems so counterintuitive and contradictory to everything that they have said since they left.

Prince Harry, right, and Meghan walk along the boardwalk during a visit to Bondi Beach, Australia, on April 17. (Jonathan Brady/The Associated Press)

Royal expert Phil Dampier told The Sun the King's statement was a "warning shot" not to overshadow the Royal Family.

"It’s really sending out a message — a warning shot across their bows, you could say. What they’re [the palace] emphasizing is that nothing has changed as far as they’re concerned," Dampier said.

"Now that they’ve come back and might start turning up to various charity events or doing commercial activities, it’s got to be absolutely clear to everyone that they are doing it as private individuals and not as royals.”

On Monday, Meghan posted a photo on her As Ever Instagram account, in which she relaxes on a lawn with the couple's black lab, Pula. "Long weekend plans," notes the caption.

World.title: Survivors of an apartheid-era massacre are suing South Africa's government
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | Interview with Sharpeville resident Vincent Thamae: As It Happens 7:30 Survivors of apartheid-era massacre sue South Africa's government

Vincent Thamae remembers his grandfather telling stories about the Sharpeville massacre.

On March 21, 1960, South Africa's apartheid police opened fire on unarmed protesters in a township south of Johannesburg, killing dozens of men, women and children.

"My grandpa told me that those people who did that were not humans," Thamae, a Sharpeville resident, told As It Happens host Nil Köksal. "It's only when I grew up that I began to understand what he meant."

Thamae has been collecting testimonies from survivors and victims' families since 2018 for the organization Voices of Sharpeville . Now, he's a liaison between those survivors and a team of lawyers helping them launch a class-action lawsuit against the government.

The suit seeks compensation for victims and their descendants and calls on the government to strike down an apartheid-era law that shields South African officials from liability related to the massacre.

'Not possible to forget'

Thousands of people in Sharpeville were protesting apartheid pass laws, which restricted people's movement and enforced racial segregation, when police opened fire.

Police records from the time say 69 people were killed and 180 injured, while research cited by the plaintiffs puts the count at 91 dead and more than 238 wounded.

Abram Mofokeng, 87, was 20 when he was shot in the foot and back as he fled the gunfire. A bullet remains lodged in his back.

"It is not possible to forget what happened in 1960," Mofokeng said. "I cannot go a day without thinking about how we have been affected."

Abram Mofokeng, 87, one of the survivors of the Sharpeville Massacre, poses for a photograph at the memorial site for the victims in Sharpeville, on Sept. 3, 2026. (Phil Magakoe/AFP/Getty Images)

Mofokeng is one of three Sharpeville residents acting as representative plaintiffs for a wider group in the case brought by Lawyers for Human Rights.

The others, Paulina Mathinye and Ishmael Poho, both lost their fathers in the massacre when they were young children.

More than 70 survivors and relatives have expressed support for or interest in joining the litigation.

The government did not respond to requests for comment.

Why now?

Those impacted have long been seeking compensation. In the aftermath of the massacre, around 258 claims were filed. But in 1961, the government enacted the Indemnity Act, shielding officials from legal liability and extinguishing the claims.

Apartheid officially ended in South Africa in 1994. But that shielding law remains in effect today.

Lawyers for the Sharpeville plaintiffs are calling for it to be struck down, arguing it violates their clients' constitutional right of access to the courts.

They also said the case seeks to address gaps left by the Truth and Reconciliation Commission process, under which only 51 Sharpeville survivors were formally awarded reparations.

Dan Leader, a partner at British human rights law firm Leigh Day, which is supporting the plaintiffs, called the case part of South Africa's "unfinished business."

"This is a time of reckoning for modern South Africa," Leader said.

Performers stand after re-enacting the 1960 Sharpeville Massacre at the memorial site for the victims in Sharpeville on Thursday. (Phil Magakoe/AFP/Getty Images)

If they succeed in overturning the Indemnity Act, the plaintiffs' claims for damages can proceed. The lawyers did not give a total figure for the claim but said it would vary for each claimant and would be worked out with the help of experts.

Thamae, a member of the Pan Africanist Congress political party, is hopeful that reparations could go beyond money and include more long-term benefits, like guaranteed access to education for the plaintiffs' children.

Many Sharpeville residents from that era, he says, were dispossessed of their lands by South Africa's apartheid government, the impact of which has reverberated through generations.

"They could not be part of the economy of the country," he said.

Thamae says collecting stories from survivors and victims' descendants has been slow and painful work that reopens old wounds that never fully healed.

"We still don't ... understand how other human beings can do the act that the government did to the people. We still haven't come to terms with what has happened."

World.title: 'That’s not storytelling': Olympians hope proposed guidelines eliminate sexualization on broadcasts
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When Kate Van Buskirk made her Olympic debut at Tokyo 2021, she clocked her second fastest time in the women’s 5,000 metres in a sweltering 41 C.

It was a massive feat, and afterward, she collapsed onto the track to soak it all in.

Five years later, Van Buskirk recalls the moment to be the most “egregious” time she was captured on camera, with photos posted online of her “sprawled out” on the track from extremely invasive angles .

“I've just finished the biggest race of my life … I just remember looking at those and thinking, ‘these live on the Internet forever,’” Van Buskirk said, adding that there were other photos of the moment that didn’t show her inappropriately.

Instances like this aren’t rare in women’s sports.

A report from The Representation Project from the Tokyo 2021 Olympics found that women were sexualized nearly 10 times more than male athletes at the Games, despite Olympic broadcasters encouraging "sport appeal, not sex appeal" to camera operators ahead of the competition.

“It should be about performance, not appearance,” said Van Buskirk, who has since retired and works as a track and field analyst. “Even if it's passive and unintentional, there should be thought put around how we position photographers so that we're not giving them just that one angle.”

For decades, women’s sports uniforms have been a point of conversation regarding coverage and fit, such as the controversy ahead of Paris 2024 when Nike unveiled its new Team USA track and field kit for women as a high-cut bodysuit.

Van Buskirk refers to her track uniform as her “equipment,” opting for bottoms called “bunners.”

“I want to wear as little fabric as possible while still feeling like I have the dignity to do what I'm doing and be taken seriously as an athlete, but also not have to be distracted by that and worry about am I literally covering my private areas,” she added.

WATCH | More athletes speaking out about invasive camera angles : When does a sports replay go from storytelling to sexualization? | Duration 1:30 More athletes are speaking out about invasive camera angles at women's athletics competitions.

Europe pushing for change from broadcasters

In July 2026 the European Broadcasting Union and European Athletics created new guidelines to improve coverage in women’s athletics, calling out problematic broadcasting habits that “add zero narrative value.”

Lingering close-ups on specific body parts, low-angle camera placements, and excessive slow-motion replays with no storytelling purpose are the main “culprits” the report, Raising The Bar, cited.

“The way people consume sport today can amplify that impact. A single frame from a live

broadcast can be clipped, zoomed in and shared around the world within minutes,” Elissavet Arapi, women's sport lead for the European Broadcasting Union, said.

“Those images can then attract sexualized comments and abusive behaviour online, and athletes have told us they are increasingly concerned about that.”

Above is a photo created by the European Broadcasting Union and European Athletics to show the encouraged standard camera angles in the broadcasting of women’s athletics. (European Broadcasting Union)

Van Buskirk shared that some of her peers in athletics have found highly sexualized photos taken of them in competition on “soft core porn” sites.

“I have seen, again, many replays over the years of myself and others where there's no commentary over top of it … It’s a slow motion pan up, usually starting around the calves and coming up really slowly,” she said.

Arapi says that navigating editorial decisions like this is a collaborative effort amongst directors, video operators, and camera operators who need to “react quickly if their shot gives us a sexualized image.”

Michele Donnelly, associate professor of Sports Management at Brock University, is quick to call out the limitations of the guidelines.

“Why can't it be a policy? The entire document makes the case for why this is necessary. It should rise to the level of something that is a requirement, not simply a guideline,” Donnelly said. “The IOC (International Olympic Committee) needs to be the first one to demonstrate this is how you do it and to hold themselves accountable.”

As Canada’s official broadcaster of the Olympic Games, Paul McDougall, CBC Sports’ head of production and content, said the organization’s priority is always athletic excellence above all else.

"Broadcasters don’t just owe women athletes a spot on the screen; they owe them a broadcast that honours their power, skill and dignity. Visibility inspires participation. By adopting respectful production guidelines, we move beyond representation and commit to a landscape where athletic excellence is always the primary lens." McDougall said.

The Olympic Broadcasting Services (OBS), the permanent host of all Olympic and Paralympic Games, said they also have guidelines in place to ensure respectful coverage of athletes.

“Respectful and appropriate portrayal of all athletes in all sports is an integral part of OBS’ Olympic Games coverage. This is reflected in the OBS guidelines for venue production teams and is also taken into account through our production quality control processes when supervising OBS coverage,” the OBS shared in a statement to CBC Sports.

Germany's Gina Lückenkemper, right, calls the upward facing cameras intrusive and uncomfortable while wearing her competition attire. (Petr David Josek/The Associated Press)

Education versus information

Back in 2019, the World Athletics Organization introduced two miniature cameras inside the starting blocks for sprint and hurdle events at the world championships in Doha.

While the goal was to provide “trailblazing” angles capturing the runner's explosion off the starting blocks, several sprinters heavily criticized the camera placement. Most notably German athletes Gina Lückenkemper and Tatjana Pinto, who said the upward facing cameras were intrusive and uncomfortable while wearing their competition attire.

“When your body is exposed…there's a presumption of access and ownership and being able to use images of women's bodies for whatever purposes people want to use them for. But also, that translates to in real life interactions with athletes and expectations of them,” Donnelly said.

In response to the push back, the International Association of Athletics Federations (IAAF) agreed to only show shots from the block cameras right at the starting pistol and to delete video data at other times each day.

“We have noted some specific feedback about the block cameras and we have confirmed we have appropriate measures in place to protect athlete privacy during the process of selecting images for broadcast,” the IAAF wrote in a statement. “We also have strict editorial guidelines for what is broadcast and these have been observed since the beginning of the championships.”

While sexualization isn’t limited to women athletes, men in sport often celebrate when their bodies are captured on camera, rather than being at risk of threat, says Donnelly.

“Without diminishing the negative effects that there may be for many athletes, often when men's bodies are being sexualized in a celebratory way. Like, think of the poor high jumper [Anthony Ammirati] right, from Paris 2024 where it was all about his manhood and his masculinity.”

On Friday, the world's top track stars will compete at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest where heated rivalries and new stars will emerge in the leadup to LA 2028.

With all eyes on athletics as one of the most watched sports at the Summer Olympics, establishing broadcasting expectations may be more important than ever.

“There's a difference between informing and educating, versus entertaining. And I think as soon as we slip into entertainment, as the thing that we're focusing on, that's when it can really quickly devolve into hyper sexualization,” Van Buskirk said.

“That's not storytelling, that's objectification,” Van Buskirk said.

World.title: Liberal Party joins Colombia’s far-right to form majority coalition
World.content:
The Liberal Party announced that it had joined the congressional coalition of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella.

The party, which also supported De la Espriella’s presidential bid, said that it would join the coalition after “extensive deliberation and arduous debate among representatives, senators, and leadership” of Colombia’s oldest political party.

It is worth noting that the discussions between representatives and senators over the past several weeks have revealed disagreements among some members of our caucuses with the current administration, but they also acknowledge President Espriella’s ability to work toward stimulating economic growth, building a talent pool to provide real opportunities for Colombians, and restoring security and respect for institutions. Liberal Party

The liberals’ decision gives the government broad support in Congress and marginalizes the opposition led by the leftist Historic Pact Party.

In the senate, De la Espriella’s right-wing coalition can count on the support of 63 of 103 lawmakers. In the House of Representatives, the coalition consists of 123 of 183 lawmakers.

The Historic Pact, which won the elections and became the biggest party in Congress, was abandoned by the left-liberal Green Alliance party and can count of the support of 28 senators and 44 representatives.

The opposition party has been able to make temporary anti-government alliances with, for example, the far-right Democratic Center party of former President Alvaro Uribe.

World.title: Colombia’s president appoints controversial new spy chief
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella appointed retired army General Jorge Andres Zuluaga as director of the National Intelligence Directorate (DNI) despite pending criminal investigations.

Zuluaga, who spent 30 years with military intelligence, is best known for his participation in Operation Jaque, which liberated former presidential candidate Ingrid Betancourt, three American military contractors and 11 soldiers.

Throughout his career, the 61-year-old former general was deputy commander of the now-defunct Charry Solano intelligence school, commander of the Regional Intelligence #5 and the director of the National Army’s Technical Intelligence Center (CITEC).

Zuluaga received training in the United States and was a diplomatic aide at the Organization of American States.

He was removed as CITEC director in 2014 after prosecution investigators found out that he received intelligence illegally obtained from “Andromeda,” a clandestine intelligence unit that operated from a Bogota internet café.

In October 2024, war crimes tribunal JEP ordered the Prosecutor General’s Office to investigate Zuluaga for his alleged participation in the extermination of the leftist Patriotic Union party when he was the CITEC’s director between 2004 and 2005.

The prosecution has yet to decide whether or not to formally charge the retired general with the crimes he allegedly committed.

Zuluaga, who became a member of the far-right Democratic Center party after he was ejected from the army, has always sustained that he acted within the boundaries of the law.

World.title: Colombia’s government clashes with human rights office over De la Espriella walking among corpses
World.content:
Colombia’s chief ombudsman, Iris Marin, clashed with the national government after she criticized President Abelardo de la Espriella for walking among the corpses of people killed by the military.

In a public statement, Marin reiterated that “in recent days, we saw the president of the Republic walking among the bodies—in white body bags—of people who were killed during Operation “Azarías” in Guaviare.”

“I don’t recall ever seeing a president walking among the dead and taking pride in those deaths,” said the ombudsman, whose office is independent from the government.

The state and the government cannot allow themselves to be drawn into a competition to see who can be the cruelest. They cannot compete with armed groups over who instills the most fear, who humiliates the adversary the most, or who turns death into a display of power. Ombudsman Iris Marin

According to Marin, the military has the right to kill citizens, but must do so with respect for the Constitution and International Humanitarian Law, and is responsible for “the way that the State exercizes power and communicates its results.”

In a response, Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara said that the Ombudman falsely equated the State with “narcoterrorist groups as if it wer competing with them in cruelty.”

“Such an equivalence is inappropriate,” said Lara and called on the Ombudsman’s Office to be “an ally of the victims and of our mission to protect them and to liberate them from the terror regime of crime.”

Marin told Lara that she trusted that “the President and the Government will reflect on the way they communicate operational results, as I requested in my statement.”

De la Espriella’s stroll through the 23 body bags, including those of two minors, was also fiercely criticized in independent and foreign media.

World.title: Judge orders Colombia’s military to suspend air strikes on illegal armed groups
World.content:
A court ordered the government and the military to suspend air strikes on suspected members of illegal armed groups while studying the risk of harm to child forced recruitment victims.

In a preliminary sentence, the Bogota family court in response to a lawsuit that was filed by a civilian who claimed the State ignored its obligation to protect children when carrying out air strikes on illegal armed groups.

TO ORDER the PRESIDENCY OF THE REPUBLIC, the MINISTRY OF NATIONAL DEFENSE, the GENERAL COMMAND OF THE MILITARY FORCES, the NATIONAL ARMY, the COLOMBIAN AEROSPACE FORCE, and the NATIONAL NAVY, through the appropriate channels and within the scope of their respective authorities, that, pending a decision on the merits in this constitutional protection action, they refrain from conducting offensive air operations against targets regarding which there is certain, objective, or reasonably verifiable information regarding the presence of children or adolescents recruited or used by armed groups, until the necessary precautionary and protective measures have been adopted and verified, and it has been determined, based on the available information and applicable operational protocols, that there is no less harmful operational alternative that would allow the legitimate military objective being pursued to be achieved Bogota family court

According to Radio Caracol, at least 107 minors were killed in air strikes on illegal armed groups since they were resumed by former President Ivan Duque in 2018.

The sentence comes a day after President Abelardo de la Espriella announced the military killed 23 “narcoterrorists” in the deadliest air strike during the peace process that started in 2016.

The president vowed to resume bombing campaigns that were all but suspended by former President Gustavo Petro as he sought peace and demobilization talks with multiple illegal armed groups, a strategy rejected by the new far-right government.

Following the killing of at least three children in an air strike carried out in August, Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora blamed guerrilla organizations for the deaths, claiming they were recruiting children for human shields and combatants.

World.title: Colombia’s education minister resigns after less than a month
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella replaced his education minister after she resigned, claiming “an unexpected family situation.”

De la Espriella announced on social media platform X that he had accepted the resignation of the evangelical Education Minister Viviane Morales, who took office on August 7, the first day of the administration.

I bid a nostalgic farewell to my dear friend Viviane Morales. God’s designs are inscrutable, and she must leave us early to take charge of a personal situation that I sincerely hope she can resolve very soon. President Viviana Morales

In the same post, De la Espriella said he had appointed Ilva Myriam Hoyos, stressing that “I am confident that she will be an outstanding minister and that she will serve Colombia with dedication, character, and conviction.”

While in office, Morales lead the government’s Culture War in education and vowed to remove “gender ideology” from Colombia’s classrooms, and proposed a law that would allow churches to provide public education services.

Hoyos, a catholic, warned in 2016 that a peace deal between the government of President Juan Manuel Santos and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC promoted gender ideology.

The new education minister used to work with Alejandro Ordoñez, Colombia’s notoriously far-right former Inspector General and the country’s current ambassador to the Organization of American States.

World.title: De la Espriella claims Colombia’s military killed 23, arrested 6 EMC guerrillas
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella claimed Wednesday that Colombia’s armed forces killed at least 23 members of FARC dissident group EMC and captured another six.

In a video, De la Espriella said that “Operation Azarias,” targeted the EMC’s Carolina Ramirez Front and killed one of its commanders, a man called “Tigre” or “Pintado,” in the south of the Guaviare province.

A second guerrilla commander, “Victor,” was among the six alleged EMC members who were arrested during the operation, which included air strikes.

The president claimed that Victor carried out attacks against the military “during the elections, as part of the ‘gunpoint vote’ strategy launched by the previous regime to skew the popular verdict.”

That narcoterrorist, whom we have now taken out of circulation, carried out attacks against members of the National Army and the Navy. During the elections, as part of the “gunpoint vote” strategy launched by the previous regime to skew the popular verdict, this criminal ambushed a unit that was on the move precisely to protect citizens’ right to vote freely. President Abelardo de la Espriella

There is no evidence to suggest that De la Espriella’s predecessor, former President Gustavo Petro, employed illegal armed groups to coerce voters into voting against his would-be successor.

One minor allegedly survived the attack and was surrendered to family welfare agency ICBF. The Medical Examiner’s Office is expected to investigate how many minors were among the alleged “narcoterrorists.”

At least three minors were killed in a previous operation in Guaviare that killed at least nine alleged members of the EMC’s main rival, FARC dissident group EMBF, the Medical Examiner’s Office said earlier this week.

Air strikes against illegal armed groups are controversial as they could imply the blanket killing of victims of child recruitment, a war crime according to international humanitarian law.

The government has long insisted that those recruiting children and minors are responsible for the deaths of their victims.

World.title: 1 killed, 15 injured in northeast Colombia car bomb attack on police station
World.content:
At least one person was killed and another 15 injured in a car bomb attack on a police station on the outskirts of Cucuta, the capital of Norte de Santander.

According to the National Police, the bomb exploded on Monday evening outside of the police station in Los Patios, a municipality that is part of Cucuta’s metropolitan area.

Apart from the casualties, the blast also damaged buildings and vehicles that were parked near the police station, police told local media.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said on social media platform X that he had convened a security council meeting “with the entire top brass of the security forces.”

“Wherever the terrorists try to sow fear, that is where the State will be with all is might,” said De la Espriella.

We will pursue with an iron fist those who threaten Colombians, until we capture them, dismantle their networks, and restore peace to our communities. Abelardo de la Espriella

In the region around Cucuta, guerrilla organizations ELN and EMBF have been fighting each other. Organized crime groups operate mainly inside the urban area of the capital of the Norte de Santander province.

No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack.

World.title: Evacuations ordered in Chile as wildfires run amok
World.content:
Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred) Wednesday ordered the evacuation of 14 communes in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, including Nacimiento, Purén, and Contulmo, which have all been particularly affected by the forest fires.

In messages broadcast through the Emergency Alert System (SAE), the authorities also called on residents to leave their homes to avoid further damage to their health.

It has already been a week since the first wildfires ran amok in south-central Chile despite efforts to contain them. High temperatures, dryness, and strong winds add to the plight of local people and some 5,600 firefighters deployed in the area while helping flocks in from abroad.

”We are entering this part of the week which is the most complex. Today, tomorrow, and the day after we have an alert for high temperatures in several regions of the country that has mobilized a very large effort (…) to prevent the fires from spreading,“ Interior Minister Carolina Tohá said regarding the 311 active fires, of which 89 are being fought. The Senapred also said 180 fires were under control, and 309,747 hectares have been affected.

”If the temperature rises and the wind increases we can indeed have more problems, and we already have many fires,” Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Carlos Javier Martín Traverso told AFP. Traverso’s Air Operations Section of the Military Emergency Unit (UME) arrived in Chile on Sunday to join the firefighting efforts.

Over 309,000 hectares have been consumed in the regions of Maule, Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía with the death toll standing at 24, plus 2,180 people injured as 1,180 houses were destroyed, leaving 5,560 people homeless.

There seems to be a seamless scientific consensus that fires are the result of human actions, either by intentionality or carelessness, although the drought that has hit Chile for 13 years adds to the aggressiveness of the fires.

In this scenario, President Gabriel Boric Font has announced a curfew in the areas of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía where a state of catastrophe is in force, in order to guarantee the security and tranquility of

the families affected by the crisis. Defense authorities working on the sites will determine the restriction’s schedule.

“We have 24 people dead nationwide, three are from Santa Juana and we do not want there to be even one more,” Boric told reporters after visiting the area.

The number of fatalities was updated to 24 after two bodies were determined to belong to people who had died before the fires broke out.

Meanwhile, Biobío Governor Rodrigo Díaz said he was certain about “people criminally setting fires.”

“I have reports from police, firefighters, of people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols,” he insisted in a radio interview.

“We have fire outbreaks at the southern exit of Contulmo, different places where fires were set 300 meters away from each other, I could see it, nobody told me about it. The mayor of Mulchén told me how fires were lit in the four cardinal points, I have reports from the police, the Fire Department, from people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols in the area,” he explained.

President Boric’s Regional Delegate Daniela Dresdner said eight people had been arrested for “irresponsible and suspicious attitudes with respect to the setting of fires. This was due to citizen complaints and patrols by the Navy.”

“We are asking that all these conducts be denounced and we are filing a lawsuit for all these denunciations to [be] prosecute[d],” she added.

The Biobío Regional Prosecutor’s Office called on the citizenry to e-mail all data regarding criminal behavior to fiscaliaincendios@gmail.com, including pictures, videos, audios, or written information as to the probable causes of the fires, which will be handled confidentially. (Merco Press)

World.title: Chile’s wildfires death toll reaches 24
World.content:
Chilean authorities spoke Sunday of 24 fatalities, nearly 1,000 people injured, and some 800 houses destroyed in the past five days by wildfires spreading fast in amid a highly-irregular heat wave with strong winds and temperatures above 40°C in areas 500 km south of Santiago.

The death toll reached 24 after the death of one of the injured people who had been hospitalized in Angol, Undersecretary of the Interior Manuel Monsalve explained. “The risk situation in the country remains” in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, and in certain localities of the central region of Maule, he said. A red alert was also decreed Sunday in communes of the southern regions of Los Ríos and Los Lagos due to the appearance of new fire outbreaks. He also pointed out that 26 of the 997 people injured were in serious condition.

“I came home from work and I was already without anything, without a house. I was left on the street, with my arms crossed, now with my son, and my wife, in a tent. I have no fodder for my animals,” a resident of the town of Purén, in the Araucanía region, told Televisión Nacional de Chile (TVN).

Meanwhile, President Gabriel Boric Font attended the wake of a firefighter in the town of Coronel. ”Chile is crying with you. I am here to tell you that you are not alone, that the family of Yesenia (Muñoz, the deceased firefighter) will not be alone,” he said.

According to Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred), the number of fires being fought went down from 87 to 51. “We are experiencing a small window of improving weather conditions during Sunday and Monday. That means that we are not with extremely high temperatures,” Monsalve said.

Undersecretary Monsalve also told reporters that 10 people have been arrested for their responsibility in starting some of the fires for which the red alert was still maintained. Of the total number of fires, 22 occurred Sunday for a total of 283 active fires, of which 151 were under control and 71 are being fought.

Given the magnitude of the fires in size and number, international help has been summoned. “We have just sent a plane to Chile with a contingent of the Military Emergency Unit to collaborate in extinguishing and controlling the fires that are raging in the country. All our support to the Chilean people,” tweeted Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

Chile’s Foreign Ministry also said assistance was being coordinated with Argentina, Brazil, Ecuador, the United States, and Mexico, while Boric’s administration has declared a constitutional state of catastrophe in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío and La Araucanía, to speed up additional resources while restricting free transit and involving military forces to contain the disaster.

In 2017, another chain of fires destroyed some 460,000 hectares, left 11 people dead, nearly 6,000 injured, and more than 1,500 homes burned.

Monsalve also warned that this week high temperatures will continue, as well as the risk of low humidity and strong gusts of wind, which will make it difficult to extinguish the flames. – MercoPress

World.title: Parts of Chile under red alert for major forest fires in central region
World.content:
The Government of Chile has declared a “red alert” in the central part of the country due to the heat wave stemming from 39 major forest fires as the wave keeps spreading throughout the country, most of them in Araucania (17) but also in Bío Bío (7), Ñuble (7), Maule (4), Los Lagos (3), and one in the Santiago Metropolitan Region.

The National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response reported that in addition to the 39 fires currently being fought, there were four others under observation, while 141 were already under control, and 20 had already been extinguished.

Authorities ordered a series of preventive evacuations in several towns, as well as the interruption of highway traffic in the most affected areas where 181 hectares of scrubland and pastureland were burned out, threatening nearby homes.

The main cause for the fires is said to be the summer high temperatures which reached 41 degrees Celsius in the Chillán area.

Meteorologists forecast that the heat wave will last until Sunday. The last major fires to affect Chile were recorded in the summer of 2017 when the flames swept through entire villages, causing 11 deaths and more than 580 thousand hectares affected.

The state-owned National Forestry Corporation (Conaf) reported that in the Ñuble region, the fire has already affected some 550 hectares in the area of Chillán Viejo and another 200 hectares in another town near the regional capital, burning infrastructure and some houses.

Agriculture Minister Esteban Valenzuela told reporters that in addition to the heat wave, the dry and hot Puelche wind from the eastern cordillera was also expected in the central-southern zone. Valenzuela also announced the temporary closure of seven national parks from Santiago to the south in the Metropolitan, Ñuble, Biobío, La Araucanía, and Aysén regions to prevent new fires, and also ordered the evacuation of rural areas of Ñuble, where simultaneous forest fires were reported.

– MercoPress

World.title: Chilean airlines will reimburse cost of boarding taxes under certain conditions
World.content:
Chile’s national Consumer Service, Sernac is calling all consumers who purchased tickets directly from airlines between 2015 and 201l and did not make use of them, to claim from the companies the reimbursement of the boarding taxes paid.

Following on a Voluntary Collective Procedure reached at the beginning of 2020 with LATAM, and at the end of 2021 with Sky, Avianca, Jetsmart, Aerolineas Argentinas and COPA, the airlines agreed to reimburse the boarding taxes cost for flights not done between May first 2015 and 24 December 2021, with the exception of Jetsmart, which only started operations in Chile in July 2017.

Accordingly the universe of beneficiaries reached 1.108.416 passengers and involved some US$ 12 million for domestic flights and US$ 1,4 million for international flights. The amount to be reimbursed to each potential passenger depends on the distance to travel and if it was domestic of international travel.

In Chile the domestic boarding tax is equivalent to some US$ 14 and overseas US$ 50. Allegedly following the agreement the companies were to inform the beneficiaries of their reimbursements.

Reimbursements can also be checked by filling forms at the airlines’ offices. For further information on the agreement and the sums involved consumers are invited to check the web.

World.title: Remembering Steve Anderson
World.content:
BENJAMIN WITTE

I was neither the first nor the last of the many interns and editors who peopled the office of the Santiago Times during the quarter century founder Steve Anderson captained the ship. But for whatever reason, I stuck around longer than most, and it was with great sadness that I learned yesterday about the automobile accident that ended his life.
