If you live in Chile and follow K-pop, this is the biggest booking the country has taken in years. It is also the one that nearly did not happen.

Three Nights, Not Two

The promoter DG Medios and Ticketmaster Chile both list three dates: October 14, 16 and 17. The venue is the Estadio Nacional Julio Martínez Prádanos in the Ñuñoa district of Santiago.

The October 14 show was added in April, after the first two sold quickly. Listings that still show two nights are out of date.

The promoter writes the tour as BTS World Tour “ARIRANG” in Santiago. Live Nation Latin America bills the same run as “ARIRANG” in Latin America.

Santiago sits in the middle of a South American leg. Reported stops also include Bogotá, Lima, La Plata and São Paulo, though we could only verify the Chilean dates from primary sources.

The Month Chile Nearly Lost the Shows

In early July the Instituto Nacional del Deporte, the state sports agency that controls the stadium, refused permission. Its concern was the damage a 360-degree stage would do to the pitch.

By then roughly 200,000 tickets had been sold. Fans had bought seats for a venue that had no authorisation.

The government reversed course on July 21 and cleared the shows with conditions attached. The stage had to be redesigned, and cranes had to work from the athletics track rather than the grass.

The conditions also required ventilated protection over the turf and engineering studies on how long it would take to recover. This is why the production looks different from other stops on the tour.

None of that is settled trivia. It explains why Chilean coverage of these concerts has been unusually tense.

What a Ticket Costs

Ticketmaster Chile is the only authorised online seller, with DG Medios as promoter. Published prices already include the service charge.

The cheapest tier, Pacífico Lateral Sur, is 99,875 pesos (about US$107). Cancha Andes and Cancha Pacífico, the two floor sections, are 293,750 pesos (about US$315) each.

Pacífico Medio is the most expensive standard tier at 528,750 pesos (about US$566). Above that sits a soundcheck package at 676,020 pesos (about US$724).

That package bundles a Cancha Pacífico ticket with soundcheck access, a gift and priority entry. It is the only tier that includes anything beyond the show.

Conversions use 933.82 pesos to the US dollar, the Banco Central de Chile observed rate for September 8, 2026.

We could not confirm which nights are still on sale. Ticketmaster Chile blocks automated checks, and the last availability reports are from April and contradict each other.

Chile’s Nominative Ticket Rules

Every ticket carries a named holder. Ticketmaster states that all of them are nominative, without exception.

Names are assigned through the Quentro app. One change of name is allowed, and it must happen within thirty days of the show.

Entry requires the ticket and the holder’s identity card or passport, and the two must match. Bring the physical document, not a photograph of it.

The purchase limit is four tickets per person per date. Children under six are not admitted at all.

Anyone between six and sixteen needs an accompanying adult, and one adult may bring at most three minors.

This regime makes casual resale close to useless, which is the point. Sites such as entradasbts.com and btschile.com are not authorised, whatever their names suggest.

Getting to the Estadio Nacional

Metro Line 6 has a station called Estadio Nacional directly at the venue. Do not assume it will be open.

Metro de Santiago regularly closes that station on major concert days and pushes crowds to neighbouring stops. Check the operator’s notice for your specific date.

All gates open at the same time, so there is no advantage to arriving early for a particular sector. Gate times had not been published at the time of writing.

The stadium seats about 48,745 for football. Concert configurations differ, and three nights implies a six-figure audience across the run.

That scale is exactly what made the pitch dispute politically difficult. Ñuñoa is residential, and the surrounding streets fill quickly.

What We Could Not Confirm

No primary source confirms which members perform in Santiago. All seven appeared at the tour opening in South Korea in April.

At that show RM performed partly seated while recovering from a ligament injury. That was five months ago and says nothing definite about October.

Sell-out status is unverified for the same reason. Treat any claim that a specific night is gone as unconfirmed until the seller shows it.

Two Chilean outlets published figures that differ from the seller’s own table, quoting 99,850 pesos (about US$107) and 582,750 pesos (about US$624). The prices in this article come from the ticket page and sale-day reporting.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many BTS shows are there in Santiago? Three: October 14, 16 and 17 at the Estadio Nacional. The October 14 date was added in April after the first two sold quickly. How much do tickets cost? From 99,875 pesos (about US$107) for the cheapest tier to 528,750 pesos (about US$566) for Pacífico Medio. A soundcheck package costs 676,020 pesos (about US$724). Can I buy a ticket from someone else? Only through the official renaming process. Tickets are nominative, one name change is allowed within thirty days of the show, and entry requires ID matching the ticket. Why was there doubt about the venue? Chile’s national sports institute refused permission in early July over damage a 360-degree stage would cause to the pitch. The government authorised the shows on July 21 with conditions.

World.title: Rock al Parque Turns 30 in Bogotá With Three Free Days in October
World.content:
Festivals: Bogotá

Key Facts What happened. Rock al Parque returns on October 10, 11 and 12 for its 30th edition, free to enter.

Rock al Parque returns on October 10, 11 and 12 for its 30th edition, free to enter. How big it gets. The 2025 edition drew 253,000 people over three days. This year adds a fourth stage.

The 2025 edition drew 253,000 people over three days. This year adds a fourth stage. What it means. Bogotá has paid for a free rock festival every year since 1995, apart from the pandemic.

Bogotá has paid for a free rock festival every year since 1995, apart from the pandemic. The catch. The line-up is out but the running order is not. Nobody knows who plays which day.

The line-up is out but the running order is not. Nobody knows who plays which day. Who turns up. A quarter of the 2025 crowd came from other Colombian cities or from abroad.

A quarter of the 2025 crowd came from other Colombian cities or from abroad. What comes next. The city normally publishes times and entry rules about a week beforehand.

Bogotá’s free rock festival reaches its 30th edition on October 10, 11 and 12. Entry costs nothing, more than 60 acts are booked, and nobody yet knows who plays when.

Rock al Parque fills the Parque Simon Bolivar in Bogota. The 2025 edition drew 253,000 people over three days (Photo: RayScript, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Rock al Parque is the largest free rock festival in Latin America, and it is paid for by the city of Bogotá. For a visitor, that means three days of stadium-scale music without a ticket.

Three Free Days in October

The festival runs from Saturday October 10 to Monday October 12. It takes place in the Parque Metropolitano Simón Bolívar, the big park in the Teusaquillo district west of the centre.

Entry is free and there is no ticket to buy. There is also no registration, no wristband ballot and no queue for a code.

The Monday is a Colombian public holiday, which is why the festival can run three consecutive days. It has moved from its usual June slot.

Anyone planning a trip should note that shift. Guides written before this year will send you to Bogotá at the wrong time.

Thirty Editions, Not Thirty Years

The organiser, the city arts institute IDARTES, is branding this as “30 años, 30 ediciones”. The edition number is the part that holds up exactly.

Rock al Parque began in 1995, so 2026 is the 31st year. It is the 30th edition because 2020 and 2021 were cancelled during the pandemic.

The arithmetic checks out against the organiser’s own record. IDARTES called the 2025 festival “edición número 29”, and the official history page lists no 2020 or 2021.

The festival started as a piece of cultural policy rather than a promotion. Instead of policing an underground scene the city then treated as a public-order problem, Bogotá gave it a municipal stage.

Three decades on it anchors a series of nine free “al Parque” festivals, covering jazz, salsa, hip hop and joropo among others.

Who Is Playing

The poster went up on August 26 and carries more than 60 acts. IDARTES has not published a single definitive number, and press tallies differ.

The international names include Mon Laferte, Ministry, Editors, Apocalyptica and Stratovarius. Serú Girán appear in the form of David Lebón and Pedro Aznar.

Also booked are Rata Blanca, Tokyo Ska Paradise Orchestra, Triptykon, Los Bunkers and Bandalos Chinos. División Minúscula, Los Tetas, Gondwana and Desorden Público fill out the bill.

Claudio Narea, once of the Chilean band Los Prisioneros, is on the list too. Colombian acts include I.R.A., Lika Nova, Esteman, V for Volume, Skampida and Maskhera.

Twenty-six bands from Bogotá itself were chosen through the city’s grant programme. That local quota is a fixed feature of the festival, not a filler.

What Is Not Published Yet

No day-by-day schedule exists. Set times and stage assignments have not been released, and El Espectador reported in late August that they were still missing.

IDARTES has also named no headliners. Press coverage infers them from name recognition, which is not the same thing.

The official site still says more announcements are coming. Whether the line-up is final is genuinely unclear.

The practical consequence is simple. If you are travelling for one specific band, you cannot yet know which of the three days to book.

Getting In and Getting There

The rules below are from the 2025 edition, because the 2026 bulletin has not appeared. IDARTES normally issues it about a week before the gates open.

Last year entry was 14 and over with photo identification. Gates opened at 13:00 and the site closed around 21:30.

Camping and tents were banned, as were glass, cans, aerosols, pointed umbrellas, professional cameras, bicycles, skateboards and pets. Football shirts were also refused, a standard Colombian crowd-safety rule.

No re-entry policy was published either way. Assume you cannot come back the same day and plan around it.

There is no metro in Bogotá. Access is by TransMilenio, with the nearest trunk stations at 7 de Agosto, Movistar Arena, CAN–British Council and Salitre El Greco.

Each is a walk of 15 to 40 minutes to the gates. In 2025 TransMilenio ran extra frequency and pushed its last services to 23:00.

What to Bring to a Festival at 2,640 Metres

Bogotá sits at 2,640 metres and October is in the rainy season. The weather can turn from strong equatorial sun to a cold downpour within the hour.

Bring sunscreen and a rain jacket, and expect to use both on the same afternoon. The park has almost no shelter.

The realistic risk in a crowd of a quarter of a million is petty theft, not violence. Keep your phone away on the walk out after dark.

The economic weight of the festival is real. In 2025 the city counted more than 19 billion pesos (about US$6.1 million) spent in the first two days alone.

That figure uses a rate of 3,132 Colombian pesos to the US dollar, the reference rate for September 8, 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Rock al Parque really free? Yes, and there is no ticket, no registration and no wristband ballot. The festival is funded by the Bogotá city government through its arts institute, IDARTES. When and where is Rock al Parque 2026? October 10, 11 and 12, in the Parque Metropolitano Simón Bolívar in the Teusaquillo district of Bogotá. The Monday is a Colombian public holiday. Who is headlining? Nobody officially, because IDARTES has not designated headliners and no schedule has been published. The best-known names on the poster are Mon Laferte, Ministry, Editors and Apocalyptica. What is the minimum age? In 2025 it was 14 and over with photo identification. The 2026 rules had not been published at the time of writing, so check the festival site before travelling.

World.title: Ultra México Returns After Eight Years With Two Nights in Mexico City
World.content:
Festivals: Mexico City

Key Facts What happened. Ultra México returns on November 7 and 8, its first Mexican edition since 2018.

Ultra México returns on November 7 and 8, its first Mexican edition since 2018. How big a change. The two earlier editions were held in Toluca, an hour away in the State of México.

The two earlier editions were held in Toluca, an hour away in the State of México. Where it really is. On the esplanade outside the Estadio Banorte, the renamed Azteca, not inside the stadium bowl.

On the esplanade outside the Estadio Banorte, the renamed Azteca, not inside the stadium bowl. The catch. The cheap tiers are gone. Passes now cost 3,500 pesos (about US$207), up from 2,550.

The cheap tiers are gone. Passes now cost 3,500 pesos (about US$207), up from 2,550. Who gets turned away. Entry is 18 and over, and student cards are refused at the gate.

Entry is 18 and over, and student cards are refused at the gate. What comes next. Sixteen acts are confirmed as phase one, and no running order has been published yet.

Ultra México comes back on November 7 and 8, after eight years away. It moves into the capital for the first time, and the venue is not quite what the posters suggest.

The Estadio Banorte, formerly the Estadio Azteca, seen from the air before its renovation. Ultra México takes place on the esplanade around it, not inside the bowl (Photo: ProtoplasmaKid, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

If you live in Mexico City and have watched Ultra pass the country by since 2018, this is the return. It is also the first edition inside the capital rather than an hour up the road.

A Festival Returning From an Eight-Year Gap

Ultra México is the Mexican edition of Ultra Worldwide, the touring arm of the electronic-music festival held in Miami since 1999. Mexico has had two editions, in 2017 and 2018.

Both were staged at Foro Pegaso in Toluca, in the State of México. That is a different city about an hour from the capital, which mattered a great deal for anyone without a car.

The 2026 edition moves to Mexico City itself. Organisers are billing it as the first electronic-music festival held at the site.

The 2018 edition ended badly, with Mexican outlets reporting chaos and accusations of fraud. That history is worth knowing before you buy, even though the promoter has changed the venue and the format.

The Venue Is the Esplanade, Not the Stadium

This is the detail most listings get wrong. The festival takes place on the explanada, the open plaza outside the Estadio Banorte, and not inside the stadium bowl.

The official ticket seller states the venue as “Estadio Banorte, Explanada”. Every Mexican outlet that has visited says the same thing.

The difference matters, because a stadium show and an esplanade show are not the same size of event. The stadium’s own capacity of about 80,000 does not apply here.

The Estadio Banorte is the former Estadio Azteca. Banorte, a Mexican bank, bought the naming rights in March 2025 and paid for the renovation before the World Cup.

The address is Calzada de Tlalpan 3465, in the Santa Úrsula Coapa neighbourhood of the Coyoacán borough.

Who Is Playing

Sixteen acts make up phase one: Afrojack, Alesso, Armin van Buuren, ARTBAT, Boris Brejcha, Boys Noize, CamelPhat and Eric Prydz. The list continues with Hardwell, Klangkuenstler, Levity, Marlon Hoffstadt, Miss Monique, Sara Landry, Steve Angello and Subtronics.

The festival has confirmed three stages. Two are named, the Main Stage and RESISTANCE, and the third has not been announced.

No day-by-day split has been published. Which artist plays which night is genuinely unknown at the time of writing.

Organisers have said Mexican acts will be added. No second phase had appeared by early September.

Tickets, and the Tiers That Have Already Gone

Only two-day passes are sold, called abonos. There are no single-day tickets, and none have been promised.

Four price tiers have run so far, and the first three are sold out. General admission started at 2,550 pesos (about US$151) and is now 3,500 pesos (about US$207).

The VIP pass has followed the same path. It opened at 4,400 pesos (about US$260) and now costs 6,000 pesos (about US$354).

Those figures are before service charges and tax, which the festival states separately. Earlier tiers carried roughly fourteen per cent on top, so budget for more than the headline price.

Prices are converted at 16.93 pesos to the US dollar, the reference rate for September 8, 2026. Rates move, so check on the day you buy.

The seller is Fanki, not Ticketmaster. Several listings say otherwise and they are wrong, which matters because resold tickets get cancelled.

The Rules That Catch Foreign Visitors Out

The festival is strictly 18 and over. There is no concession for anyone younger, accompanied or not.

A passport is the safest identification. Foreign driving licences are accepted, but the terms also ask for a passport photocopy alongside them.

Student cards, consular IDs, expired documents and photocopies on their own are all refused at the gate. So are birth certificates.

Tickets can be transferred to another person, but resale is banned outright. The organiser states that any ticket found in improper use will be cancelled with no right of appeal.

There is no re-entry. Once you leave the site your pass is spent, so plan the evening as one continuous stretch.

Getting There and Getting Home

Take Metro Line 2 to Tasqueña, then the Tren Ligero south. The station is still signposted Estadio Azteca, because it was not renamed with the stadium.

That mismatch confuses visitors every time. Look for the old name on the platform signs.

Doors open at 16:00 and the night runs to roughly 02:00. Metro and light rail will have stopped long before the end.

Calzada de Tlalpan and Periférico Sur clog badly on event days. Book a ride in advance or agree a meeting point away from the gates.

Mexico City sits at 2,240 metres and November nights are cold. This is an outdoor event running past midnight, so bring a layer you do not mind carrying.

Frequently Asked Questions

When and where is Ultra México 2026? On Saturday November 7 and Sunday November 8, on the esplanade outside the Estadio Banorte in Coyoacán, Mexico City. Doors open at 16:00 and the night runs to about 02:00. How much does a ticket cost? A two-day general admission pass costs 3,500 pesos (about US$207) and a VIP pass 6,000 pesos (about US$354), both before fees. The three cheaper tiers have sold out. Where do I buy tickets safely? Only from Fanki, the festival’s official seller, linked from ultramexico.com. Resale is banned and resold tickets are cancelled, so avoid third-party sites. Can I get in with a student card? No, the festival is 18 and over and student cards are explicitly refused. Bring a passport, or a foreign photo ID together with a passport photocopy.

World.title: A Hunting Lodge Just Tested Mozambique’s Gas Wager
World.content:
Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy . We never share your email.

One email, every weekday morning. African markets, politics and business — filed from our newsroom in Rio.

GLOBAL BACKDROP · ENERGY & SECURITY

Key Facts —What happened: Insurgents raided a hunting camp at Marangira, Niassa province, on Thursday 3 September, killing one or two people and abducting between 11 and 20. —Not a first: Niassa has been attacked since November 2021. A raid on the Mariri centre in April 2025 killed nine. —The gap: Marangira is one province from TotalEnergies’ Afungi site, which sits behind its own fence and its own guards. —The project: The US$20 billion Mozambique LNG scheme restarted on 29 January 2026 after a five-year freeze, on the argument that security had improved. —The numbers: ACLED counts 2,397 political-violence events and about 6,624 deaths in Cabo Delgado since October 2017, of which 2,768 were civilians. —The parallel: Peru learned the same lesson at Camisea in 2012. A company can fence a wellhead; a government cannot fence a province.

A hunting lodge in Niassa has just shown what the Mozambique gas restart actually bought. Not a pacified north, but a very well guarded perimeter inside one.

A raid, and what it did not prove

The attackers hit Marangira, near the Niassa Special Reserve, on Thursday 3 September. They looted and burned the hunting camp and damaged the medical centre, the police post and the telecommunications tower.

Reports put the dead at one or two and the abducted at between 11 and 20. A South African mechanic, a chef and a third member of staff are among them, and three American hunters were flown out by helicopter.

No hostages have been released. The spread of targets reads as planned rather than opportunistic.

What Marangira does not show is a new frontier. Niassa has been absorbing this war since November 2021, and the April 2025 raid on the Mariri Environmental Centre inside the reserve killed four rangers and five soldiers.

The analyst Peter Bofin described Marangira as the group’s first incursion into Niassa since May 2025. The province’s respite lasted sixteen months, not nine years.

The economy behind the raids

Islamic State Mozambique has spent 2025 building what one specialist assessment calls a mobile, revenue-driven model. It runs convoy ambushes, road taxation along National Road 380 and levies on artisanal mining.

Kidnapping accounted for roughly ten percent of the group’s recorded activity last year. A hostage economy once confined to the Cabo Delgado coast has found new ground to work.

Filmmakers on the ground reported that insurgents had been moving west from Cabo Delgado for an extended period before the raid.

Fighter numbers have fallen from several thousand in the insurgency’s early years to what one recent assessment calls a few hundred. The same analysis insists the insurgency is not near its end.

The ghost of Palma

In March 2021 more than a hundred Islamic State-linked fighters overran Palma town, some ten kilometres from TotalEnergies’ Afungi construction site. Dozens were killed and the settlement was gutted.

TotalEnergies declared force majeure that April, citing “the evolution of the security situation in the north of the Cabo Delgado province”. The US$20 billion project sat frozen for close to five years.

Mozambique’s anticipated windfall froze with it. President Daniel Chapo’s government now puts the lifetime figure at up to US$35 billion in state revenue.

Seven Palma survivors and victims’ relatives filed a criminal complaint against TotalEnergies in France in October 2023. It alleges involuntary manslaughter and failure to assist persons in danger.

The restart was announced by Chapo and chief executive Patrick Pouyanne at Afungi on 29 January 2026. It rested on the claim that “security is deemed to have improved in Cabo Delgado, particularly with the deployment of Rwandan soldiers”.

Two perimeters, one province

Industry assessments now concede that Afungi’s safety and Cabo Delgado’s safety are different products. One review calls the site a highly securitised enclave.

It is a fenced concession expected to hold some 17,000 workers at peak construction, with minimal contact with surrounding communities. Around 3,000 of the roughly 5,000 Rwandan troops in the province are stationed around it, alongside private security contractors whose headcount and mandate have never been disclosed.

Rwanda’s commitment has grown from the 1,000 soldiers first deployed in July 2021. A Status of Forces Agreement signed by the two defence ministers in late August 2025 formalised it, with a duration that has never been made public.

The regional SADC force it effectively replaced began withdrawing in April 2024 and closed out in July, over funding disputes and friction with Kigali.

ACLED recorded eight political-violence events and eight deaths in Cabo Delgado in the second half of May 2026 alone. Since October 2017 it counts 2,397 events and about 6,624 deaths, of which 2,768 were civilians.

One independent review describes the July and August 2025 attack wave as the most significant escalation since 2022. The fence has held. The province around it plainly has not.

Chapo’s formula and its price

Chapo’s public doctrine is to fight on the ground while working to identify the insurgency’s leadership. That reads less like an exit strategy than an admission that the war has no fixed end date.

A first-gas target of 2029 runs alongside it regardless.

The financing terms are not fully visible to Mozambique’s own government. TotalEnergies claims roughly US$4.5 billion in costs accrued during the suspension, close to a quarter of the project’s original value.

The restart proceeded before an audit the government itself had requested was concluded or published.

One assessment warns that force without governance and stability buys only weeks of calm, not years of peace. What Chapo is selling investors is not an end to the war but a tolerable rate of incident.

London registered its doubt in the clearest language a government has, withdrawing US$1.15 billion in export finance shortly before the January ceremony. Friends of the Earth called the relaunch a carbon timebomb.

What this means from Latin America

Rio Times readers have seen this split screen on their own continent.

On 9 April 2012 Shining Path remnants operating out of Peru’s VRAEM valley kidnapped as many as thirty workers from a hotel in Kepashiato. Most were employed by the Swedish contractor Skanska, servicing the pipeline that carries gas out of the Camisea fields.

The government had spent a decade calling that corridor secure. Twenty-three hostages were released within hours and Peru’s energy exports never paused.

The message was not about the gas. It was the group’s first major kidnapping since 2003, and a military officer said at the time that the rebels had taken the hostages to halt the army’s advance.

A decade on, Lima was still treating the VRAEM as an active emergency zone. In April 2022 it proposed only to begin closing counter-subversion bases there, not to declare the valley pacified.

Camisea never stopped flowing, exactly as Afungi’s construction will not stop for Marangira. A company can fence a wellhead far more easily than a government can fence a valley or a province.

The gap between those two achievements is where every hostage story like this one gets written.

More: Africa news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did the attack reach the LNG site? No. Marangira is in Niassa, the province next to Cabo Delgado, one province from the Afungi construction site. There is no indication of contact with the LNG perimeter. Was this the first insurgent attack in Niassa? No. The first recorded attack in Niassa was in November 2021, and a raid on the Mariri Environmental Centre in April 2025 killed nine. Marangira is the first incursion since May 2025. Why did TotalEnergies suspend the project in 2021? It declared force majeure in April 2021 after more than a hundred fighters overran the nearby town of Palma that March. The freeze lasted close to five years. Is Cabo Delgado safer than in 2021? Assessments diverge. The government and TotalEnergies point to roughly 5,000 Rwandan troops, while one independent review calls the July and August 2025 attack wave the worst escalation since 2022. How many people has the conflict killed? ACLED counts about 6,624 deaths across 2,397 political-violence events in Cabo Delgado between October 2017 and June 2026, of which 2,768 were civilians. Around 1.3 million people have been displaced.

World.title: Nepal Changed Its Politicians and Kept Its State
World.content:
Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy . We never share your email.

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

GLOBAL BACKDROP · POLITICS & DISASTER

Key Facts —The anniversary: One year ago this week, Gen Z protests burned part of Singha Durbar and forced out a prime minister. Seventy-six people were killed. —The mandate: Balen Shah, a 35-year-old former rapper, was sworn in on 27 March 2026 with 182 of 275 seats. —The test: A glacier collapsed on 26 August. The flood has killed at least 1,385 people across Nepal and Tibet, with more than 5,400 still missing. —The hesitation: Nepal initially held back foreign rescue teams. An industry body says approval came too late. —The pledge: The governing party banned nepotism at its June convention. Its own appointments have tested that within weeks. —The detainees: More than 900 people arrested during last year’s protests are still held on arson-related charges.

Nepal replaced its political class and kept its state. A glacier has since tested the difference, and Latin America has run this experiment three times already.

A mandate without a method

Balen Shah took the prime minister’s oath on 27 March 2026. His Rastriya Swatantra Party holds 182 of the 275 seats in the House of Representatives.

The 5 March election drew more than 800,000 first-time voters on turnout of around 60 percent. Shah is a rapper turned civil engineer turned Kathmandu mayor, and at 35 the youngest prime minister Nepal has had.

A majority is an instrument, not a diagnosis. Nepal’s Gen Z movement never specified which institutions were supposed to change.

Sushila Karki, the former chief justice who ran the country as interim prime minister before handing it to Shah, made the gap explicit on the anniversary. “Even a two-thirds majority in Parliament cannot provide stability if there is no good governance,” she said on 8 September.

Bishnu Raj Upreti of the Nepal Centre for Contemporary Research told Al Jazeera that “leadership change has started. It is good, but not enough.” He added that structural change has to begin with changing laws and writing new ones.

Professor Dinesh Paudel was blunter. “The fundamental concerns and issues raised by the young protestor last year are still the same, and there are no governance style changes even after the new elected government.”

The pledge and the appointments

Within days of the swearing-in, the government appointed Kumar Byanjankar, known as Kumar Ben, as the prime minister’s chief advisor. Shah considers his father, Narsingh Byanjankar, his political mentor.

Kumar’s brother Siddhi Byanjankar became chief advisor to Education Minister Sasmit Pokharel on 1 April. On his first day in office Shah moved his entire Kathmandu city secretariat into the Prime Minister’s Office.

Only in June, at its Chitwan convention, did the Rastriya Swatantra Party pass a resolution banning nepotism and favouritism outright. The vocabulary was the movement’s own.

The appointments that followed came within weeks of that pledge. Kumar’s sister Siddhi Laxmi Byanjankar joined the Calendar Determination Development Committee in early July, and a 68-year-old ally, Kishore Thapa, was named to chair the Tribhuvan University Service Commission without a competitive process.

None of this is illegal, and little of it is unusual in Nepali coalition politics. It is unusual only in whose signature is on it.

Governing by ordinance

The government did move on paper. It published a hundred-point agenda for its first hundred days and set up a commission to investigate former officials’ assets.

It abolished civil-service trade unions. It removed more than 1,500 political appointees through ordinance, without individual legal review.

The method is what critics have seized on. Courts have since released several of the government’s headline detainees, a pattern one Nepali assessment said risked “creating the impression of politically dramatic but legally fragile enforcement”.

More than 900 people arrested during the 2025 protests remain in custody on arson-related charges, with unofficial estimates running past 1,600. A government born of a street uprising is still the jailer of the people who put it there.

Two further episodes never reached the official scorecard. A prime ministerial comment appeared to question Nepal’s border with India and was walked back, and riverbank settlements were cleared in Kathmandu.

Water finds the old cracks

On 26 August 2026 roughly 0.2 square kilometres of ice and rock broke off the Langtang Lirung glacier and fell about 1.2 kilometres. The United States Geological Survey attributed the seismic signal to the collapse itself, not to any earthquake before it.

The impact melted enough ice to send a flood down the Trishuli river system. It destroyed the Gyirong Port border crossing in Tibet within seven minutes.

Nepal’s upstream monitoring stations were swept away before they could send an alert. Debris travelled up to a hundred kilometres downstream.

Five districts lie along the flood path: Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha and Chitwan. The worst destruction was upstream, in Rasuwa and Nuwakot.

In Chitwan, some 160 kilometres downstream, more than 250 bodies washed ashore. Only nine could be readily identified.

A toll that keeps climbing

The United Nations reported roughly 900 dead and 4,247 missing on 31 August. By 4 September Nepali authorities were citing 1,287 dead inside the country.

By 6 September the combined figure had reached at least 1,385 dead, 1,342 in Nepal and 43 in Tibet, with more than 5,400 still missing.

Among the missing are 583 foreign nationals from 39 countries in Nepal, and 261 more from 23 countries in Tibet. At least 17 further bodies have been recovered from rivers in India and are not in the official count.

South Korea sent a response team and one million dollars in aid. Nine of its nationals are missing at a hydropower construction site in Rasuwa.

The hesitation that cost time

Nepal has mobilised some 21,465 security personnel and declared a three-month disaster zone. Relief funds passed 7.77 billion rupees by 3 September, up from 5.44 billion five days earlier.

On paper that is a far better organised response than 2015. In practice the government initially held foreign help at arm’s length.

Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle said aid was accepted “according to the needs on the ground”. Bhim Gautam of the Independent Power Producers Association said the government lacked “enough technology, equipment and expertise”.

Gautam added that late in the week the government approved rescue teams from China, India and Australia. “But it is so late now,” he said.

The analyst Chandradev Bhatta traced the hesitation to 2015, when China and India competed openly for reconstruction influence and China “managed to gain a geopolitical foothold in the country”. A state that spent a decade guarding against foreign leverage built the delay that cost it time in a different emergency.

What this means from Latin America

Rio Times readers have watched this experiment run to its conclusion twice on their own continent.

Chile’s October 2019 estallido social produced an elected Constitutional Convention and a new president in Gabriel Boric. The rewrite the plazas demanded was rejected twice, by 61.87 percent in September 2022 and 55.76 percent in December 2023.

The amended Pinochet-era charter is still in force. The faces changed and the operating system did not.

Peru offers the harsher version. After Pedro Castillo’s December 2022 self-coup collapsed and Dina Boluarte took office, protests demanding early elections were met with force that killed 49 people, including eight children, between December 2022 and February 2023.

Congress rejected every attempt to bring the vote forward. Peru ran the calendar out to 2026 under the same political class the protesters had tried to remove.

Colombia sits between the two. The April 2021 paro nacional forced President Ivan Duque to withdraw a tax reform within days, and the disillusionment fed into Gustavo Petro’s election the following year.

Nepal has so far delivered the Chilean pattern rather than the Colombian one. New faces, an unrewritten state, and a flood asking the question a ballot box usually asks first.

More: World news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How old is Balen Shah? He was born on 27 April 1990. He was 32 when Kathmandu elected him mayor in May 2022 and 35 when he was sworn in as prime minister on 27 March 2026. What caused the August 2026 floods? About 0.2 square kilometres of the Langtang Lirung glacier collapsed on 26 August and fell some 1.2 kilometres. The impact melted enough ice to send a flood down the Trishuli river system. How many people have died? At least 1,385 as of 6 September, 1,342 in Nepal and 43 in Tibet, with more than 5,400 still missing. The count is still rising. What sparked the 2025 protests? Anger at corruption combined with a ban on major social media platforms, since reversed. The demonstrations killed 76 people and forced Prime Minister K.P. Sharma Oli to resign within days. Has the government kept its anti-corruption promises? Only partly. It created an asset-investigation commission and abolished civil-service unions, but it has also placed its chief advisor’s relatives in public posts and seen courts release several of its own headline detainees.

World.title: The Party Elon Musk Backed Just Won a German State by 26 Points
World.content:
Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy . We never share your email.

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

GLOBAL BACKDROP · POLITICS

Key Facts —The result: Alternative for Germany, the anti-immigration party known as the AfD, took 43.8 percent in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday 6 September, the largest share a populist-right party has won in a German state election since 1945. —The seats: It holds 39 of 83. The four parties that refuse to work with it also hold 39. A majority needs 42. —The hinge: One small left-wing breakaway party, the BSW, has the remaining five seats and has not said what it will do. —Not final: This is the preliminary official count. The state electoral committee certifies the result later this month. —The collapse: The Christian Democrats, Germany’s main conservative party, fell to 17.2 percent from 37.1 percent, losing 25 of their 40 seats. —What comes next: Two more German regions, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Berlin, vote on 20 September.

Elon Musk said only this party could save Germany. On Sunday it took 43.8 percent of one German state, a landslide in a system built to prevent them, and 26 points clear of the conservatives who had governed there since 2002. It still cannot govern, because the parties refusing to work with it hold exactly as many seats. Latin America has spent twenty years learning what that kind of arithmetic does to a country.

Nothing Like This Has Happened Since 1945

Saxony-Anhalt, a state of about two million people in the former East Germany, voted on Sunday 6 September. Alternative for Germany, an anti-immigration party usually called the AfD, took 43.8 percent of the preliminary official count.

No party of that kind has won a bigger share in any German state election since 1945. Chatham House makes the same point in the same words.

The raw number is not the record. Eight German state elections have produced 43 percent or more since 2006, two of them as recently as 2022.

What has no precedent is the speed. The party took 20.8 percent here five years ago, so it has added 23 points in a single cycle.

Its own previous best anywhere was 32.8 percent, in Thuringia in 2024. It has just beaten its own ceiling by 11 points.

No party that a German domestic intelligence agency has classified as confirmed right-wing extremist has ever won a share like this. The Saxony-Anhalt branch has carried that classification since November 2023.

And no party in Western Europe since 1945 has crossed 40 percent while every other party in its parliament refused to govern with it. Belgium’s cordon peaked against a party on 24 percent, Austria’s against one on 28.9.

The share converts to 39 of the state parliament’s 83 seats. In 2021 the party took 20.8 percent and 23 seats, in a chamber that then held 97.

The Christian Democrats fell to 17.2 percent from 37.1 percent. The governing party lost more than half its vote in a single election, and 25 of its 40 seats.

The party had governed Saxony-Anhalt since 2002, under Reiner Haseloff from 2011. Sven Schulze only took over as minister-president in January of this year.

And Now Nobody Can Govern

Winning on that scale has not delivered power, and that is the second half of the story. Add the conservative Christian Democrats’ 15 seats to the centre-left Social Democrats’ eight, the Greens’ eight and the left-wing Die Linke’s eight. That is 39.

The AfD also has 39. Neither side can reach the 42 seats a majority needs.

Between them sits the Bundnis Sahra Wagenknecht, or BSW, a breakaway from Die Linke with 5.3 percent and five seats. The Free Democrats took 2.6 percent and lost every seat they had.

The BSW’s federal leadership has ruled out installing either the AfD’s Ulrich Siegmund or Schulze as minister-president. It has floated a candidate from outside the parties instead.

Its regional lead candidate, Thomas Schulze, has left the door open to working with the AfD bill by bill. “This tiny party could now play a decisive role in determining the future of Saxony-Anhalt,” the analyst Volker Resing told the Associated Press.

Four parties that agree on almost nothing must now govern together, or hand the state to the party they exist to exclude. There is no third option that does not involve the five seats in the middle.

Every earlier test of the firewall lasted a week, or covered one district, or turned on a single ballot. This is the first time the arithmetic itself makes the wall unworkable.

Washington Is Cheering

The party has powerful admirers abroad. Elon Musk wrote in December 2024 that only the AfD could save Germany, then hosted its leader Alice Weidel on a livestream.

He posted “Gut gemacht”, German for well done, after Sunday’s result. Richard Grenell, Donald Trump’s envoy and a former US ambassador to Berlin, called it a new day in Germany.

Trump himself shared the result on his own platform without comment. He has never endorsed the party, and in 2025 said he was not disappointed it had lost.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio went further than his president. After German intelligence upgraded its assessment of the party in May 2025, he called the move tyranny in disguise.

That assessment no longer stands nationally. A Cologne court blocked it in February 2026, and the federal party is again treated only as a suspected case.

The Saxony-Anhalt branch is the exception. The state intelligence service has classified it as confirmed right-wing extremist since November 2023.

The Wall Was Never a Law

The Brandmauer, German for firewall, is an understanding rather than a statute. Germany’s mainstream parties agreed not to govern with the populist right or to accept its decisive votes.

An understanding lasts exactly as long as the people keeping it. This one has cracked before.

In February 2020 the Free Democrat Thomas Kemmerich became Thuringia’s premier on a ballot that passed only because all 22 AfD deputies backed him. Chancellor Angela Merkel called it unforgivable, and he announced his resignation the next day.

In 2023 the AfD’s Robert Sesselmann won the Sonneberg district administration, the first populist-right politician to run a German county since the Nazi era.

The Rosa Luxemburg Foundation counted 121 cases of mainstream parties voting alongside the AfD in eastern councils between 2019 and 2023. Most concerned building, infrastructure and social policy rather than migration, which accounted for only eight.

Every Earlier Crack Was Small

On 29 January 2025 the Bundestag passed a non-binding migration motion by 348 votes to 345. Friedrich Merz brought it as opposition leader; he is now chancellor.

It carried only because AfD votes supplied the margin. It was the first time a Bundestag majority had rested on the populist right.

Between 160,000 and 250,000 people protested in Berlin within days, depending on whether the count comes from the police or the organisers.

Every previous breach was absorbed inside a week, a district or a single ballot. Saxony-Anhalt is different in scale, and scale is what containment was never built to survive.

Where the Vote Came From

The state’s economy supplies the mood. Population is down to 2.12 million since reunification, and unemployment runs at 8.2 percent against 6.5 percent nationally.

Company insolvencies rose about 18 percent in 2025, against 4 percent nationally on the same measure. The pressure sits in the Leuna and Bitterfeld chemical belt the state still treats as its identity.

Voters name migration rather than unemployment as the problem. Foreign nationals are 7.9 percent of the state population, against 14.9 percent nationally.

What changed was belief. Some 36 percent told pollsters in July they trusted the AfD most to fix the state, against 9 percent five years earlier.

Siegmund’s campaign converted that into an estimated 157,000 former non-voters and 83,000 former Christian Democrat voters. Turnout climbed to 77.8 percent from 60.3 percent.

Marcus Boick, a historian of Germany at Cambridge, argues that “voting for right-wing populists is a very rational thing to do in the rural areas” of the east.

A Movement, Not a Swing

Vote shares move all the time. Movements show up in a different number, which is how many people they pull into an election that was not going to have them.

Seventeen and a half points of extra turnout, in a state that has been losing population since reunification, is that number. So is a jump from 9 percent trust to 36 in five years.

The party also beat its own ceiling by 11 points, having never passed 32.8 percent anywhere before. That is not a swing between two established blocs.

The closest comparison anyone reaches for is American. The Washington Post described the winning candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, as a German politician with a MAGA touch, and Make Germany Great Again caps have become common at the party’s rallies.

Almut Moller of the European Policy Centre put it more carefully. There is ideological alignment on key issues, she said, and the party is also learning from the MAGA movement.

The differences are real and worth stating. The party is pro-Moscow in a way the American movement is not, and its leaders have publicly criticised Washington on tariffs, Iran and Greenland.

Berlin Braces, Warsaw Fumes

Merz called Sunday’s result “the most serious election defeat that the CDU has had for years, for decades”. He said his party was “deeply shocked” and that “giving up is not an option for me”.

Schulze, the outgoing minister-president, chose defiance over concession. “Some say this is a dark day for Saxony-Anhalt. I say this is democracy.”

The result travelled. Poland’s prime minister Donald Tusk posted that “in Poland, only idiots or traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD in Germany”, adding that “quite a few of them have gathered in Confederation and PiS”.

The reply was personal. The Confederation MP Konrad Berkowicz told Tusk it was his own camp that should worry about German money drying up, and the AfD member of the European Parliament Tomasz Froelich told the Polish prime minister to eat a Snickers.

The AfD’s roughly 576,000 second votes are about one percent of Germany’s national electorate. The party still leads the Social Democrats 35 to 32 in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, which votes on 20 September.

What This Means From Latin America

Rio Times readers do not need a German dictionary to recognise this problem. They need only look at their own legislatures.

Peru has removed or forced out six presidents since 2018. The most recent was Jose Jeri in February 2026, four months after he replaced Dina Boluarte.

That happens inside a Congress split across a dozen shifting blocs. Each vote requires a new coalition, so nobody governs for a term.

Brazil’s answer has a name and a price. President Lula da Silva’s government depends on the Centrao, a bloc with no fixed ideology and a documented appetite for cabinet posts and budget earmarks in exchange for votes.

That is the kingmaker role the BSW has so far declined to play for free. Brazilian politics has priced it in for a generation.

Argentina ran the opposite experiment. Javier Milei took office in December 2023 with a small fraction of Congress and was not walled out but invited in, first through decree powers and then through seat-by-seat deals.

Latin America never wrote a doctrine as explicit as the Brandmauer. Exclusion here has always been improvised, coalition by coalition.

Saxony-Anhalt makes the same point from the other end. Even an explicit doctrine comes down to whichever five seats hold the balance.

More: World news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did the AfD win control of Saxony-Anhalt? No. The preliminary official count gives it 39 of 83 seats, three short of a majority. The four parties that exclude it also hold 39, so the BSW’s five seats decide who can reach 42. Is this the first time a populist-right party has topped a German state election? No. The AfD topped Thuringia in September 2024 with 32.8 percent. What is new in Saxony-Anhalt is the size of the share, 43.8 percent, the largest since 1945. Is the result final? Not yet. This is the preliminary official count. The state electoral committee meets later this month to certify the final result. What is the Brandmauer? It is an informal commitment by Germany’s mainstream parties never to govern with the AfD or accept its decisive votes. It has cracked before, in Thuringia in 2020, in Sonneberg in 2023 and in the Bundestag in January 2025. Does this affect Chancellor Merz? Not directly, because a state parliament has no say over Berlin. Indirectly it is real: Merz called it his party’s worst defeat in decades, and two more states vote on 20 September.

Connected Coverage We covered the regional read-through in Global Economy Briefing — September 8, 2026 and the wider European policy picture in Europe Intelligence Brief.

World.title: Latin America China Ties Survived the Region’s Right Turn
World.content:
LATIN AMERICA · ECONOMY

Key Facts — The expectation Milei, Kast, Fujimori and de la Espriella were all read as a turn away from Beijing.

— Argentina Milei renewed the central bank swap with China in August and extended it from three years to five.

— The catch The clearest rollbacks of Chinese positions were done by left governments and by courts.

— Colombia President de la Espriella rode the Chinese-built Bogota metro in September and confirmed lines two and three.

— Peru President Fujimori’s government has said nothing about Chancay or Chinese investment since taking office.

— The real shift Chinese direct investment in the region fell to US$8.66 billion in 2025, around 55 percent below its 2019 peak.

The Latin America China relationship was supposed to shrink under the region’s new right. The record of the past year says something stranger.

The port of Valparaiso. China takes about a third of Chilean exports. (Photo: “Puerto de Valparaíso, Chile” by Marca Chile, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.)

The story writes itself. Argentina, Chile, Peru and Colombia all elected right-wing governments aligned with Washington.

Chinese influence should therefore be in retreat. The Latin America China relationship has instead been remarkably steady.

Where it has shrunk, the cause is usually not the new governments. It is Chinese balance sheets, Latin American courts, and in one case a left-wing president.

Argentina Renewed the Swap and Made It Longer

Javier Milei campaigned on refusing to trade with communists. In office he has been considerably more practical.

On 5 August 2026 the central bank renewed its currency swap with the People’s Bank of China. The facility is 130 billion renminbi, around US$19.3 billion.

The term was extended from three years to five, running to 2031. That is longer than any previous renewal.

It was agreed over sustained objections from the United States Treasury, which had offered a competing facility. Both simple readings of this are wrong.

Argentina did wind down the money it had actually drawn, from about US$5 billion to US$675 million by mid-January. It repaid the drawn portion and lengthened the facility.

In May the government admitted a lithium project led by China’s Ganfeng into its flagship investment incentive regime. The project is worth about US$1.24 billion.

The economy ministry announced the approval without naming the companies. A government aligned with Washington gave its best tax terms to a Chinese lithium major, quietly.

Colombia’s President Rode the Chinese Metro

Abelardo de la Espriella has reversed his predecessor on almost everything. Israel, the Golan Heights, Western Sahara, Venezuela and United States military access have all moved.

China is the exception. He has said he will maintain strategically important infrastructure regardless of ideological differences.

In early September he rode Bogota’s metro line one, built by a Chinese consortium and more than eighty percent complete. He confirmed the viaduct finishes in January 2027 and committed to lines two and three.

Reports that Colombia will leave China’s Belt and Road Initiative come from the incoming United States ambassador. No Colombian official has said it.

Peru Has Simply Gone Quiet

Keiko Fujimori took office on 28 July 2026. Her inaugural address promised significant space for cooperation with Washington.

It said nothing about China, and nothing about Chancay. Her prime minister’s eighteen-page policy programme in August did not mention mainland China either.

It did promise to bring a Hong Kong trade agreement into force this year. Silence plus continuity is not the same as a reversal.

The threat to the port is legal rather than political. Its operator is fighting at the Constitutional Tribunal over whether Peru’s regulator may supervise it at all.

The Latin America China Rollbacks Came From Elsewhere

Two Chinese positions in the region were genuinely cut back this year. Neither was cut back by a right-wing government.

In Chile, the state lithium deal that diluted Tianqi’s position at SQM was struck under Gabriel Boric. The Supreme Court rejected Tianqi’s final appeal in January, before Jose Antonio Kast took office.

In Panama, the Chinese-linked port operator lost its concession because the Supreme Court ruled it unconstitutional. The much-discussed sale of that portfolio to a Western consortium has still not closed.

The one telecommunications casualty was the China Mobile submarine cable to Chile. Approval was rescinded under Boric after Washington revoked the visas of three Chilean officials.

Kast’s government has since said the project continues to be assessed. The pattern is consistent and counter-intuitive.

What Has Actually Changed Is the Money

Chinese direct investment in Latin America was US$8.66 billion in 2025, across 46 transactions. That is down from US$9.8 billion in 2024 and about 55 percent below the 2019 peak.

The number of deals held up. Average deal size fell from US$427 million in 2019 to US$188 million last year.

Policy bank lending effectively stopped. The main academic database recorded nothing new in 2021 and US$1.3 billion in 2023, and has published no figure since.

But infrastructure engagement went the other way. Chinese infrastructure investment in the region reached US$19.8 billion in 2024, its strongest year of the decade.

So the accurate summary is not retreat. China is lending less and building more, in smaller and greenfield-heavy pieces.

Washington Has Rhetoric and Few Instruments

The State Department warned in February that cheap Chinese money costs sovereignty. No sanctions, financing offer or alternative port investment accompanied it.

A hemispheric summit in Miami in March drew twelve heads of state. Only one concrete economic deliverable is documented, a minerals agreement with Chile whose value was not disclosed.

A widely cited fifty-billion-dollar infrastructure compact is a think tank proposal, not announced policy. Marco Rubio’s regional tour this week is built around narcoterrorism and migration.

China and infrastructure do not appear on its published agenda. Trade is where the asymmetry shows most clearly.

China took 31.6 percent of Brazil’s exports in the first half of 2026. The United States took 9.4 percent.

What to Watch

The first marker is Peru’s Constitutional Tribunal. Whether a Peruvian regulator can supervise the country’s newest port is a sovereignty question with no electoral component.

The second is deal size. If average Chinese ticket sizes recover, the retreat thesis fails outright.

The third is whether Washington produces an instrument rather than a warning. So far the carrots have been proposals and the sticks have been visas.

More: Latin America news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Has Latin America’s right turn reduced Chinese influence?

Not so far. Argentina renewed and lengthened its currency swap with China, Colombia’s president publicly backed the Chinese-built Bogota metro, and Peru’s government has made no statement on Chinese investment.

What has actually changed in the Latin America China relationship?

The money. Chinese direct investment fell to US$8.66 billion in 2025, about 55 percent below the 2019 peak, with average deal size dropping from US$427 million to US$188 million. Infrastructure investment rose to US$19.8 billion in 2024.

Who has rolled back Chinese positions in the region?

Courts and left-wing governments. Chile’s Supreme Court and the Boric government diluted Tianqi’s lithium position, and Panama’s Supreme Court voided a Chinese-linked port concession.

Sources: Red ALC-China and UNAM Cechimex Monitor de la OFDI china, Boston University Global Development Policy Center, Inter-American Dialogue, CEBC, Central Banking, SCMP, Caixin, La Republica, Wilson Center, Rio Times.

World.title: The Isaac Accords Have One Member, and No Way to Join
World.content:
LATIN AMERICA · DIPLOMACY

Key Facts — The membership Argentina is the only state to have joined, as of 8 September 2026.

— The mechanism There is no accession instrument. No treaty text, no signature page, no depositary and no ratification.

— The catch About twenty legislators signed a non-binding resolution. That became twelve countries in the retelling.

— The count The organisers’ own materials variously say ten, twelve, thirteen and fourteen countries.

— What was signed A framework launch in Jerusalem on 19 April 2026, plus three bilateral memorandums with Argentina.

— Who funds it A New York non-profit created by the Genesis Prize Foundation, seeded with Javier Milei’s declined US$1 million prize.

The Isaac Accords are described as a regional realignment. Argentina is the only state that has joined, and no mechanism exists for a second.

The Argentine National Congress in Buenos Aires, where the June resolution was signed. (Photo: “Atrio del Palacio del Congreso de la Nación Argentina” by Cámara de Diputados de la Nación Argentina, via Wikimedia Commons, Public domain.)
