World.title: Documentary on James Bond creator Ian Fleming to premiere at GoldenEye
World.content:
Portrait taken in the early 1960s of Ian Fleming, a British journalist, secret service agent, writer, whose most famous creation was the superhero James Bond, agent 007. (Photo: AFP)

Ian Fleming and the Curse of James Bond, directed by Adam Low, a new feature documentary exploring the life, imagination and enduring legacy of James Bond creator Ian Fleming, will premiere at GoldenEye, Fleming’s former Jamaican home, during the 80th anniversary year of the villa’s construction.

The documentary explores Fleming beyond the legend of 007, considering the contradictions, pressures and fascinations that shaped both the man and the charged literary world he created, according to a press release by Gross Media, which executive produced the project.

Presented at GoldenEye by Gross Media, the premiere weekend – November 19 to November 22, 2026 – brings together biography, place and mythology in a setting deeply connected to the Bond story.

“GoldenEye’s enduring legacy as a center of Jamaican art and creativity is rare and compelling,” said Gross Media founder David M Gross. “So much new has originated here and radiated outward — through music, painting, literature and the performing arts. Our film invites a new generation to come to Oracabessa, St Mary, to understand that legacy and be inspired by it.”

Built in a uniquely Jamaican architectural style, the iconic villa features whitewashed walls, wooden louvers and has no glass windowpanes.

Upon returning from espionage duties during World War II, Fleming built the villa in 1946 on Jamaica’s famed North Coast. GoldenEye became the creative sanctuary where he wrote each of the 12 James Bond nov els and the stories that introduced one of the most recognizable characters in modern popular culture.

Eight decades later, the property remains a living landmark: part legendary literary site, part cultural myth and an enduring symbol of Jamaica’s oversized place in the Bond story and the wider cultural world.

“Fleming built GoldenEye as a place where he could write, and every James Bond novel was written here. Eighty years later, it remains the spiritual birthplace of Bond. To screen a film that looks so closely at Fleming himself, during GoldenEye’s 80th year, is very special,” said Chris Blackwell, Founder, and Marika Kessler, CEO, Island Outpost.

Adam Low, the film’s director, said he was “determined to put Jamaica at the centre of the story” with the project.

“Even the Bond books not set there are infused with the island’s atmosphere, landscape and history. By including Jamaican voices — from Fleming’s longtime gardener Ramsay Dacosta to novelist Marlon James as well as Minister Olivia ‘Babsy’ Grange whose relative Aunt Violet was Fleming’s house manager — the film shows how deeply Jamaica shaped Fleming’s imagination and the world of Bond,” Low said.

“As Minister Grange says in the film, ‘Jamaica is the star of the Bond films,’ and the documentary makes a compelling case that without Jamaica, there would be no James Bond,” said Low, underlining the Jamaican connection.

The perspective of the film deepens the premiere’s connection to GoldenEye by positioning Jamaica not simply as Fleming’s retreat, but as a defining creative force behind Bond’s settings, sensibility and mythology.

“By weaving together Jamaican voices, landscapes and history, the documentary underscores the island’s central place in both Fleming’s imagination and the continuing cultural life of 007,” said film editor Joanna Crickmay.

According to the release, the film’s opening sequence features a moving benediction in the Rastafari tradition by author, journalist and cultural liaison Barbara Blake-Hannah, while driving the vibrant streets through Oracabessa, St Mary, en route to GoldenEye with Desmond Dekker & The Aces’ legendary rocksteady and reggae track “007 (Shanty Town)” on play.

The premiere film weekend will bring guests from around the world to the place where Fleming’s daily writing ritual helped launch the Bond phenomenon, the release stated, adding that the programme includes a screening at PlayScape, a cocktail party at the GoldenEye villa with a Jamaican jazz band, a classic Jamaican BBQ on Button Beach with members of the film’s crew and Ian Fleming-themed morning breakfasts: scrambled eggs, toast, guava jelly, local fruits and Blue Mountain coffee.

Together, the events offer guests a rare opportunity to experience the film in the setting most closely associated with Fleming’s creative life, according to the press release.

World.title: Stronger schools
World.content:
Education Minster Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon walks with students of Maud McLeod High School in Westmoreland where she filmed her back-to-school message to the nation.

After a school year battered by Hurricane Melissa, particularly in western Jamaica, but capped by improved results in the country’s major examinations, Education Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon is looking to the new school year with optimism, pointing to increased investment, and stronger infrastructure as Jamaica pushes to transform its education system.

The scale of the challenge facing schools remains stark.

According to Morris Dixon’s back-to-school message, more than 688 schools were damaged by Melissa, 313 of them severely, while almost $26 billion is being spent on repairs and reconstruction. As she has repeatedly done in the past few weeks she acknowledged, however, that the work is not advancing as quickly as the Government would like.

Still, she said preparations were being made to get schools open, including contingency arrangements for institutions where repairs have not yet been completed.

“Thanks to the excellent work of our principals, boards, and the ministry team, we are working to have all schools open tomorrow. I have to thank all who have worked so hard over the summer and who have put in place contingency plans to support reopening even where repairs are not completed,” she said.

For Morris Dixon, however, rebuilding after Melissa is only part of the task.

The Government is entering the new school year with more than $835 million in operational support for schools, representing an average 55 per cent increase in funding. The minister said all schools received the first tranche of the increased funding in June, ahead of the reopening.

More than $1 billion is also being invested in educational resources, including workbooks, readers, textbooks, e-books, virtual learning solutions, and supplementary materials.

The increased spending comes against the backdrop of what Morris Dixon described as a strong finish to the last academic year, despite the disruption caused by the Category 5 storm.

“Despite the historic, once-in- a- 100-year devastation caused by the passage of Hurricane Melissa, we ended the last academic year with improved results across our major exams — PEP, CSEC and CAPE. Jamaica’s children did so well despite so much being thrown at them!” she said.

The minister is now betting on that resilience, alongside new investments, to drive further gains. In her speech she reminded the country of plans already in place.

Among the biggest initiatives is a $400-million investment in technical and vocational education at high schools. Technical high schools are to receive state-of-the-art laboratories in areas including autonomous robotics, renewable energy, virtual welding, electrical engineering, industrial controls, and optoelectronics.

The Government is also retooling science laboratories, while more than 150 satellite systems have been distributed to schools to improve Internet access, with additional devices being procured, particularly for rural institutions.

Morris Dixon said the hurricane recovery programme is similarly being used as an opportunity to improve schools beyond simply repairing the damage.

“Our Melissa reconstruction programme has not only presented an opportunity to make our schools more resilient, but it has also provided an opportunity to upgrade and renovate staffrooms for educators across Jamaica. The Staffroom Renovation Programme covers 74 institutions in the first phase, with work concentrated heavily in the parishes hardest hit by Melissa,” she said.

And while buildings, equipment and technology are central to the push, the minister also highlighted the needs of students outside the classroom.

More than 160,000 students are projected to benefit from the traditional cooked lunch programme, while another 69,000 students in the most challenged schools are expected to receive both breakfast and lunch. Meanwhile, 316 school cooks were trained and received range cook certification over the summer.

Psychosocial and psychological support, including trauma-informed services and Psychological First Aid, will also continue into the new academic year, after being intensified during the previous one.

Morris Dixon said the ambition extends beyond simply getting schools reopened and students back into classrooms.

“The ministry’s commitment is to continue transforming education so that every child, regardless of where they live or their circumstances, has a fair opportunity to learn, grow and succeed,” she said.

World.title: Far right’s rise in rapidly re-arming Germany gives Poland cause for concern
World.content:
“But we remember all too well where a rearmed Germany in the hands of a far-right, pro-Russian party can lead — and that is exactly what the AfD represents,” he added.

For Warsaw, the prospect of a far-right party gaining power in a heavily militarized Germany hits a deep historical nerve.

Parts of present-day Poland were occupied by Imperial Germany during World War I, and Nazi Germany invaded Poland in 1939, triggering World War II in Europe and subjecting the country to a brutal occupation.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk struck a similarly stark note after the Saxony-Anhalt vote, saying “only idiots or traitors” in Poland could celebrate the AfD’s triumph.

Merz pledged at the beginning of his term in 2025 to turn the Bundeswehr into “the strongest conventional army in Europe.” Germany also spent $114 billion on its military last year — almost as much as France and Poland combined — and Berlin is planning further increases.

As part of that wider rearmament drive, Germany is also planning for nearly €12 billion in long-range weapons capable of striking military targets hundreds or thousands of kilometers away, part of Berlin’s effort to deter Russia in the war against Ukraine.

World.title: La France plaide pour 60 milliards d’euros de nouvelles taxes européennes
World.content:
Certains craignent toujours qu’un accord budgétaire défavorable à la France ne profite au Rassemblement national, dont la candidate à la présidentielle, Marine Le Pen, est actuellement en tête dans les sondages et plaide pour réduire de moitié les contributions de Paris au budget de l’UE.

L’Irlande prépare une liste plus “light”

Lors d’une discussion à huis clos mardi, le représentant permanent de la France auprès de l’Union européenne (sorte d’ambassadeur tricolore auprès de Bruxelles), Philippe Léglise-Costa, a énoncé à ses collègues que les nouvelles taxes européennes devraient être de plus de 60 milliards d’euros — un seuil élevé pour la plupart des autres pays, selon des diplomates ayant une connaissance directe des discussions. Aucun des autres pays n’a précisé le montant qu’il souhaitait générer grâce à ces nouvelles taxes.

Si la plupart des gouvernements sont favorables à la mise en place de nouvelles ressources propres, ils émettent toutefois des réserves quant aux propositions concrètes qui sont sur la table.

La proposition de la Commission européenne, présentée en juillet 2025, prévoyait cinq nouvelles taxes qui pourraient générer jusqu’à 66 milliards d’euros de recettes supplémentaires. Mais ce plan s’est heurté à la résistance des Etats membres.

La présidence irlandaise du Conseil de l’UE, qui pilote les discussions sur le prochain cadre financier pluriannuel (CFP, l’appelation technique du budget à long terme de l’Union), a pour objectif de réduire la liste des ressources propres jugées acceptables par les pays européens lors d’un sommet des chefs d’Etat et de gouvernement qui se tiendra à Bruxelles le 15 octobre.

Lundi, Dublin s’est félicité du “consensus” atteint entre les gouvernements pour instaurer de nouvelles taxes visant les pollueurs étrangers — appelée mécanisme d’ajustement carbone aux frontières (MACF) — et les déchets électroniques. Celles-ci pourraient générer respectivement 1,64 milliard et 17,9 milliards d’euros par an en moyenne entre 2028 et 2034.

Au cours de la discussion de mardi, la Commission a laissé entrevoir la possibilité d’ajuster certaines propositions fiscales afin de générer davantage de recettes que ce qui était initialement prévu, relate l’un des diplomates.

Mais coup dur pour la France : d’autres propositions fiscales — visant les produits du tabac, le chiffre d’affaires des entreprises et les recettes issues du marché carbone (ou système d’échange de quotas d’émission) — se sont heurtées à l’opposition de plusieurs pays, d’après une note de l’Irlande consultée par POLITICO.

World.title: AI is helping gangs grow illicit tobacco networks, EU auditor warns
World.content:
It’s just one of the many challenges facing EU and member countries as they grapple to clamp down on illicit tobacco networks, which cause at least €13 billion in lost revenue in the bloc annually. In 2023, almost one in 10 cigarettes in Europe was illegally produced or smuggled in.

The report also lands as EU countries' attempts to find agreement on raising minimum tobacco and vape taxation levels have slowed after snus-loving Sweden — which is holding a general election next week — rebuffed a levy on nicotine pouches. The aim of the law is to harmonize prices across the bloc, strengthening the single market while nudging smokers to quit.

A lack of coordination and intelligence sharing between EU agencies and member countries’ authorities is hindering the bloc’s response to new cigarette factories, meaning “most alarmingly” the true size, structure and economic impact is unknown, Sarvamaa said.

To clamp down on this illegal activity, “it all starts with the Commission,” Sarvamaa said. “Better intelligence sharing between all relevant actors is essential.”

And the Commission needs to take a greater role in coordinating a strategic response of these actors, he added, including: the European Anti-Fraud Oﬃce OLAF, Europol, Eurojust and the European Public Prosecutor's Oﬃce, EPPO.

The Commission broadly accepted ECA’s recommendations, bar areas it said were beyond its role. It pushed back on defining strategies for the various EU authorities, noting that OLAF and others are responsible for setting their own strategic priorities. And it said it was not possible to provide a robust approach to assessing the size and economic impact of illicit trade, since no single method could do this.

“The union cannot afford to lose this fight,” Sarvamaa warned, saying that public health, safeguarding the integrity of the single market and preventing organized crime were all at risk.

But he stopped short of recommending how Europe should proceed with its overhaul of tobacco products and excise legislation, saying this was a role for policy and lawmakers.

World.title: Hungary expels 10 Russian diplomats amid espionage concerns
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar also said the diplomats “have committed unacceptable activities in Hungary.” Neither he nor Orbán specified the nature of their allegations. The Hungarian foreign ministry declined to make further comments.

The move “does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia,” Orbán said.

Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said Moscow’s response would be “harsh and painful,” according to Russian state news agency Interfax.

Magyar has sought to sever ties with Moscow since taking over from Viktor Orbán in May, a sharp shift from his predecessor’s coziness with the Kremlin.

In July, authorities opened an investigation into former Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó over allegations that he shared sensitive information with Russian officials.

In August, Magyar’s government said Russia was “a threat to Hungary, Europe and the global order” to Hungary, Europe and the global order” in its instructions to Hungary’s delegation to the U.N. General Assembly.

World.title: EU pursues closer Israel ties on air defense and space
World.content:
"It's very hard to do things on your own," Maman told POLITICO, warning that the militarization of space "is already happening — we just don't realize how much" and that Israel is seeing more interest from allies in "dual-use" technology for both civilian and defense purposes.

"One of the things we are working on is early warning systems," she said. "We saw that very nicely in the last round [of missile strikes] we had with Iran, for example. How we are managing to get [warnings to] all the civilians in Israel and not have that many casualties. That's part of that system. We are working on that very wide look that you're able to warn in advance, have that system warn the citizens."

A string of recent deals have seen the EU pursue closer military and technological relations with Israel, after several years of effective disengagement as a result of political tensions that have followed the war in Gaza. However, competition from Washington and strategic rivalries with Moscow and Beijing have created a need for allies with advanced industrial capabilities.

In 2024, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen backed calls from Polish and Greek Prime Ministers Donald Tusk and Kyriakos Mitsotakis to create an EU-funded air defense shield.

However, three senior officials involved in the discussions told POLITICO the plans did not move ahead after the Commission and a handful of capitals concluded it would need to rely on Israeli air-defense technology, which they deemed too sensitive a year into the Gaza conflict.

Now though, in a major expansion of its operations in Europe, Israeli firm Rafael Advanced Defense Systems confirmed Monday that it will open a factory producing its Iron Dome air-defense system in a former Volkswagen factory in Germany. One week ago, Greece struck a €3 billion deal with Israel’s Defense Ministry to build a new multilayered air defense network designed to take down drones, hostile jets and rockets.

World.title: France and Canada join UK in issuing trade sanctions on Israeli settlements
World.content:
The U.K., France and Canada are among 12 countries which issued a joint statement Tuesday warning the Israeli government’s actions in the West Bank are threatening the two-state solution.

Miliband told MPs the British government “agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank,” adding that “all too often the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this.”

He said the U.K. will take action against specific companies and individuals who provide services such as construction, infrastructure, financing, or real estate for settlement expansion.

U.K. sanctions legislation will take between six and nine months to implement, meaning the effects will not be felt immediately.

Britain will “act in concert with others in a broad international coalition,” he said, adding that France and Canada will also ban the import of goods from illegal settlements.

Confirming France’s involvement in a post on X, the country’s foreign affairs minister Jean-Noël Barrot said: “France cannot, through its trade, support a situation that threatens the security of both Israelis and Palestinians.”

World.title: France calls for new EU taxes to raise €60B
World.content:
There are lingering concerns that a bad budget deal for France could boost the far-right National Rally, which is ahead in the polls and has campaigned to halve Paris’ contributions to the EU budget.

During a closed-door discussion on Tuesday, France’s ambassador to the EU, Philippe Léglise-Costa, told colleagues that new EU-wide levies should generate over €60 billion — a high threshold for most other countries, according to the diplomats, who have direct knowledge of the talks. None of the other countries specified how much money they want to generate through the new taxes.

While most governments support introducing new own resources, they have misgivings about the specific ideas on the table.

The European Commission’s proposal from last July envisaged five new levies that would generate up to €66 billion in extra revenue. But the package has been met with resistance from national governments.

The Irish Council presidency, which is steering discussions on the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), aims to narrow down the number of own resources that are acceptable for EU countries during a leaders’ summit in Brussels on Oct. 15.

Dublin on Monday hailed “consensus” among governments to introduce new levies on foreign polluters, known as the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), and electronic waste that could respectively generate €1.64 billion and €17.9 billion per year on average from 2028 to 2034.

During Tuesday's discussion, the Commission opened the door to tweaking some of the tax proposals to generate more revenue than initially foreseen, one of the diplomats said.

But in a significant blow for France, other tax proposals — targeting tobacco products, corporate turnover and revenues from the Emissions Trading Scheme — have faced opposition from several countries, according to a note from Ireland seen by POLITICO.

World.title: Ursula von der Leyen condemns ‘shocking’ Ratko Mladić funeral in Serbia
World.content:
Mladić was the commander of the Bosnian Serb Army during the 1992-95 Bosnian War and was found responsible for the Srebrenica genocide, in which more than 8,000 Bosniak Muslim men and boys were killed in July 1995.

The Serbian government said that it had no hand in organizing the funeral, however Mladić’s body was flown to Serbia on a government plane and his coffin was escorted by members of the Serbian Armed Forces.

“The elements of official support and the presence of some senior Serbian officials at the funeral are deeply regrettable,” von der Leyen said, adding that “they demonstrate a failure to confront a dark chapter in Europe’s recent history.”

“The images from Ratko Mladić’s funeral yesterday in Belgrade were shocking,” wrote European Council President António Costa. “Ratko Mladić was a convicted war criminal. He was responsible for genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity.”

The EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas struck an similarly hard line, calling the public glorification of Mladić “an affront to the memory of the victims” and warning that “true reconciliation cannot be built on revisionism, the denial of genocide or the honouring of perpetrators.”

Serbia, which is an EU candidate country, has not opened a new negotiating chapter with the bloc since December 2021. The process is blocked by eight member countries over its rule-of-law record and its refusal to sanction Russia for its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

This story has been updated with comments from Kaja Kallas. Milena Wälde contributed to this report.

World.title: Technical glitch leads to more than 1,000 flight cancellations across UK
World.content:
Passengers travelling to and from the UK on Tuesday faced severe disruption after a technical glitch affected air traffic control systems.

 

More than 1,000 flights have been cancelled so far, according to flight-tracking website Flightradar24, with the issue impacting airports including London Heathrow, London Gatwick, Manchester, and Birmingham.

Air traffic control operator NATS said earlier that it had identified a "technical issue" with its flight processing system and that its engineers were on site and working on a solution.

"Our system issue is now resolved, we are operating normally and working as hard as possible to clear the backlog of flights," NATS later said in a post on social media, while also apologising for the disruption.

The incident has also hit flights at Dublin, London Luton, London Stansted, Liverpool, and Edinburgh airports, among others.

Flight disruptions are likely to continue throughout the rest of Tuesday, airports say.

In a statement on Tuesday evening, Manchester airport said it expected a full flight schedule to operate on Wednesday but warned that the airport may be busier than usual as flights were rescheduled.

Airports are advising passengers to check with their airlines before travelling.

Writing on X, British Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said she was "pleased" NATS had remedied the problem and thanked all those "working to get people moving."

"It will take time to fully resume flights, so continue to check with airlines," she wrote, adding: "I am seeking assurances that lessons will be learned and systems that support aviation are up to the job."

World.title: Israeli TV series 'Fauda' returns to Netflix with new season set during aftermath of 7 October attacks
World.content:
Israeli TV show Fauda returned to Netflix on Tuesday with its fifth season.

 

In its early seasons, the series sought to portray human stories on both sides of the Israel-Palestine conflict.

The show's newest iteration, created by Avi Issacharoff and Lior Raz, takes place two years after the 7 October 2023 attacks by militant group Hamas on southern Israel.

It follows the story of Doron Kavillio, a commander of an undercover Israeli military unit hunting down a Hamas operative he thought he had killed.

Doron also heads to France's Marseille after discovering that an old friend has gone rogue on an unsanctioned revenge mission.

In this Thursday, May 30, 2019 photo, an actor waits for his scene on the set of Israel's hit TV show "Fauda," in Tel Aviv, Israel. AP Photo/Oded Balilty

Raz, who plays Doron, told Netflix's official companion site Tudum that season 5 was “not about trying to show what happened."

“It was about trying to tell a story, to see how we can implant our characters inside those situations and in that story that really happened," Raz said.

"So for us, it was important to be very accurate to what happened in real life, but also to put our characters into this unpredictable situation".

Raz added that he hoped viewers would understand "how peace is important, and how we need to think differently and how war is ruining the universe."

"It’s ruining our region, it’s ruining our country, and their countries, for sure. We know that people see this show all over the world — in the Arab world, in Israel — [and they’ll see] that the price of the war is hard, and we need to have hope to solve this situation," he said.

Hamas' 7 October attacks on Israel killed around 1,200 people, while another 251 were taken hostage into the Gaza Strip.

In response, Israel began an air campaign against Gaza, while also launching a ground invasion of the territory.

Israel's offensive has resulted in the deaths of more than 73,600 Palestinians in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run Gaza Health Ministry. The United Nations considers the ministry's figures reliable, and Israeli officials have since stated that the numbers are broadly accurate.

World.title: 'Turning blind eye' to AfD win further angers voters, political scientist warns
World.content:
Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his coalition government's response to the historic victory of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in the Saxony-Anhalt state election will be pivotal in deciding the future of the federal government, political scientist Nicolas Spohn told Euronews.

 

Final results following last Sunday's election in the eastern German state showed AfD received 43.8% of the vote, more than double its showing five years ago in the region of 2.1 million people. Merz's party, the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), slumped to 17.2%.

"First of all, it really is a historic victory for the AfD, and it is an earthquake for the rest of the parties," Spohn, an expert on East German state politics, said.

The pro-Kremlin, anti-immigration party's win marks the first time ​a far-right party is within reach of power at the state level since WWII.

Questions have been raised about what this means for national politics in Germany. Thorsten Frei, the leader of the CDU in Germany's federal parliament, or Bundestag, denied that the result suffered by the CDU in Saxony-Anhalt would have consequences on the national level.

"But this is what frustrates people," Spohn said, adding that "turning a blind eye to the warnings of elections like in Saxony-Anhalt could give the AfD more votes."

Voter discontent

Failure to deliver on promises made ahead of the 2025 elections — notably his vow to revive Germany’s stagnant economy — saw Merz's popularity sink. A recent YouGov poll showed just 16% of Germans have a favourable opinion of Merz.

"The election here shows that the CDU must, on the national level, correct their political course," the political scientist explained. "A lot of people are frustrated with the work of the CDU. They promised different things than what they achieved after the elections. The economy is doing worse than before the last election on the national level."

He recognised that some factors are not under the control of the CDU, such as the ongoing wars in Ukraine and Iran. "These are issues that Chancellor Merz can't do a lot about, but still, Germans feel this economically."

This discontent is particularly visible in Saxony-Anhalt, where Merz's popularity sank to just over 9%. Spohn believes this was more of a decisive factor in the election than support for the AfD's policies was.

"It is not genuine support for the AfD's agenda, but rather for the [idea associated with the party] of doing everything differently."

Saxony-Anhalt, whose territory was formerly part of the German Democratic Republic (East Germany), has experienced the largest population decline of any German state over the past 35 years, losing a quarter of its inhabitants since German reunification in 1990. This is particularly visible in rural areas and among young people, who bear the brunt through teacher shortages and poor career prospects.

"What I'm trying to say is that 40% of the voters do not vote for the AfD because of its far-right policies, but rather despite such policies. People in eastern Germany are not more right-wing; they are simply more frustrated."

The party now has strong momentum heading into regional elections in Berlin and another eastern German state, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, in just under two weeks. The AfD is leading in voter intent polls in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, with about 35%.

To turn the tide, Spohn argued, Merz's CDU party will have to provide a positive outlook for voters. "At the moment, we don't have this positive vision, and the AfD is the only party giving voters some kind of positive outlook, which was, 'everything is possible'. So, everything can also be different."

World.title: Ceuta President urges the EU to take firm action against Morocco, as the city is 'on the brink of collapse'
World.content:
Ceuta’s president, Juan Jesús Vivas, has accused Morocco of a “policy of harassment” towards the city and urged the EU to take a tougher stance and fund border security after some 80,000 migrants entered the exclave on 30 July, distancing himself from Spain’s cooperative approach to Rabat.

 

Vivas met three EU commissioners and several lawmakers in Brussels on Tuesday, urging help to return irregular migrants and restore normality in the exclave, where thousands of third-country nationals, including unaccompanied minors, remain. "Ceuta is on the brink of collapse," he said.

The Ceuta leader broke with the national government, accusing Pedro Sánchez’s administration of failing to respond adequately before, during and after the July incident, which left more than 150 people dead at sea.

“The EU should tell Morocco that any fruitful and mutually beneficial cooperation begins by respecting our borders,” he said at a press conference at the European Parliament, where EPP lawmakers and staff greeted him with applause.

Spain has not blamed Morocco for the Ceuta incident, despite calling it a violation of its territorial integrity.

Instead, Madrid has pointed to false claims on social media and human traffickers as the main drivers of the mass influx, while continuing to describe Rabat as a “trusted partner” in tackling irregular migration — a position echoed by the European Commission.

“The government should explain why it refuses to hold Morocco responsible, whether directly or through inaction, for the invasion,” Vivas said, after being asked about a leaked police report suggesting Moroccan forces played a role in the crisis.

He claimed that Rabat maintains a “policy of harassment” towards the city and that his fellow citizens now live in fear that a sudden major influx could happen again.

Vivas stopped short of calling for the suspension of EU funds to Morocco, a request made in recent days by Spain’s far-right party Vox. The EU is currently financing Rabat’s migration management strategy with €160 million until 2027.

In his talks with the Commissioners, he also asked for financial support to build border infrastructure and manage the humanitarian crisis that erupted after the mass influx.

According to Vivas, EU Commissioners Andrius Kubilius, Magnus Brunner, and Dubravka Šuica expressed support for Ceuta, but the Commission made no specific commitments.

Brussels is now set to send a technical mission to Ceuta this week to "assess the situation", a Commission spokesperson said on Tuesday.

As Europe’s only land border with Africa, Ceuta, along with Melilla, should have a “special status," within the EU and migration rules adapted to their circumstances, Vivas said.

Another request is for a “permanent presence” in Ceuta of the EU asylum agency (EUAA) and Frontex, the agency responsible for the bloc’s external borders.

“The situation is untenable. We need EU support to restore normality. If Ceuta falls, Europe falls,” Vivas said.

World.title: UAE warned Netanyahu of 7 October attack, Israeli newspaper reports
World.content:
UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed allegedly warned Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that Hamas was planning a major offensive in Israel just days before the militant group launched its attack on 7 October 2023, Israeli daily newspaper Haaretz claimed on Tuesday.

 

Haaretz reported that at the end of September 2023 — 10 days before the attack — the UAE president spoke with Netanyahu for 45 minutes and said the leader of Hamas in Gaza at the time Yahya Sinwar was planning a major operation.

The newspaper reported that Bin Zayed told Netanyahu that the attack would lead to bloodshed and could destabilise the region and undermine the Abraham Accords, the normalisation agreements between Israel and several Arab and Muslim-majority nations.

The Haaretz report claims Netanyahu “reacted with relative calm” and assured bin Zayed that Israel was prepared for any scenario and a possible attack was more likely to come from the occupied West Bank.

Netanyahu's office called the report by the left-leaning newspaper "an absolute lie" and denied he spoke to the Emirati leader at that time.

The Haaretz newspaper based its report on a new book, “Kidnapped: 843 Days of Abandonment,” by journalists Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yuval in which they investigate the circumstances and intelligence failures of the 7 October attacks.

Election campaign heating up

The revelations come at a time when Israel’s election campaign is heating up for the vote next month, and Netanyahu’s actions around the time of the 7 October attack are a key issue in the campaign.

Israel’s opposition leaders immediately launched a series of scathing attacks on Netanyahu, culminating in a joint statement calling for an investigation.

“The Israeli public is entitled to know: What did Netanyahu know, when did he know, why he didn’t update the security establishment, and why he didn’t act to protect Israeli civilians?” the joint statement by Naftali Bennett, Gadi Eisenkot, Yair Golan and Avigdor Lieberman said.

“Netanyahu bears personal and direct responsibility for the failure that led to the deaths of thousands of Israelis on his watch," Bennett, who leads the B’Yachad party, said.

Eisenkot, a former chief of the General Staff of the Israel Defence Forces and a rival to Netanyahu in the upcoming legislative elections, had earlier said the Israeli leader "received dozens of warnings for 7 October and ignored them all."

"He is unfit for office," he added in a post on X.

In a video address, Golan, the leader of the Democrats party, also accused Netanyahu of "endangering Israel" and "leading us to disaster."

"You knew, you ignored, you failed, you are to blame, Netanyahu. The excuses are over," he said.

Netanyahu's office denied the report's veracity on Tuesday evening.

"The press reports are false. No warning was given to the prime minister from the United Arab Emirates before 7 October," the office said in a statement, while adding it was possible the two countries exchanged messages through intelligence channels.

The UAE's foreign ministry said on Tuesday it would not comment on the Israeli media report.

In a statement, the ministry said "the UAE government does not comment on media stories or speculation."

"When necessary, all relevant intelligence has been and continues to be communicated between the relevant entities."

'Basic strategic failure'

Former Israeli government spokesperson Eylon Levy told Euronews that the 7 October attacks were a "strategic failure" on Israel's part.

"If this report is true, it's hard to say why he wouldn't pass that on, other than that he didn't think it was credible. And that's because Netanyahu was really convinced that Hamas was deterred," Levy said.

"It was a basic strategic failure to understand the nature of the enemy facing Israel, its true intentions and its real capabilities".

Israelis are due to head to the polls on 27 October for a national election to determine the 120-seat Knesset (parliament).

On election day, voters are asked to choose a political party and its list of candidates, rather than choosing individual candidates directly.

Asked about the Haaretz report's impact on Netanyahu's chances in the elections, Levy told Euronews that it was "too early" to rule him out, but that the vote would ultimately be about "responsibility for 7 October."

Netanyahu has so far rejected multiple calls for an official government inquiry into the events surrounding the 7 October attack following other accusations of his handling of the crisis.

During the surprise attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, Hamas-led militants killed some 1,200 people and took another 251 hostage, triggering the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza that ended in a US-brokered peace deal in October 2025.

Israel's offensive resulted in the deaths of more than 73,600 Palestinians in the Strip, according to the Hamas-run Gaza Health Ministry, whose figures do not distinguish civilians and combatants.

The United Nations considers the ministry's figures reliable, and Israeli officials have since stated that the numbers are broadly accurate.

Hundreds of Israelis, mostly soldiers, have been killed in continued fighting in wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

World.title: Laundry, backflips and panda suits: Humanoid robots take over IFA 2026
World.content:
IFA is all about technology and innovation, with companies from around the world presenting their visions for the future.

 

In 2026, many of those visions include humanoid robots, and companies brought plenty of them to Berlin.

Across the exhibition halls, visitors repeatedly came across robots walking, waving, interacting with crowds or demonstrating individual tasks, with some being presented to European audiences for the first time.

"Alongside artificial intelligence, robotics is one of the key future topics at IFA 2026," Leif Lindner, CEO of IFA Management GmbH, said. He pointed to humanoids, physical AI and robotic systems for the home as examples of how quickly the technology is developing.

But beyond simply showing that robots can walk, talk or wave, companies are increasingly trying to demonstrate what they could actually be used for. With the trade fair drawing to a close, Euronews gathered some of the robotic highlights from this year's IFA.

Practical applications

Perhaps the most ambitious vision came from South Korean electronics company LG, which presented its idea of a "Zero Labor Home".

At the centre of its IFA presentation was CLOiD, LG's home robot, which the company used as the symbolic conductor of an "AI Orchestra" connecting appliances, entertainment systems and other devices across the home.

LG says its longer-term goal is to reduce the amount of household work people have to do, with robots and connected appliances taking over more everyday tasks.

Chinese home appliance and consumer electronics company Haier also focused on how robotics could be used around the home. At IFA, the company presented humanoid robots designed to interact with people and appliances, alongside cleaning and companion robots.

Another example came from US-based SwitchBot, which demonstrated a robot loading clothes into a washing machine.

US-based SwitchBot demonstrated a robot loading clothes into a washing machine. Euronews

The robot was able to pick up clothes, place them inside the machine and close it, showing one possible use for humanoid robots in the home. But the process was noticeably slow. So while the robot could take the laundry off your hands, for now, you would need plenty of patience.

Chinese company Pudu Robotics, meanwhile, is looking more towards commercial applications. The company has so far focused largely on service and cleaning robots, which it says are used in sectors including hospitality, retail, healthcare and logistics. At IFA, it also presented its PUDU D7 humanoid robot.

At its booth, the robot demonstrated relatively simple interactions. It could pick up objects on request, pose for pictures with visitors, take selfies from its own perspective and form a heart shape with its hands.

Such demonstrations remain a long way from robots independently, and quickly, handling complex everyday tasks. But they do offer an indication of where manufacturers see potential uses for humanoid robots beyond the exhibition floor.

Companions

But not every company is trying to make robots look or behave like humans. Some are moving away from the humanoid form altogether, developing smaller, often animal-inspired robots designed less as household helpers and more as companions.

Chinese electronics manufacturer TCL presented AiMe, an AI companion robot designed to interact with people and respond to voices, expressions and emotional cues.

The company says it can interact with users through conversations, games and storytelling, while remembering previous interactions over time. It can also be personalised and, with its rounded design and soft-looking appearance, resembles something closer to a teddy bear than a conventional robot.

A similar idea comes from Chinese company OlloBot with its OlloNi SS1, which it describes as a "Cyber Pet". The company says the small robot can learn from a user's voice, habits and interactions over time and adapt its responses accordingly.

OlloBot describes its OlloNi SS1 as a "Cyber Pet". Euronews

Its appearance also deliberately moves away from the traditional image of a robot. With a rounded body and movements designed to mimic those of a pet, the SS1 is intended to feel more like a companion than a piece of technology.

Other manufacturers stuck more closely to companions people are already familiar with, taking inspiration from the animal world. MagicLab Robotics brought several humanoids to Berlin dressed in panda costumes, although their skills were less typical of their real-life counterparts, with the robots repeatedly performing backflips.

In fact, entertainment and spectacle were difficult to separate from the more practical ambitions surrounding humanoid robots at IFA.

Many companies used dancing, acrobatics and interactions with visitors to demonstrate what their machines could already do, even if those skills may not have an obvious place in everyday life.

Robots on stage

Nowhere was that more apparent than at IFA's Robot Show.

Humanoid robots and robotic pets came together on the runway to dance, perform Tai Chi, do backflips and even the splits.

Judging by the crowds, it was one of the most popular attractions at the trade fair. The area was packed with visitors, with cheers and applause accompanying the robots as they performed.

Humanoid robots and robotic pets came together on the runway to show their skills. Euronews

But the show also provided a reminder of how far the technology still has to go.

Some of the robots appeared noticeably unsteady after their performances. One that had just completed the splits looked particularly shaky when getting back onto its feet, while a robotic dog fell over during another demonstration.

The robots certainly managed to entertain the crowd. But for now, at least, they may not quite be ready for the big stage.

World.title: Growth nearing 1% of GDP and higher revenues: what it means for the 2027 Budget Law
World.content:
The Italian economy could grow more than expected in 2026, approaching 1% of GDP.

 

That is the assessment of Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti, who on the closing day of the Teha Cernobbio Forum said that Italian GDP would exceed the 0.6% growth indicated in the government’s planning documents.

"For now we have secured 0.8%," the minister explained, adding that if the indicators continue to be favourable, "growth could come close to 1%."

For Pietro Reichlin, economist and professor at LUISS University, interviewed by Euronews, this is a "realistic estimate", but still not a result that allows us to speak of a turning point for the Italian economy. Growth remains held back by structural problems, from low productivity to unfavourable demographic trends.

It is not yet a new official government forecast, but the figure is significant because it comes on the eve of the drafting of the 2027 Budget Law and is accompanied by another positive signal for the public finances: rising tax revenues.

More growth, higher tax revenues

In the first seven months of 2026 the state recorded tax revenues of €346.1 billion, €9.4 billion more than in the same period of 2025, an increase of 2.8%, according to the bulletin (source in Italian) from the Finance Department of the Ministry of Economy and Finance (MEF).

"As GDP increases, revenues increase," the economist explains, a trend "accompanied by positive employment data". Higher employment and wages mean a broader tax base and therefore, under normal conditions, more income tax.

According to MEF estimates, between January and July 2026 direct taxes amounted to €200.7 billion (+€6.175 billion, or +3.2%) and indirect taxes totalled €145.5 billion (+€3.182 billion, or +2.2%).

Tax revenues up, January–July 2026

Among the various items, personal income tax (Irpef) revenues came to €138.5 billion (+€3.7 billion, or +2.7%). VAT revenues totalled €100.3 billion (+€3.6 billion, or +3.8%).

Excise duties on energy products in the period January–July stood at €12.7 billion (-€1.2 billion, or -8.5%); in July alone they amounted to €2.2 billion, down 3% on July 2025, also as a result of temporary reductions introduced to limit the impact of higher energy prices.

Why Italy is still lagging behind other EU countries

Reichlin warns that "we should not celebrate the growth figure too much".

Looking at the international picture, he notes that the improvement is "fairly widespread" across the European Union, but that Italy "remains at the tail end, together with Germany and France".

"Growth, for example in Spain, is higher than ours," Reichlin says, stressing that the Italian figure is not "so brilliant", especially if we take into account the support provided by investment financed under the Pnrr.

According to the researcher, at the root of Italy’s backwardness there is a historical factor that dates back to the late 1990s: very low productivity. A feature shared with other peripheral EU countries.

In Reichlin’s view, part of Spain’s stronger growth is also linked to the large inflow of migrants, which has helped drive employment, a phenomenon common in southern European countries and one that also benefits Italy. But, the economist warns, employment growth "is not strong enough to allow us to offset" the problem of low productivity.

"So more work, more workers, but with little added value," he explains.

Without tackling this underlying issue, the professor argues, we cannot expect a corresponding increase in wages and a rise in prosperity.

What will change in the 2027 Budget Law

The higher revenues recorded in the first seven months of the year cannot automatically be regarded as resources available for next year’s Budget Law.

It will be necessary to determine how much of the increase in revenue is structural and can therefore be used to finance new measures in subsequent years.

If revenues perform better than expected, the economist warns that "we must not harbour illusions" regarding the 2027 budget. "To keep the public accounts in order, exit inflation and keep the deficit under control" or "to increase spending or adopt costly measures" revenues alone are not enough.

According to the professor, it will be a "very cautious budget law, because there is very little room for manoeuvre".

Besides productivity, growth is also undermined by the fact that "demographic trends are very unfavourable", he explains.

Italy is experiencing an ageing population and falling birth rates, and "this weighs on the public finances through the pension system, and also on the health service", causing public spending to rise naturally.

Reichlin concludes by saying that even if Italy managed to reduce the tax burden "especially on labour and businesses, as international organisations advise us", this would have a positive effect, but one major issue would remain unresolved. These measures would in fact have to be "offset by other sources of revenue, and it is not clear where these could come from".

World.title: Turkey seeks Black Sea shipping deal as attacks threaten grain trade
World.content:
Turkey is racing to restore safe passage for cargo ships in the Black Sea as attacks on shipping disrupt grain exports and push up prices. Russia and Ukraine are major global wheat exporters, but Black Sea trade has been severely disrupted as both sides step up attacks on shipping and port infrastructure.

Advertising

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan announced this week that Turkey was working on a plan to ensure safe passage in the Black Sea for commercial shipping and said he was in touch with both Ukraine and Russia.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan confirmed that he raised the issue with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, on the sidelines of a gathering of regional leaders in Kyrgyzstan.

The Turkish move comes as Ukraine and Russia have ramped up their attacks on shipping and ports in and around the Black Sea. In 2022, Turkey and the United Nations brokered a deal between Ukraine and Russia to ensure safe passage for Ukrainian grain exports through the Black Sea.

The agreement lasted a year.

While Turkey has maintained good ties with both sides, reaching another agreement will be much harder, warned international relations professor Huseyin Bagci of Ankara’s Middle East Technical University.

“The tension is increasing more than ever before,” Bagci said. “It's not enough to have good relations, because the two sides – the Ukrainians and Russians – should sit down and talk about a common solution to this problem. Turkey cannot solve this problem alone.”

What the SDF’s dissolution means for Syria’s Kurds and neighbouring Turkey

Growing attacks

In August Ukraine offered a ceasefire on commercial shipping, but the offer was rejected by Moscow, which said it wanted a broader deal. Ukrainian drones continue to strike Russian shipping, while Russia has continued missile attacks on Ukrainian ports and ships.

This surge in attacks comes as both nations rush to export their grain harvests.

Grain prices have risen sharply, by as much as 30 percent, international grain broker Can Atbasoglu said, even as both sides scramble to find new routes for their exports.

“Russia will do their best to export as much as they can, both from Russian Baltic ports and EU Baltic ports like Latvia and Lithuania; they're also exporting,” Atbasoglu said.

“Ukraine will also export as much as they can from Romania as well and through the Danube ports. But the export pace will be definitely lower. So it will definitely stay bullish for the markets. Prices are definitely going to stay like this or can have a further increase.”

Fears of wheat price surge amid Ukraine-Russia clashes in the Black Sea

Ships staying put

At one of Istanbul's many shipyards, the docks are crowded with ships that once braved the Black Sea. One vessel bears the scars of a drone attack and is under repair. Others undergo routine maintenance as shipowners hesitate to risk new journeys into dangerous waters.

The superintendent of one ship, speaking anonymously, says repairs are nearly finished, but uncertainty clouds the future.

“We wanted to take the ship out to the Black Sea before entering the shipyard, but because of that risk, we didn’t enter the Black Sea and didn’t take on any cargo. We’ve been in the shipyard for 50 days for repairs, but we don’t know what will happen once the repairs are finished,” the superintendent said.

Turkish shipowners warn that many are on the brink of bankruptcy, as idle ships rack up costs of up to 50,000 euros a month in mooring and crew expenses.

Ziya Ustel, CEO of Turkish shipping company VI-ZA STAR, says high freight rates are being offered for Black Sea routes, but the risks are too great.

“They are offering high freight rates, etc,” Ustel said.

Without a diplomatic solution, few shipowners will be prepared to risk their vessels, Ustel warned.

“The main thing is to find out a real solution,” Ustel added. “Otherwise, no one will try anything anymore.”

Turkish diplomacy

Ankara is expected to step up its efforts to find a solution.

Grain brokers say hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough may be one reason prices have so far remained below the record highs seen at the start of the war.

But if Turkish efforts fail and attacks on Black Sea shipping continue, higher grain prices could have a considerable impact, especially on the world’s poorest nations, many of which depend on Russian and Ukrainian grain.

World.title: German economy frets about Saxony-Anhalt election results
World.content:
The AfD won the election in the eastern German state by a wide margin. While politicians and election analysts are still debating the reasons for the far-right party's popularity, economists are sounding the alarm.

The results came in as predicted: The AfD, which is considered far-right extremist in parts, won the election in Saxony-Anhalt and could now put forward the state’s minister-president and take over the state government.

What hardly anyone expected, however, was this: The governing CDU is now barely half as strong as it was, while the other parties have been left far behind. Calling it a landslide victory for the AfD is no exaggeration. And many commentators go so far as to call it a turning point in Germany’s postwar history.

Keep calm and carry on?

"A state government led by the AfD would certainly be seen by many as a turning point and would further fuel the debate over how best to deal with the party," Commerzbank economist Ralph Solveen told Reuters.

At the same time, he advises waiting to see what happens, saying that things are rarely as bad as they seem.

"Many of these decisions are unlikely to affect the economy until the medium to long term," he said. "Decisions on most taxes, the structure of the labor market and social security systems are made at the federal level. That is why the AfD, in many of its pledges, only promises to advocate for something in the Bundesrat, which is unlikely to succeed given the foreseeable isolation of an AfD-led government."

What next after far-right AfD win in regional election? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Local political pragmatism?

Many business community concerns had already been raised before the election. It also became clear that there are differing views within the AfD, which could lead to unpredictable policies.

For example, DW reported two months ago that Hannes Loth, a member of the AfD and the mayor in Raguhn-Jessnitz, Saxony-Anhalt, sought to have six new wind turbines installed. This pledge puts him at odds with the official stance of his own party.

Whether this is a sign of internal party pluralism or simply local political pragmatism will become clear during the coming legislative term, especially if the AfD ends up in the state government. It is not, however, serving to reassure business leaders.

Consequences of xenophobia

One issue the AfD campaigned on was a promise to limit the number of foreigners. But will the party actually be able to implement its goal? On this point, Michael Berlemann, director of the Hamburg Institute of International Economics (HWWI), remains skeptical.

"A large part of the measures it has promised cannot be implemented at the state level because the federal government is responsible for them," he said. "Another part would be illegal and would be overturned by the courts after some delay: The AfD cannot restrict the immigration of foreign skilled workers in Saxony-Anhalt."

ING chief economist Carsten Brzeski pointed to the national shortage of skilled workers: "Forced deportations in Saxony-Anhalt would probably be limited. However, the symbolic effect cannot be underestimated. As with Trump, such headlines would act as a deterrent for foreign skilled workers."

Wido Geis-Thöne, an economist at the German Economic Institute in Cologne, sees it the same way.

He told DW that the AfD would "do everything in its power to pursue its migration policy goals." However, it could only "do things that actually fall under the responsibility of the state rather than the federal government."

Economic fallout for Saxony-Anhalt

Geis-Thöne said the state itself would be the main victim of such a policy: "With an anti-immigration state government, Saxony-Anhalt will become significantly less attractive a destination for foreign skilled workers, regardless of whether anything actually changes for them from a legal perspective."

For HWWI Director Berlemann, the indirect impacts of the AfD's plans are particularly problematic. The measures announced would mean "that many skilled workers who are particularly needed in health care and nursing, hospitality and tourism, the food industry and agriculture and in construction and logistics will avoid the state in the future."

This would exacerbate the shortage of skilled workers and widen the state's economic gap.

Openness and diversity are key

Saxony-Anhalt must remain a state where people from around the world want to live and work and where companies want to invest and new technologies can emerge, Bitkom President Ralf Wintergerst warned.

He told the Catholic News Agency KNA: "The digital economy thrives on openness, diversity and international cooperation. Companies invest where they find good conditions and where skilled workers from Germany and abroad are welcomed."

Regarding foreign investment, ING Chief Economist Carsten Brzeski told Reuters: "Sure, there could be a symbolic effect on foreign investors. But let's not forget: Saxony-Anhalt is not the entire German economy."

What the AfD's Saxony-Anhalt win means for Germany To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How should Berlin react

DIW President Marcel Fratzscher painted a bleak picture of the economic future after the Saxony-Anhalt election.

"Regardless of the makeup of the next state government, a controversial or weak government and the polarization during the election campaign are likely to accelerate the departure of people and companies from Saxony-Anhalt, thereby significantly worsening conditions in the state," he said.

He told Reuters that the election result was "above all a vote of no confidence in the federal government." The consequence, he added, must be "that the federal government changes course and implements far-reaching structural reforms involving subsidies, bureaucracy, taxes, the social security system and Europe."

Tanja Gönner, managing director of the Federation of German Industries (BDI), took a similar perspective. Following the state election, she called on the federal government to be single-minded in pursuing a reform agenda.

"The response to this state election result must not be political paralysis at the federal level," she said.

The federal government must now consistently implement and expand reforms to boost investment, innovation and growth, she told RedaktionsNetzwerk Deutschland, adding that "the positions of radical parties are not suitable for this."

The political center must now show that it is capable of taking action, BDI's managing director said, adding that what is needed is a policy focused on competitiveness and growth at both the state and federal levels. A single state election result must not distract from that goal, she concluded.



This article was originally published in German.

World.title: EU, UK express dismay over Mladic funeral in Serbia
World.content:
The EU is deliberating an official response to the glorification of war criminal Ratko Mladic in Belgrade. The UK, meanwhile, summoned Serbia's charge d'affaires over the display.

Both the EU and UK on Tuesday expressed dismay over the funeral in Belgrade, Serbia of late war criminal Ratko Mladic a day prior.

Thousands of people, including at least six Serbian ministers, attended the event on Monday which was seen as glorifying Mladic. He received military honors at the funeral, with the head of Serbia's Orthodox Church presiding over the ceremony.

The Bosnian Serb commander died last month at The Hague, where he had been imprisoned for life. Mladic was convicted in 2017 of genocide, having orchestrated the July 1995 Srebrenica massacre, where 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed.

Mladic, called the "Butcher of Bosnia" by some international press, is a revered as a war hero by many Serbian nationalists in both Serbia and Bosnia.

EU leader call Mladic state funeral 'deeply regrettable'

EU leaders condemned the funeral, with the bloc weighing an official response to the event.

"The elements of official support and the presence of some senior Serbian officials at the funeral are deeply regrettable," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa said in statements posted on X.

"They demonstrate a failure to confront a dark chapter in Europe's recent history and contradict the values underpinning Serbia's path towards the European Union," they added.

A European Commission spokeperson, in comments to German news agency DPA, said next steps were being evaluated.

EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas added: "Serbia's path into the European Union requires an unequivocal commitment in fundamental European values and historical truth."

Serbia first applied for EU membership in 2009. Serbia's EU candidacy was confirmed by the European Council in 2012.

Serbia: Thousands attend 'Butcher of Bosnia' funeral To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

UK summons Serbian envoy

The UK, meanwhile, summoned Serbia's charge d'affaires in response to the funeral.

"As a military commander, Mladic presided over crimes that are among the worst committed in Europe since the Second World War," the British Foreign Office said in a statement.

"The thoughts of the UK Government are with Mladic's victims and their families. They deserve respect, compassion and accountability, not efforts to rewrite proven history," the statement added.

The UK said that the "glorification of a convicted war criminal directly undermines trust, fuels division, and is incompatible with the process of reconciliation within Bosnia and Herzegovina and the region."

Bosnia expels Serbian diplomats, says Belgrade crossed 'red line'

In its reaction to the funeral, neighboring Bosnia expelled two Serbian diplomats, saying Serbia crossed a "red line" in its display of reverence for Mladic.

"They crossed every red line with what they did yesterday, the day before, and in the days leading up to the reception," Bosnian Foreign Minister Elmedin Konakovic told a Sarajevo press event.

Konakovic had also said he would withdraw most staff from the Bosnian Embassy in Belgrade in an effort to reduce ties to "the lowest possible level"

Serbian President Aleksander Vucic was not present at Mladic's funeral, although his son Danilo, did attend the event. Vucic rejected allegations that Mladic was being glorified at the funeral and said the event was put together by Mladic's family rather than the state.

Can Serbia's student movement turn protest into power? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The controversial funeral comes ahead of snap elections next month. Serbia has faced a political crisis in the past two years triggered by the collapse of a concrete canopy at a railway station in Novi Sad.

World.title: Fifty years after Mao’s death, China has transformed. DW looks at why his political legacy still matters.
World.content:
Mao Zedong was perhaps the most influential, and certainly one of the most controversial, figures in 20th-century China. Even five decades after his death, the legacy of his era continues to influence China today.

On September 9, 1976, Mao Zedong died. The revolutionary leader who led the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) to power and founded the People's Republic of China left behind a profoundly contradictory historical legacy.

He shaped the narratives of revolution, nation-building and national independence, but also left behind immense social trauma as a result of successive political campaigns and persecutions.

50 years of transformation: How far has China moved away from Mao?

Over the past five decades, China has undergone radical changes.

When Mao died, China was still a poor and relatively isolated communist state. Today, it is the world's second-largest economy, deeply embedded in the supply and value chains of global capitalism, with a vast private sector, a large urban middle class and a highly digitalized society.

Zhang Lun, a professor at Cergy-Paris University, said Mao left behind four major political legacies: the authoritarian and highly centralized political system; a model of governance that relies on revolution and political campaigns to solve social problems; populist tendencies marked by anti-elitism and anti-rationalism; and utopian visions of egalitarianism and moralism.

From the perspective of political legacies, Zhang told DW, the most fundamental change in China over the past five decades has been "de-Maoization" — while its greatest challenge has been that this process was never fully completed.

Mao's insistence on the CCP's supremacy is still a fundamental principle in China today Image: akg-images/picture alliance

The legacy that never left: the party's supremacy

Mao's name remains written into the CCP's constitution, while his thought remains part of China's official ideology and his portrait still hangs in Beijing's Tiananmen Square.

Mao helped forge the Chinese Communist Party, and his insistence on the party's supremacy over the state and society has remained a fundamental principle throughout the decades, said Jean Christopher Mittelstaedt, professor at the University of Zurich.

Veteran journalist and political commentator Chang Ping agrees, adding that what has truly endured is the institutional core of the principle that "the party leads everything," serving a state vision of being able to "concentrate resources to accomplish major tasks."

The CCP, he said, can pursue such objectives "at all costs" — meaning the interests of ordinary people can be sacrificed to the maximum extent necessary to preserve the regime.

A return to the 'Mao era?'

Under current leader Xi Jinping, a number of political concepts and methods of governance associated with the Mao era — such as ideological unity and the spirit of "struggle" — have again attracted attention.

Xi's actions such as abolishing the presidential term limits, strengthening his personal authority and the incorporation of his political thought into the party and state constitutions have invited comparisons between him and Mao.

Chang argues that the very term "return" is misleading, since elements of the Mao era have never fully disappeared.

Zhang holds a similar view.

Authoritarian rule, political rigidity, weak rule of law and the lack of effective guarantees for citizens' rights, he argues, are not only important elements of Mao's political legacy but also among the most significant continuities between the Mao era and China's current political system, he underscored.

And Xi, who personally suffered during the Cultural Revolution, seems even move closer to Mao-era policies.

"What Xi learned from the Cultural Revolution was not the lesson of a victim, but the lesson of power," Chang told DW.

The lesson was not that "such a system must never exist again," but rather that "whoever loses power is at the mercy of others," he added.

Felix Wemheuer, professor of modern China studies at the University of Cologne, echoed this view.

"The conclusion Xi appears to have drawn from his own experience of the Cultural Revolution was clearly not that Mao should be completely abandoned," he told DW, "but rather that, for political reasons, Mao's historical status as the founder of the state, the military and the party must be upheld."

Wemheuer views the current CCP leadership's approach to Mao as "fundamentally Machiavellian and pragmatic."

In economic policy, for instance, there is no sign of a return to the Mao era, he said. Today's China operates a highly dynamic model of state capitalism, with a mix of ownership forms coexisting and maintaining a strong private sector. Nor is there any indication that China intends to return to the Mao-era model of a communist welfare state.

The same applies to the idea of "self-reliance." Today's China could hardly afford to withdraw from the global economy and international supply chains.

Trump, Putin or Xi: Who really runs the world? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Xi remains a product of the system Mao created

Experts say similarities between Mao and Xi can be seen in areas such as the emphasis on the CCP's supremacy, the elevation of a core leader, and populist elements that stress a close connection between the people and the leadership.

Wemheuer argues that Xi possesses neither Mao's historical authority nor his personal charisma.

The two also exercise power in fundamentally different ways. Mao could bypass party institutions, go for years without convening a party congress and mobilize the masses against the party and state apparatus.

Mao himself was a populist with certain anarchic tendencies, Wemheuer said, and even tolerated the temporary collapse of the party-state system at the grassroots level in 1966-67.

Xi, by contrast, would never allow such a situation to occur, the expert stressed. Xi places greater emphasis than Mao on control and top-down governance, consolidating power by strengthening institutions and the party apparatus.

Mittelstaedt likewise cautions against equating Xi with Mao.

First, Mao was a revolutionary who destroyed existing institutions during the Cultural Revolution and was fundamentally anti-bureaucratic in his political orientation. Xi, Mittelstaedt argues, does the opposite.

Second, Mao stood above the party. His power came from "being Mao himself" rather than from the party's institutional structures.

Xi, by contrast, is "a party man through and through." His authority derives from party institutions, and he governs through those institutions, Mittelstaedt pointed out.

"At the end of the day," he told DW, "Xi Jinping remains a product of the system Mao created."

Mao nostalgia among younger generations?

China has also seen recurring waves of Mao nostalgia, with some Chinese citizens invoking Mao online and expressing longing for what they describe as an era without social inequality, when everyone supposedly had enough to eat.

Chang argues that what they are longing for is neither Mao himself nor the real Mao era.

The actual Mao era, Mittelstaedt said, was marked by rigid hierarchies, pointing to the urban-rural household registration divide, different levels of privileges and supplies for officials, and a system in which one's family background could determine one's fate. It was, in many respects, more unequal than China today — and voicing grievances could be fatal.

The imagined vision of a more equal world, he underlined, is therefore actually an indictment of the present situation, with widening inequality, soaring housing prices and persistently limited social mobility.

Still, many express the dissatisfaction with contemporary reality through Mao's image and language.

In Chang's view, this is connected to the continuing contraction of space for public criticism in China. When forms of political expression such as independent trade unions, street protests, free media and opposition parties are tightly restricted, Mao remains a historical symbol that official ideology cannot entirely exclude.

The result is a striking irony, he said, pointing to some people invoking Mao's language of anti-bureaucracy, resistance to oppression and even "rebellion" to criticize what they see as corruption, inequality and abuses of power in Xi's China today.

Mittelstaedt said this makes Mao a double-edged sword. He remains an important symbol of the CCP's political legitimacy — but parts of the revolutionary language he left behind can also be turned into standards by which contemporary reality is measured and criticized.
