World.title: Penélope Cruz, sobre Javier Bardem en Venecia: “Tenemos un buen equilibrio entre lo personal y lo profesional”
World.content:
Los dos actores presentan en el festival ‘Búnker’, de Florian Zeller, en la que encarnan a un matrimonio que entra en crisis tras aceptar el marido, arquitecto, un polémico encargo

Ante una sala de prensa abarrotada, Penélope Cruz y Javier Bardem defendieron este martes en Venecia su nuevo trabajo juntos, Búnker, del francés Florian Zeller. La película gira alrededor del dilema de un arquitecto de éxito español afincado en Londres (Bardem), que recibe el encargo de construir un búnker de lujo para un tecnooligarca y cómo la posibilidad de ese encargo erosiona la relación con su pareja (Cruz), una editora que no acaba de encajar en el ecosistema inglés. El conflicto con un vecino por una ventana en la medianera de su lujosa casa londinense cierra el círculo de un guion que habla de la paranoia de los ricos y la desconexión social, “del búnker invisible en el que nos estamos metiendo”, añadió Zeller en el encuentro.

Más información Javier Bardem y Penélope Cruz, una historia de amor de cine

Los dos intérpretes españoles hablaron en el Lido junto a sus compañeros de reparto: Stephen Graham, que da vida a ese vecino víctima de la gentrificación; Paul Dano, en la piel del tecnooligarca; y Patrick Schwarzenegger, en la de un escritor del catálogo del personaje de Cruz. En el centro de la conferencia estuvieron en todo momento Bardem y Cruz quienes, según explicaron, aceptaron hacer una nueva película como pareja de ficción por todos los temas de actualidad que Zeller toca en el guion de Búnker. “Nos convenció la calidad del material”, dijo Bardem. “Florian es un gran escritor de teatro y cine y la historia que trata afecta a parejas, hermanos e hijos. Y además lo hace transmitiendo esperanza”.

Javier Bardem, este martes en Venecia. Scott A Garfitt (AP Photo/Scott A Garfitt)

Florian Zeller explicó por qué escribió el guion pensando en la pareja y qué quería de ellos en una película que muestra las fricciones de un matrimonio que gira más alrededor del trabajo de él que el de ella. “Pensé en ellos porque son dos de los grandes y, para ser honesto, porque al tenerlos juntos en pantalla interpretando a una pareja le da un valor único a la película por todas las capas de realidad y ficción que aportan. Me interesaba llegar a esa autenticidad desnuda que solo poseen los intérpretes que son como ellos, ambiciosos y sin miedo”.

Sobre cómo les afecta en su intimidad trabajar juntos y qué pusieron de su propia vida en la pantalla, Bardem dijo: “Somos buenos creando realidad y creando ficción, de otra manera no seríamos capaces de sobrevivir en esta profesión”. Por su parte, Penélope Cruz añadió que para ella es un proceso muy natural y más cuando confían en la mediación del director. “Nosotros amamos nuestra profesión y tenemos un buen equilibrio con lo personal. Cuando conocimos a Florian, en la primera reunión con él, sentimos que nos iba a proteger. Fue importante sentir que no iba a entrar en nuestra intimidad, aunque a la vez toda nuestra experiencia vital está en esos personajes. Tenerle en medio era muy relevante para sentirnos a salvo, sobre todo en las secuencias más emocionales, que pueden llevarte a un lugar engañoso. Sin invadirnos nunca, Florian estuvo muy cerca y eso fue muy bonito vivirlo”.

Penélope Cruz, ante los fotógrafos en Venecia. Scott A Garfitt (AP Photo/Scott A Garfitt)

En Búnker Cruz y Bardem hablan en inglés con sus vecinos, colegas y amigos y en español entre ellos. “Eso era impensable hace unos años”, señaló la actriz española. “Hace diez o quince años nadie hubiese financiado proyectos multiculturales como este. Nosotros hemos tenido que hacer de colombianos en inglés, y por fortuna eso cada vez ocurre menos y hoy las películas hablan muchos idiomas”.

En ese sentido, y ante una pregunta sobre la carrera internacional de La bola negra, en la que Cruz tiene un importante papel secundario, y El ser querido, protagonizada por Bardem, el actor celebró el buen momento de la industria. “El cine español siempre ha tenido mucha calidad y este año es un ejemplo más”, dijo. “Aunque es una maravilla y hay que celebrar la victoria de que el cine español viaje y viaje tan bien, que se recibe con tanto gusto y respeto”.

Penélope Cruz, Florian Zeller y Javier Bardem, en la presentación ante la prensa de 'Búnker'. Scott A Garfitt (AP Photo/Scott A Garfitt)

Sobre el tema central de la película, el miedo y la paranoia como arma de desconexión humana, los dos intérpretes coincidieron en su necesidad de alzar la voz. Cruz apuntó: “Para mí era importante hablar a través de mi personaje de la manipulación en la que vivimos, del riesgo de perder la conexión humana. Nos tratan como marionetas y, pese a ser algo obvio, no reaccionamos. Y me da pena y rabia. Yo soy una persona optimista; sin embargo, veo todo esto como algo muy oscuro y preocupante. Lo único que me salva es observar a la gente joven. Les veo reaccionar, hablan más de política que antes y veo que se empiezan a dar cuenta de la falta de empatía en la que vivimos”.

Nos tratan como marionetas y, pese a ser algo obvio, no reaccionamos. Y me da pena y rabia” Penélope Cruz

Para Florian Zeller, la idea de la construcción del búnker de lujo funciona en la película como una metáfora sobre un aislamiento que afecta a todo el mundo. “El punto de partida de esta película fue el miedo. Leí la historia de un tecnomillonario muy famoso que se estaba construyendo un secreto búnker en Hawái. Me pareció una paradoja que un hombre que presumía de haberse hecho rico conectando a la gente a la vez se construyera un búnker para aislarse de todo el mundo. Creo que hemos abrazado un estilo de vida que es una ilusión creada por otros, una ilusión que nadie se cuestiona. Ya nadie quiere explorar el resto del mundo y eso nos conduce a ese otro búnker invisible del que también habla la película”.

Bardem y Cruz, en Venecia. Yves Herman (REUTERS)

A la pregunta de si los artistas tienen un compromiso con la sociedad, Bardem respondió: “Como artistas tenemos la responsabilidad de hacer que las historias de los directores ocurran, pero como individuos tenemos otra responsabilidad, que es la misma que tiene un taxista o un fontanero. Y es ser fieles a nuestra verdad. Yo tengo la suerte de tener un altavoz y lo aprovecho”.

World.title: Los pantalones ‘barrel’ de Zara y el “motín” de las mujeres perimenopáusicas: “¿Sería mucho pedir existir?”
World.content:
He aquí la breve historia de la nueva silueta que está en todas partes y el debate que ha despertado en las redes sociales

Zara es un poco como la Coca Cola, todo el mundo conoce la marca, pero nadie más tiene su fórmula. La que sí ha dado en una de las teclas de Zara (al menos en la de ciertas clientas) ha sido la psicóloga afincada en Zaragoza Pilar Cebrián, gracias a un vídeo cómico que publicó en su perfil de Instagram en los últimos días de agosto: “Querida Marta Ortega, tenemos que hablar”, comenzaba.

“Estoy en un punto de mi vida en el que Zara y yo hemos tomado caminos diferentes. Y yo me pregunto, Marta, ¿por qué? ¿Por qué los pantalones barrel?”. Pilar se refiere a esos pantalones “que no quedan bien a las mujeres que [hemos pasado de los 40]”, un diseño que desde hace unos meses inunda la colección de la marca de Inditex (y de todas las demás cadenas de moda asequible, para ser más precisos). “Mujeres perimenopáusicas!! Levantémonos en armas!! Fuimos las primeras en comprar en sus tiendas y en lucir sus prendas! Y ahora vamos a permitir que nos dejen en la cuneta de la moda de Inditex?”, bromeaba en el pie del vídeo.

Historia de los barrel

Primero, una cuestión de nomenclatura. El pantalón balloon fit o barrel fit debe su nombre a la forma de su pernera, que recrea la de un barril o un globo. Al vestirlo, dibuja una silueta ovalada: gana volumen en la zona del muslo, se curva hacia fuera y vuelve a estrecharse en el tobillo.

Su origen está salpicado de referencias. Algunos sitúan sus primeros antecedentes en los uniformes de trabajo franceses de los años 20 y 30, que incorporaban pantalones amplios y estructuras cónicas. Otros los relacionan con los pantalones de los vaqueros de principios del siglo XX, cuya silueta abombada tendría que ver con la posición de las piernas al montar a caballo. Y hay quien sitúa su salto definitivo a la moda en los años 80, de la mano de la cultura hip-hop y el streetwear, cuando las prendas amplias y con movimiento se convirtieron en parte esencial de la estética urbana.

El vaquero de tipo 'barrel', un modelo muy popular en las marcas 'fast fashion'. Moritz Scholz (Getty Images)

Lo que sí sabemos es que la silueta no nació ayer y que su actual reinado tiene bastante que ver con el cansancio colectivo de los skinny. Tras años de pantalones pegados al cuerpo, y al calor de la “nueva comodidad” que llegó tras la pandemia, la moda empezó a ensanchar las perneras: primero llegaron los rectos, después los wide leg, los baggy y, finalmente, esos pantalones que tienen a internet dividido.

Uno de los modelos que contribuyó a popularizar esta silueta fue el Horseshoe de Citizens of Humanity, lanzado en 2021. Sus perneras anchas y curvas, con el bajo ligeramente cónico y corto, resultaron demasiado vanguardistas para muchos consumidores en un primer momento. En redes sociales hubo risas, burlas y referencias a los Looney Tunes. Pero la resistencia fue durando lo que suele durar cuando hablamos de tendencias de moda: hasta que este corte de pantalón dejó de parecer extraño. Y así, el Horseshoe pasó de ser una rareza a convertirse en un modelo de culto de la firma.

Un salto en el tiempo nos lleva hasta aquí: con los barrel ocupando escaparates y catálogos y con la industria de la moda explicándonos que, en realidad, son unos pantalones muy democráticos. Que se ajustan en la cintura, dejan espacio en la cadera y el muslo y se estrechan en el tobillo. Que no ciñen. Que no restringen. Que funcionan para distintos tipos de cuerpo. La teoría es estupenda. La práctica, por lo visto, tiene sus matices.

Invisibles más allá de los 40

Lo que pudo ser una publicación entre tantas acabó convirtiéndose en una pequeña “trama” viral (con giro de guion incluido: tras una serie de críticas muy encendidas, Pilar se grabó probándose unos que, para su sorpresa, al final le quedaban bien) y abriendo un debate entre los miles de comentarios que despertó el tema. Muchos de ellos eran mujeres alrededor de los 40 que siempre consumieron ropa de Zara y que hoy, para su disgusto, no encuentran prendas que se adecúen a sus cuerpos en esta etapa.

Porque quizá el problema no sea exactamente que los barrel sienten mal. Quizá sea que, cuando una mujer llega a los 40, empieza a preguntarse si la ropa que lleva toda la vida comprando sigue estando pensada para ella.

Algo parecido comentó días después, en su perfil de Instagram, Ana Santamarina, experta en dermocosmética y creadora de su marca homónima de cuidado de la piel. “Tengo 48 años y no me siento representada en ninguna de las marcas que yo consumo. Somos casi 50 millones de personas en España y seis de cada diez tiene más de 35 años. Y no solo eso: más de la mitad de las personas que trabajan y están afiliadas a la Seguridad Social tienen más de 45 años. Trabajamos, consumimos, compramos ropa, accesorios, perfume, maquillaje, skincare, de todo… pero somos invisibles. ¿Sería mucho pedir existir en el imaginario de las marcas?”. Y proponía a sus seguidores fijarse en las tiendas de los centros comerciales a ver si alguna de las modelos de los anuncios y escaparates tiene más de 25 años.

La pregunta resulta especialmente pertinente si tenemos en cuenta que las mujeres empiezan a desaparecer de la imagen pública justo cuando empiezan a tener más poder adquisitivo, más criterio y, probablemente, menos paciencia para que le digan qué debería ponerse.

No es que la moda no haya intentado corregirlo. Zara, de hecho, fue noticia precisamente por hacer algo bastante poco habitual en 2017. Aquel año lanzó Timeless, un editorial protagonizado por Malgosia Bela, de 40 años; Yasmin Warsame, de 41; y Kristina de Coninck, de 53. Las tres hablaban, además, del paso del tiempo y de cómo se sentían con respecto a envejecer.

Fue un gesto celebrado porque rompía con la imagen habitual de las modelos veinteañeras que pueblan los e-commerce de moda. Y Zara no fue la primera: Celine había convertido a Joan Didion en una de sus musas, Mango había contado con Lyn Slater, de 63 años, y Desigual había recurrido a mujeres de edades muy superiores a las que solemos ver en una campaña de moda.

El problema es que una campaña puntual no necesariamente cambia el imaginario de una marca y quizá por eso el pequeño motín de los barrel resulta más interesante de lo que parece. Porque no estamos hablando solamente de unos vaqueros difíciles. Estamos hablando de una generación de mujeres que ha crecido comprando en las mismas tiendas que sus hijas y que, de pronto, siente que las prendas ya no están diseñadas para el cuerpo que tiene. El cuerpo cambia, pero la moda parece seguir dibujando el mismo cuerpo de siempre.

En resumen, las mujeres mayores de 40 están pidiendo espacio en el escaparate. Y, ya puestos, en los pantalones.

World.title: Far-right broadcaster ON switched off over licensing breaches
World.content:
Culture minister Rianne Letschert has confirmed that she intends to take far-right broadcaster Ongehoord Nederland off the airwaves after the media regulator asked her to withdraw its licence.

Letschert said the decision was the “most serious means at my disposal” and followed a series of breaches of broadcasting rules since ON started showing programmes on the Dutch public networks in 2022.

“There are clear rules for broadcasters that want to make programmes with public money,” the minister said. ”And if you repeatedly fail to abide by them, there comes a point where it has to stop.”

The breaking point was a panel discussion posted on ON’s YouTube channel in July that featured a clip from a speech by Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler in which he fulminated against the ”rootless international clique”, referring to the Jews.

Panellists, including editor-in-chief Joost Niemöller, agreed with a proposition that the “cosmopolitan elite” was “essentially hostile” to ordinary people, though they also rejected Hitler’s anti-Semitism.

Vlemmix called the decision a “very worrying day for Dutch public broadcasting” and said he would fight for “the interests of everyone who welcomes our views, but also public broadcasting and the views of the right in general.”

Regulator call

Letschert had previously rejected demands to take ON off the air, arguing that as a government minister she could not interfere in its editorial line.

Her legal position changed when the media regulator CvdM wrote to her last week telling her that ON was not fulfilling its obligations under Dutch broadcasting law.

The NPO, which is responsible for the three Dutch public TV channels, also asked the minister to intervene because ON was not prepared to work as a partner organisation.

The broadcasting ombudsman has reprimanded the channel several times for disseminating untrue information and mixing fact with opinion.

ON has also been fined twice in the last year by the media regulator, once for breaching conflict of interest rules and once for breaching its own editorial code.

Letschert said those three reasons were enough for her to pull ON’s licence, though the broadcaster will not be taken off the air immediately because it has the right to appeal against her decision.

Rules of freedom

“The Netherlands is a democratic state that observes the rule of law. That obliges us to take great care with the decisions we make,” she said. “Ongehoord Nederland will therefore have the opportunity to respond to my proposal and I will consider that response carefully before I make a final decision.

“A free public broadcasting system should have space for difference, debate and for views that clash and sometimes cause offence. But that freedom is only strong if everyone observes the rules that protect it.”

World.title: ASML begins building new 20,000-workplace Eindhoven campus
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Chip machinery maker ASML has begun building a second industrial campus in Eindhoven, with the first buildings due to open in 2029.

The site will be developed in phases and could eventually cover 350,000 square metres, with room for up to 20,000 workplaces, the company said.

Prime minister Rob Jetten attended a ceremony at the site on Tuesday at Brainport Industries Campus North, close to Eindhoven Airport and the A58 motorway.

The first phase will house at least 3,000 staff and combine production, logistics and offices in one location. Most of those posts will be filled by teams moving from ASML’s existing locations rather than new hires, and the company said later phases would depend on future demand for its machines.

Growing demand

“The growing global demand from the semiconductor industry requires continuous investments,” chief executive Christophe Fouquet said in a statement. “BIC North provides the space and flexibility we need to continue innovating and supporting our customers around the world.”

The new campus will include what ASML calls a “flow factory”, a production line for its chip lithography machines modelled on methods used in the car and aircraft industries.

Eindhoven city council approved the zoning plan for the site in March, after the government pledged €2.5 billion in 2024 for housing, roads, education and power grid upgrades in the region to persuade the company to expand in the Netherlands rather than abroad.

ASML’s headquarters are in nearby Veldhoven. In January it announced 1,700 job cuts, mostly in the Netherlands, despite a record year.

World.title: Mind the gap: how 30% ruling changes may affect your paycheck
World.content:
If you are one of those clever people who spent years studying abroad and is now contributing skills to the Dutch economy, there’s good and bad news.

Some economists in the Netherlands have raised alarm bells at the drop in highly-skilled migrants since the failed “hard right” government in 2023. The first international scientists have landed in the Netherlands as the result of a new “tulip” fund to support top thinkers.

But at the same time, the country is winding back a ruling to compensate some temporary highly-skilled workers for their costs, and it will in future be restricted to people with even higher salaries.

From next year, for new highly-skilled migrants and everyone who arrived after January 1, 2024, the 30% ruling for people with rare skills will be cut to 27%. This means that for five years, the first 27% of their salary will be paid untaxed – an incentive to make this high-tax country more attractive and compensate top international talent for costs such as expensive housing.

“This will make a difference of between €50 and €100 a month for most of the people we help,” said a tax adviser for Blue Umbrella. “One more dinner at home each month, perhaps, but it is still money.”

The tax break, which has strict conditions and must be applied for by the employer, will also only be valid for salaries from just over €50,000 from 2027, or for masters students under 30, earning from around € 38,000. This is a slight rise from the current levels.

It is also limited at the top end to what is known as the Balkenendenorm, the top salary for civil servants and quango employees – €262,000 this year. There are around 100,000 people nationally with the “expat” ruling for skills that cannot be found locally and most Blue Umbrella clients and internationals, of course, earn nothing like this amount.

“Typically, it’s around €60,000 to €80,000,” says the Blue Umbrella adviser, who points out that this may be a family’s single salary after an international move. “Every month, the expat ruling might save €500 on the usual tax rate. And they will lose an extra 3%.”

While there is sometimes criticism of highly-skilled migrants in Dutch media for living in local housing, Blue Umbrella points out that these people are vital for the economy.

“Fewer of them are coming to the Netherlands in general because the mood is one where we say: no migrants,” he said. “But we need highly-skilled migrants. Companies are closing in the games industry and IT specialists are going to other countries that try to attract them, like Portugal.”

The tax climate is less conducive to starting a business too, he added, meaning that entrepreneurs may be less likely to choose the Netherlands. But Blue Umbrella is hopeful that there will be a greater realisation that this small country is competing for global talent.

“We are a knowledge economy, we are known for technology and trading, and you need smart people,” he said. “There’s a battle going on around the world because other countries want them too. We are known for our schools and education, the cyber war is coming, and this should be a moment of change.”

Find out more about your personal tax situation and the 27% ruling by contacting Blue Umbrella.

World.title: IND pays out €99m in seven months for missing asylum deadlines
World.content:
The immigration service IND paid out around €99 million in court-ordered penalties in the first seven months of this year for failing to decide on residency and asylum applications on time, already exceeding the record €79 million it paid in the whole of 2025.

Asylum minister Bart van den Brink revealed the figures in a written response to requests from MPs.

The IND paid €36.8 million in penalties in 2024 and €79 million in 2025, when the average waiting time for an asylum decision reached 67 weeks. The 2026 total is running at about €14 million a month, against €6.6 million a month last year.

The answers also show the number of individual payments above €3,000 has risen from 858 in 2023 to 6,368 in 2025. By July 2 this year the IND had already made 5,442 such payments.

How the penalties work

The IND is required by law to decide on an application within six months. If it misses the deadline, the applicant can ask a court to set a new one, and the court can attach a daily penalty if that deadline is also missed.

Courts normally set the penalty at €100 a day up to a maximum of €15,000, rising to €250 a day and a €37,500 cap where a “strong incentive” is needed, according to the minister’s answers. Applicants can go back to court as often as they like for as long as no decision has been taken, so the totals in individual cases can build up over time.

Between the start of 2024 and May 11 this year, 143,190 people filed an appeal against a late decision, and 16,570 of them won two or more times, the minister said.

By July 29, courts had ordered the IND to pay a total of more than €80,000 to 46 individuals for failing to decide on their applications, and nine people received over €100,000.

Abolishing penalties

Boomsma, who submitted the questions, told the Telegraaf the system was “completely bankrupt”, with court rulings making decisions ever harder to reach and taxpayers then paying for the resulting delays.

The IND has called for the penalties to be scrapped, saying they do nothing to speed up decisions and that dealing with the court cases takes staff away from processing applications.

An amendment abolishing court-imposed penalties in immigration cases, tabled by the orthodox Protestant SGP and JA21, was passed by the lower house of parliament in June as part of a wider bill on the detention of foreign nationals. The bill is now before the senate, which rejected the previous asylum emergency measures law containing the same measure in April.

Van den Brink said no date has been set for the senate debate and he could not estimate how much more the IND would have to pay before any abolition took effect. He also declined to forecast the total for 2026.

A previous attempt to scrap the penalties was struck down by the Council of State in 2022 as a breach of EU law, and refugee organisation VluchtelingenWerk has told MPs it considers the new amendment unlawful on the same grounds.

World.title: Dutch children’s literacy falls further behind European average
World.content:
Nearly four in 10 Dutch children are at risk of leaving school with a low level of literacy, according to an international study that shows a steep decline in educational performance across Europe.

The Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), carried out every three years in more than 90 countries, shows the Netherlands has fallen behind the European average over the past decade.

Dutch children still outperform their peers in most European countries in maths and science, where the figures show a less pronounced downward trend. In science they have dropped to the average level for the 23 nations in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) used for long-term comparisons.

The figures, which compare educational performance in 91 countries altogether, show a general worldwide decline in literacy standards since 2015, but the picture is especially stark in the Netherlands.

Some 39% of 15-year-olds had a reading level deemed inadequate to function in society, up from 33% the last time the report was compiled in 2022.

The points score used to grade performance has fallen from 503 in 2015 to 441 last year, including an 18-point drop between 2022 and 2025.

Three years behind

A drop of 20 points is seen as the equivalent of falling a year behind in educational development, meaning today’s 15-year-olds are learning at the same level as 12-year-olds a decade ago.

The 14 European countries which took part in the study – 13 EU nations plus the UK – had an average score of 464, with Ireland and Latvia topping the table. Singapore topped the global rankings with 535, followed by China.

Researchers speculated last time that school closures during the pandemic might be responsible for the decline in performance, but the continuing trend since the end of lockdown has forced them to consider that they may have overestimated the impact.

The growing use of digital technology such as smartphones, social media and AI may also be holding back the development of children’s reading skills, the researchers say.

Digital media

In a paper published last year they said children’s performance in maths, sense of belonging at school and overall life satisfaction were lower if they spent more time on their smartphones and called for more support for families to manage digital leisure time out of school.

The figures for science show Dutch students’ performance fell by three points to 485, one point lower than the OECD average, while in maths the Netherlands is still above the average despite dropping 10 points to 483.

Junior education minister Judith Thielen promised earlier this year to come up with an action plan in the autumn to tackle low literacy.

“It is my ambition to stop the downward trend and turn it around,” she said. “I want to see better results in three years’ time.”

World.title: Rutte: coronavirus curfew and school closures were “unavoidable”
World.content:
Former prime minister Mark Rutte has defended the nationwide curfew imposed during the coronavirus lockdown, insisting it was “unavoidable”.

Giving evidence to the parliamentary inquiry into the government’s pandemic response, Rutte said there was “no alternative” to the drastic measure, which was in force for three months until the end of 2021.

Earlier witnesses including Hubert Bruls, the chair of the group of regional safety boards that were responsible for enforcing the lockdown rules, questioned whether the curfew was effective and said the government had failed to explain why it was necessary.

Riots broke out in several towns and cities during protests against the curfew, while in a poll by RTL this year 35% of people named it as the “most severe” of all the pandemic restrictions.

But Rutte said the curfew and other unpopular measures, such as shutting the schools, were essential to keep infections down and stop the health service reaching the “code black” crisis point.

He also defended the decision to close schools for a third time in December 2021 as the delta variant spread from the UK, after the education minister in his cabinet, Arie Slob, earlier said he was against the shutdown.

Delta variant

“The Delta variant meant that we had to take lockdown measures from October and November,” Rutte said.

“Then the Omicron variant appeared and all we knew was that it was highly infections. If it had been as debilitating as the Delta variant, code black would have been inevitable.”

Rutte also said he clashed with health minister Hugo de Jonge over vaccination policy. He was willing to set an example as prime minister by taking the jab, but it should be a matter of individual choice, while De Jonge believed the government should press people to take responsibility.

Rutte added that strict rules such as curfews would not have been needed if everyone had stuck to the basic rules announced at the start of the pandemic in March 2020.

“If everyone had said: I’ll keep to the one and a half metre rule, sneeze into my elbow, not shake hands and ventilate enough, then in theory we wouldn’t have had to take those measures,” he said.

World.title: Cabinet considers visa blocks for Russian athletes
World.content:
The Dutch cabinet will do everything it can to prevent athletes from competing under the Russian flag at international sporting events, including the upcoming 2030 winter games in Heerenveen, sports minister Mirjam Sterk has said.

She told De Telegraaf that the government is actively lobbying the International Olympic Committee to reverse its decision to readmit Russian athletes, which it made this summer, clearing the way for the 2028 summer games in Los Angeles.

Russians were suspended in 2023 after the Putin regime began using sports bodies from occupied Ukrainian territories.

The cabinet’s stance would have consequences for the 2030 winter games at Thialf in Heerenveen, which will be the first Olympic competition on Dutch soil since 1928.

Asked what would happen if Russian skaters qualified to race there, Sterk told the paper: “You would have to look at what that means for the visas.”

“The cabinet considers the participation of Russian and Belarusian athletes and teams under their own flag and national symbols at sporting events in the Netherlands undesirable and will do everything within its power to prevent it,” she said. “That applies to individual athletes, national teams and club teams from both countries.”

Pressure on IOC funding

The Netherlands is one of nine EU countries, led by Estonia, that asked the European Commission in July to cut the IOC and other federations that readmit Russia out of Erasmus+ and other EU funding programmes.

Sterk said the primary responsibility lies with the sports federations, but that the Netherlands is raising the issue with them directly. “Russia also uses this to make political statements,” she said.

D66 MP Hanneke van der Werf backed the minister but said the message should have been made “much more emphatically and more widely” at the time. “Sport is not separate from reality when a regime deliberately uses it for political ends,” she told the Telegraaf.

World.title: Culture minister to decide on future of far-right broadcaster ON
World.content:
Culture minister Rianne Letschert is under pressure to pull the plug on far-right broadcaster Ongehoord Nederland (ON) when she meets director-general Peter Vlemmix later on Tuesday.

The channel has been repeatedly criticised for breaching journalistic and ethical standards, most recently in an item that used footage of a speech by Adolf Hitler to introduce a discussion about the “cosmopolitan elite”.

Letschert initially said she was unable to intervene because the public broadcasting service NPO had not asked her to withdraw ON’s licence.

But last week the media regulator CvdM said in a letter to the minister that the broadcaster had failed to comply with its legal obligations, clearing the way for Letschert to take ON off the air.

More than two-thirds of MPs want the publicly funded channel to be removed in the wake of the latest controversy, including all three coalition parties D66, CDA and VVD, RTL Nieuws reported. Parliament is due to debate its future later this month.

ON’s editor-in-chief Joost Niemöller stepped down a week ago because of a ”difference of view about the editorial direction and recent programming”, according to a statement by Vlemmix.

Niemöller was one of the panellists on the show that sparked the row, after he said he agreed with “certain things of Hitler’s” but condemned the Nazi leader’s anti-Semitism.

Vlemmix has said the broadcaster will continue its “fight for survival” and accused the media regulator of overlooking improvements made over the past year.

World.title: Robots “protest” in Warsaw to demand regulation of AI and automation
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Around 30 robots protested outside Poland’s digital affairs ministry on Monday, calling for tougher regulation of artificial intelligence and robotisation. The human organisers say there needs to be greater public debate over the impact of new technologies on the labour market. Digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski met with the demonstrators, telling them that his department is working on regulations. However, one of the organisers said that plans currently being discussed by parliament contain insufficient protection for workers. Around 30 robots joined a protest in front of Poland’s digital affairs ministry, calling for stronger AI regulations. The demonstration was organised by campaigners to spark debate on how AI and robots could replace workers. pic.twitter.com/QEbvchb2RS — Al Jazeera English (@AJEnglish) September 7, 2026 Standing in several rows, the robots waved Polish flags and chanted slogans such as “We want regulations, we want rules, we want law” and “Don’t wait, regulate, protect jobs”. The organisers, a group called Democratism, said the event was intended to highlight the need for debate and legislation before automation has a more profound impact on employment. “Some people will benefit from new opportunities, while others may need to retrain or adapt to completely different roles,” they wrote. Society needs to discuss “who is responsible for preparing people for these changes, how workers should be protected during the transition and how reskilling should work”. Democratism appears to have been launched shortly before the protest, with the announcement about the demonstration among the first material published on its social media accounts. The initiative was launched by Delta Robots, a company that rents robots for events. However, a website they have set up to gather support for greater debate over the impact of AI and robotisation has so far only obtained signatures from 61 people. Grzegorz Kuliś of Delta Robots admitted to news website Gazeta.pl that their “campaign also has public relations value” for the company. However, he added that, “even though we’re deploying robots, we’re also humans, and we have a whole host of concerns that, if we don’t regulate this, we’ll soon find ourselves in an unprecedented situation that no human being will be able to cope with”. “We are constantly debating the impact of migrants on our society, whilst the vast majority of ‘migrants’ will arrive either via undersea cables across the Atlantic in the form of AI agents, or as humanoid robots in shipping containers from China,” he warned. Gawkowski, who went out to address the organisers, said the ministry’s objectives were aligned with the protesters’ concerns. “People come first, and that is what matters most to us,” he said, quoted by broadcaster Eska. The minister also announced plans to establish a committee on AI development and safety as well as to introduce so-called sandboxes, where companies will be able to test AI solutions before deploying them more widely, reports local news website O!Polska. Kuliś, however, told Gazeta.pl that a draft law on AI systems currently being considered by the Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament, contains too little practical protection for workers affected by automation. A Polish radio station that launched a channel run almost entirely by AI – including its presenters – has decided to end the project after less than a week The head of the station admitted they were "surprised by the level of emotion" the idea had caused https://t.co/9iMlRVamSF — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 28, 2024 The rapid development of AI and robotics has sparked debate around the world on how such technologies will impact humans, including to what extent and in what ways they will replace human labour. However, a number of recent reports have found that the impact of AI on jobs has so far been smaller than many previously predicted. Analysis by the Institute of Economic Policy Research at Stanford University, published in July, found that “AI’s effects on overall employment are likely small”. A further concern has been the prospect of AI “going rogue” by starting to act without or beyond human control. Those fears were strengthened after it emerged in July this year that some of OpenAI’s AI agents had autonomously hacked Hugging Face, another AI company. The incident prompted more than 100 companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Hugging Face, to sign an open letter calling on companies and governments to step up cybersecurity efforts amid emerging threats. A recent rise in unemployment in Poland has raised concern. But that headline figure does not tell the whole story, with experts arguing that the Polish labour market is actually in good shape, writes @AlicjaPtak4 https://t.co/Pk4y7BqGrs — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 24, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! The candidate of the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja), one of Poland’s main political groups, has been disqualified from Kraków’s mayoral election after over 2,000 of the signatures from local residents collected in support of his candidacy were found to be invalid. One of Confederation’s leaders, Sławomir Mentzen, admitted that the situation was an “embarrassment” and “catastrophe”. He responded by dismissing the candidate, Bartosz Bocheńczak, as head of his party’s local structures in Kraków and launching an investigation into how the blunder occurred. Podobnie jak i wielu naszych działaczy, wolontariuszy, sympatyków i wyborców, czuję się bardzo zawiedziony brakiem rejestracji kandydatury Bartosza Bocheńczaka w Krakowie. Przyczyną braku rejestracji było to, że spośród około 5000 zebranych podpisów, ponad 2000 były błędnych.… — Sławomir Mentzen (@SlawomirMentzen) September 7, 2026 Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, is holding a mayoral election this year after the previous incumbent, Aleksander Miszalski, was removed mid-term in a rare recall referendum earlier this year. Over a dozen potential candidates announced plans to stand. But, in order to be registered, they had to collect at least 3,000 signatures from residents of the city supporting their candidacy, then submit them to the municipal electoral commission by 3 September. Twelve candidates made such submissions, after which the commission began assessing all signatures to ensure that each candidate had at least 3,000 that were valid. On Monday, reports began to emerge that, although Bocheńczak had submitted just over 4,600 signatures, the commission had found that fewer than 3,000 of them were valid. That evening, the candidate himself confirmed the news. Mentzen, who is leader of the far-right libertarian New Hope (Nowa Nadzieja) party that makes up one half of Confederation, revealed that over 2,000 signatories had listed their address as their place of residence rather than where they are officially registered as living. In Poland, it is common for people to live somewhere different from where they are officially registered. That is particularly the case for young people, who are often registered at their parents’ address while residing elsewhere. Confederation is particularly popular among young people, and Kraków has a large student population. Moja kandydatura na Prezydenta Krakowa nie została zarejestrowana. Zabrakło ważnych podpisów. Nie będę snuł teorii spiskowych, szukał winnych ani przerzucał odpowiedzialności na kogokolwiek. Uważałem, że złożenie niemal 5000 podpisów zapewni nam wystarczający margines… — Bartosz Bocheńczak (@BBochenczak) September 7, 2026 Mentzen said that the regulations regarding collecting signatures for candidates are “absurd”, yet admitted that Bocheńczak’s campaign should have done a better job of complying with the rules. There must now be “consequences from this embarrassment”, said Mentzen, who announced that Bocheńczak had been dismissed as New Hope’s local leader in Kraków and that a party commission would “determine responsibility for this disaster”. Confederation also faced scrutiny last year when the National Electoral Commission (PKW) rejected its financial report for the 2024 European elections after it found irregularities. The party also failed to submit the required documents on time. As a result, it lost access to state subsidies. The Supreme Court has rejected an appeal by the far-right Confederation against the electoral commission's decision to reject its financial report for last year's European elections due to irregularities. The group will now lose access to state subsidies https://t.co/hNGu2Zvzii — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 14, 2025 Bocheńczak is not the only candidate who has struggled with collecting signatures. Last week, just days before the deadline, it emerged that over 3,000 signatures collected in support of the favourite in the elections, Łukasz Gibała, an independent, were invalid because the word “Kraków” was missing from the form. Gibała – a perennial candidate in mayoral elections who finished runner-up to Miszalski in 2024 – quickly scrambled to collect more signatures, and his team managed to gather an additional 9,000 in three days. On Monday this week, it also emerged that three other independent candidates, Marian Banaś, Stanisław Kułach and Marta Ratuszyńska, had failed to gather enough signatures. All three have taken up their right to appeal against the commission’s decision to reject their candidacies. Dziś złożymy dodatkowe podpisy do komisji wyborczej – ponad 9 tysięcy (oprócz wcześniejszych 5,5 tys.). Skala Waszego zaangażowania i pomocy była bezprecedensowa – w 3 dni zebraliśmy więcej podpisów niż którykolwiek z naszych rywali przez 3 tygodnie 💪 Bardzo Wam dziękuję i… — Łukasz Gibała (@LukaszGibala) September 3, 2026 Six candidates have so far been accepted, including Gibała; Monika Piątkowska, who is supported by the centrist Civil Coalition (KO) and Polish People’s Party (PSL); Michał Drewnicki of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS); Aleksandra Owca of the left-wing Together (Razem); and Michał Klimek of the radical-right Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP). Two candidates, Daria Gosek-Popiołek of The Left (Lewica) and Sławomir Pietrzyk of Social Democracy of Poland (Socjaldemokracja Polska), are still awaiting confirmation from the electoral commission that they submitted enough valid signatures. A decision is due to be announced today. The first round of the election will take place on Sunday 27 September. If any candidate receives over 50% of the vote, they will become mayor. If not, a run-off between the top two candidates will take place on 11 October. There has been little polling on support for candidates, but one survey by the Opinia24 agency for Polityka Insight two weeks ago showed Gibała with 25.2%, ahead of Piątkowska (15.3%) and Gosek-Popiołek (8.7%). Bocheńczak was in sixth with just 3.2%. Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. Poland wants the European Union to deny the right to asylum for migrants who cross EU borders in organised, aggressive groups, just as Poland has itself done on its border with Belarus. “This is about depriving people who illegally cross the border in organised groups, using violence or destroying border security measures, of the right to international protection,” Maciej Duszczyk, the deputy interior minister who oversees migration policy, told broadcaster RMF. Polska zabiega o to, by Unia Europejska przyjęła jej interpretację przepisów dotyczących ochrony międzynarodowej. „Chodzi o pozbawienie prawa do ochrony międzynarodowej osób, które nielegalnie przekraczają granicę w zorganizowanych grupach, z użyciem przemocy albo niszcząc… — Fakty RMF FM (@RMF24pl) September 6, 2026 The station reports that, at a meeting of the European Council next month, Poland will propose expanding the interpretation of article 33 of the United Nations’ Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees. That section outlines the principle of “refoulement”, under which states are barred from expelling or returning refugees to places where their life or freedom would be threatened. The article includes a clause saying that the principle does not apply if “there are reasonable grounds for regarding [a refugee] as a danger to the security of the country” in which they have arrived, or if they have a criminal conviction that makes them “a danger to the community of that country”. Poland wants that clause to be applied in situations where someone applies for asylum after being part of an organised and aggressive border crossing. Since last year, Poland has itself banned asylum claims from people who illegally cross the border from Belarus. Since 2021, the Belarusian authorities have encouraged and assisted tens of thousands of migrants, mainly from Asia and Africa, to try to irregularly – and often aggressively – enter the EU. Poland’s asylum ban, which has exceptions for certain vulnerable categories of people, was introduced as a temporary measure in March 2025 but has been repeatedly renewed since then. Warsaw now wants a similar interpretation of international refugee law to be applied across the EU Its proposals come in the wake of July’s incident in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta, where tens of thousands of migrants irregularly entered from Morocco. Soon afterwards, Poland urged the EU to adopt tougher measures, including making migrants who enter the bloc illegally ineligible for obtaining residence rights. Prime Minister Donald Tusk was also one of 22 EU leaders who signed a letter expressing “serious concern” at the situation in Ceuta and warning that the EU “cannot allow uncontrolled mass border crossings, the instrumentalisation of migration, or other hybrid threats to create the impression that illegal entry…is possible”. After last week's migration crisis in Ceuta, Poland has called for tougher EU measures, including an automatic ban on residence for anyone who enters illegally. It pointed to its own experience of dealing with "weaponised" migration from Belarus https://t.co/2VHn5ZUJx7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 5, 2026 Poland has long argued that the situation on the Belarus border is an example of how migration has been “weaponised” by Russia and its allies to sow social discord in EU countries. In response, Poland has invested billions in strengthening physical and electronic barriers along the border, has deployed thousands of additional officers there (and granted them expanded rights to use firearms), and has banned asylum claims. In 2021, Poland recorded almost 40,000 attempted illegal crossings from Belarus, and the figure remained as high as 30,000 in 2025. However, in the first half of this year, only 235 attempted crossings were recorded, which the Polish government has hailed as evidence of the success of its tough measures. However, Poland’s human rights commission recently raised concern at how long the technically “temporary” asylum ban has been in place. Some Polish courts have also ruled that Polish border guards acted unlawfully when forcing migrants back into Belarus. The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98% Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Has Karol Nawrocki’s first year as Poland’s president been a success?
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Aleks Szczerbiak Poland’s right-wing president has been largely successful at transforming his office into an assertive centre of resistance to the liberal centrist-led government, frustrating its agenda through extensive use of constitutional powers. He has emerged as the leading unifying figure on the fragmented Polish right but faces new challenges moving towards the next election. Scuppering the government’s reform agenda Last month, Polish President Karol Nawrocki marked the first anniversary of his inauguration following a surprise victory in the May-June 2025 presidential election over Warsaw mayor Rafał Trzaskowski, the candidate of the liberal-centrist Civic Coalition (KO), Poland’s main governing party since autumn 2023, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. A relatively unknown conservative historian and head of the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), a state historical research institute, Nawrocki ran formally as an independent but was backed by the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and currently the main opposition grouping. The election result represented a significant upset, ushering in a period of tense “cohabitation” between the Tusk government and a hostile president. The Polish presidency is not a day-to-day governing role, and in many respects largely ceremonial, but retains important constitutional powers. Karol Nawrocki has now issued more vetoes than any other president in Polish history Three vetoes on Thursday took his total to 37 in just ten months since taking office, surpassing the 35 issued by Aleksander Kwaśniewski during his ten years as president https://t.co/xf27K8Fyn6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 12, 2026 These include a legislative veto, which the government lacks the required three-fifths parliamentary majority to overturn, and the ability to suspend a piece of legislation coming into law by referring it to the Constitutional Tribunal (TK). Given that a majority of tribunal members were appointed under previous PiS-dominated parliaments, this also functioned as a de facto veto. As a result, Nawrocki was able to severely complicate the Tusk government’s plans to push through its legislative and elite replacement programme, notably efforts to roll back PiS’s judicial reforms. This, combined with the political authority that stemmed from Nawrocki’s strong electoral mandate, meant that the government faced continued resistance for the remainder of its term of office until the next parliamentary election, scheduled for autumn 2027. An assertive presidency From the outset, Nawrocki has been a much more assertive president than his predecessor Andrzej Duda, leveraging his mandate to carve out a role as an active centre of resistance to the government. Although both presidents were PiS-aligned, during cohabitation with the Tusk administration, Duda used his powers more selectively and occasionally sought common ground. Nawrocki, by contrast, interpreted his strong electoral mandate as authorising a more confrontational approach. He has surrounded himself with a strong political support base who have helped him to develop and carry forward a blaze of independent initiatives in both the domestic and foreign policy spheres. As well proposing a series of his own draft laws, Nawrocki has used the legislative veto far more frequently than Duda (who issued only 19 across two full five-year terms) or any previous post-1989 president in a comparable period. By mid-2026, he had already surpassed previous records, blocking over 40 government-sponsored laws on issues such as judicial reform, socioeconomic policy and defence financing. In foreign policy, where the president’s formal competencies are more limited, Nawrocki pursued independent initiatives that often diverged from, or complicated, the government’s line. He has, for example, prioritised close personal and strategic ties with the USA, positioning Washington as Warsaw’s primary security guarantor. He cultivated a high-profile relationship with the Trump administration that yielded commitments to ongoing US troop deployments in Poland, sometimes bypassing or challenging the Tusk government. On Ukraine, while supporting continued military and diplomatic aid, Nawrocki has adopted a more transactional and assertive approach, opposing rapid Ukrainian EU and NATO accession until bilateral issues are addressed, and taking symbolic steps such as removing a Polish state honour from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky over unresolved historical grievances. Polish President Nawrocki has announced that he will strip @ZelenskyyUa of Poland’s highest honour in response to him naming a military unit after a group that massacred Poles during WWII Ukraine's foreign minister condemned Nawrocki's "reckless" decision https://t.co/CEqj4aaHYg — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 These have drawn criticisms that he is playing into Russian hands by weakening regional unity, but were clearly in line with changing Polish public attitudes towards its eastern neighbour. Uniting the fragmented right? Nawrocki has also emerged as the most important unifying figure on the increasingly fragmented Polish right. PiS, long the hegemonic force on the conservative side, has seen radical-right challengers, the free-market Confederation (Konfederacja) and ultra-nationalist Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), gaining ground. In July, PiS also suffered its biggest ever internal split, with a significant group of parliamentarians aligned with former prime minister Mateusz Morawiecki breaking away. All of this weakened PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński’s once unquestioned authority as the central broker on the Polish right; he is now one leader among several. Jarosław Kaczyński, the leader of Poland's largest opposition party, PiS, has called on President @NawrockiKn to help unify the country’s various right-wing opposition forces ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections https://t.co/Q3BFSOSfTG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 10, 2026 Alone among leading right-wing politicians, Nawrocki possesses genuine crossover appeal across the fractured conservative landscape. His 2025 presidential victory showed that he could consolidate a broad right-wing coalition and attract support well beyond traditional PiS loyalists, capturing the vast majority of voters from both Confederations. Although he was the PiS candidate, Nawrocki operates as an independent authority outside of direct party control and has cultivated an image as an authoritative independent figure, which gives him greater moral and symbolic stature than any partisan leader. Nawrocki’s assertive use of his constitutional powers has further reinforced his position as a natural focal point around which the broader right can unite. Many conservatives now look to him as a potential patron or broker ahead of the 2027 election. Nawrocki can use the presidency to set a broad conservative agenda and mediate negotiations among the various right-wing groupings to secure pre- and post-election agreements. However, he has no unifying mandate and his ability to bring together the right depends ultimately on whether the various actors are willing to be led. Moreover, not only is the president expected to remain formally non-partisan and not engage too openly in day-to-day politics, Nawrocki lacks the party organisational levers needed to enforce messy backroom deals. Focus of government attacks The Tusk government knows that Nawrocki’s is now the most potent counterweight to its authority and potential unifier of the fragmented right, which is precisely why he has become the main focus of its attacks on the opposition. An essential element of this has been trying to portray Nawrocki’s more active presidency as destructive and undermining the unity of the Polish state. This forms a principal component of its broader “security” narrative, a calculated strategy to reframe political debate around the ongoing Russian threat. At a time of heightened geopolitical risk with hybrid threats against Poland, the government has portrayed presidential obstruction as undermining the country’s military readiness and ability to co-ordinate with its allies. Karol Nawrocki has sought to redefine Poland's presidency and become the figurehead of the right-wing opposition. So far, it is working, but questions remain over what his end goal is and whether these tactics will get him there, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/TNDRGGv2QT — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 22, 2025 The Tusk administration cites Nawrocki’s veto of legislation enabling Poland to access its €43.7 billion allocation from the EU’s Security Action for Europe (SAFE) defence procurement initiative as an apparently perfect example of this, although the president argues that the loans saddle future generations with a huge, long-term debt and undermine Polish sovereignty. In fact, Nawrocki is fairly relaxed about the government’s attempts to portray his more active presidency as obstructive. Rather, he feels he needs to be assertive because that is precisely what those who voted for him expect: action and change, not passivity or compromise. Nawrocki’s 2025 presidential victory was based on a sharp critique of the Tusk administration and framed, and widely interpreted, as a vote of no confidence in the government’s performance. The president believes that this gives him a strong mandate to confront the ruling coalition across a wide range of issues and that the greater political risk lies in undermining the political momentum that his win created and appearing weak or inactive, rather than in the government’s counternarrative that he is a “blocking” president. A clash between the right-wing president and more liberal government over Poland's receipt of EU defence loans has sharpened polarisation and turbocharged the ruling coalition’s “Polexit” and security narratives, writes @AleksSzczerbiak https://t.co/Iu7rcJfj5e — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 2, 2026 More broadly, Nawrocki is not too concerned about what the Warsaw opinion-forming elites say about him. His approach stands in stark contrast to earlier presidents, even right-wing ones such as Duda, who, conservative critics argue, paid excessive attention to elite and liberal media criticism and received no meaningful political reward or pay-off for doing so. Instead of seeking to present himself as a “president of all Poles” in the traditional, consensus-seeking sense, Nawrocki has deliberately prioritised appealing directly to his core electoral base: Polish voters living beyond the large urban agglomerations in smaller towns, rural areas, and the provinces. By maintaining an assertive, unapologetic style that resonates with this electorate’s sense of cultural and political marginalisation, Nawrocki has sought to consolidate that support rather than diluting it in pursuit of metropolitan elite approval. Poland’s most popular politician There have obviously been plenty of missteps along the way. One clear risk has been the sheer volume and sometimes seemingly indiscriminate nature of the legislative vetoes. While this has successfully blocked key elements of the government’s agenda and reinforced Nawrocki’s image as an assertive counterweight, it has also handed the Tusk administration a ready-made narrative that the president is simply an obstructive “veto machine”. A number of Nawrocki’s more high-profile vetoes, such as the cryptocurrency regulation law, have proved highly contentious. PM @donaldtusk called a classified meeting of parliament in a bid to persuade opposition MPs to overturn the president's veto of crypto-asset regulation, which Tusk said threatens national security. However, in a subsequent vote, the veto was upheld https://t.co/Vj0Zh9wxpH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 5, 2025 Moreover, some of the other constitutional instruments that he has sought to utilise have not been particularly successful or even proved counterproductive. These include attempts to introduce his own legislation or referendum initiatives that have been stymied in parliament, as well as his original idea of holding the government to account via the so-called “Cabinet Council”, a formal meeting of the Council of Ministers chaired by the president. Nonetheless, in general, Nawrocki’s strategy appears to have delivered political dividends for him. He can, for example, point to a number of foreign policy successes, particularly in cultivating close personal and strategic ties with the USA under the Trump administration and positioning himself as a significant actor on security issues. President @NawrockiKn has recorded the highest ever level of trust (54.8%, up 8.4pp since May) of any politician in the history of regular polling by @IBRiS_PL for @onetpl Foreign minister @sikorskiradek (42.6%) was second and PM @donaldtusk (38.1%) third https://t.co/POuUFR3Khk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 26, 2026 At the same time, Nawrocki has asserted a greater degree of independence from PiS than Duda was ever able to achieve. This has been helped by the simple fact that PiS is now in opposition rather than in government, which reduces the formal and informal constraints that tied his predecessor more closely to the party. As a result, Nawrocki has emerged as Poland’s most popular politician, with consistently high approval ratings that set him apart from both the government and right-wing opposition party leaders. Challenges ahead There are clear challenges ahead for Nawrocki in the run-up to next year’s election and beyond. The first is how to respond to the argument that electing a right-wing government would concentrate excessive power in one side of the political spectrum. This is an awkward point for Nawrocki because he himself used a version of this argument during the 2025 presidential campaign, presenting his candidacy as a necessary check on the Tusk government. Opponents of the right will inevitably turn this logic against the broader conservative camp in the run-up to the 2027 election, claiming that the combination of a sympathetic president and a right-wing parliamentary majority risks the very imbalance Nawrocki once warned against. A second, related strategic challenge arises if a right-wing government does take office, and Nawrocki finds himself cohabiting with an ideologically and programmatically aligned administration rather than a hostile one. In that situation, he would still need to carve out a distinct and independent role for himself. The risk is falling into the trap that afflicted Duda during the years of PiS government: being widely perceived as little more than the government’s “notary” or a passive rubber stamp for its agenda. Maintaining personal authority, visibility, and a sense of autonomy, while avoiding conflict with an ideologically allied government, would demand a different style of presidency from the approach that has defined his first year. The very assertiveness and independence that have served him well in cohabitation with the Tusk government will prove harder to sustain if the political balance shifts after 2027. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has condemned as “idiots or traitors” those among the right-wing opposition who have celebrated Sunday’s state election victory by the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). However, the response from the Polish right to the election result has so far been relatively muted. The rise of the AfD has been watched with concern by many in Poland due to the party’s attempts to downplay the significance of Germany’s Nazi history and its sympathy towards Russia. W Polsce tylko idioci albo zdrajcy mogą się cieszyć z tryumfu AfD w Niemczech. Trochę się ich nazbierało w Konfederacjach i PiS. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) September 6, 2026 The AfD came first by a large margin in Sunday’s election in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, with preliminary results giving it around 44% of the vote. The centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) of federal Chancellor Friedrich Merz is trailing in second on around 17%. The victory continues a recent rise for the AfD, which also came first in the Thuringian state election in 2024, with 33% of the vote, and second in the federal elections of 2025, with 21%, making it the main national opposition party. The AfD’s latest result was welcomed by some figures from Poland’s right-wing and far-right opposition. “Germany is waking up,” tweeted Jacek Wilk, a former member of Poland’s parliament who is part of the radical-right Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party. Wg tej prognozy AfD brakuje już tylko 3 miejsc do samodzielnej większości Landtagu Saksonii-Anhalt. Niemcy się budzą. https://t.co/oHUIkYV1aQ — Jacek Wilk (@JacekWilkPL) September 6, 2026 Zdzisław Krasnodębski, a former deputy president of the European Parliament for the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s main opposition party, described the Saxony-Anhalt elections as “a great celebration of democracy”, pointing to the almost 80% turnout. Krasnodębski called on the minister-president of the German state, Sven Schulze of the CDU, to “end the anti-democratic ‘firewall’ [Brandmauer]” policy under which mainstream German parties refuse to form administrations with the AfD. However, other PiS figures expressed concern over the AfD’s victory, including former education minister and current MEP Anna Zalewska, who said that “the AfD is a powerful threat to European values and Polish-German cooperation”. Sven Schulze ist ein besonnener, konservativer Politiker (den ich persönlich aus dem Europäischen Parlament kenne). Er sollte einer Koalition mit der angeblich demokratischen, postkommunistischen „Linken“ nicht zustimmen. The Polish prime minister called them “ominous”, especially as they were delivered hours before the anniversary of the liberation of Auschwitz. World.title: Poland’s oldest operating electric train, 63-year-old “Granny”, returns to the tracks after a refurb
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s oldest operational multiple-unit electric train, a 63-year-old vehicle nicknamed Babcia (meaning “Granny”), is returning to service after refurbishment. The train, whose official name is EN57-038, rolled off the production lines on 9 May 1963 at a factory in the city of Wrocław belonging to Pafawag, a state locomotive manufacturer. For decades, it served in the southern Małopolska province, transporting passengers in cities including Kraków, Tarnów, Nowy Sącz and Sucha Beskidzka. In 2003, it was transferred to Masovia, the province around Poland’s capital, Warsaw, where it has operated ever since. “Masovian Railways continually invests in modern rolling stock, making our fleet among the most modern in Poland,” said Czesław Sulima, the operations director for the regional rail operator. “However, we fully understand the importance of tradition and sentiment.” “Babcia has become a permanent fixture in Polish railway history,” he added. “We are delighted that after a major overhaul, this unique vehicle will once again serve passengers and delight lovers of old-time travel, combining history with modernity.” Babcia has previously undergone periodic modernisation and maintenance, most recently in 2022, when she regained her original yellow and blue livery associated with the historic Pafawag factory. The latest work included upgrades to the train’s monitoring system and toilet, which now operates in “closed circulation” (a polite way of saying that waste is no longer dropped directly onto the track). State rail operator PKP has for years been promising to phase out the few remaining old “open” toilets. Now that Babcia has been refurbished, she will return to service early on Saturday morning, running a 10 km route on weekends between the town of Tłuszcz and village of Mostówka, just northeast of Warsaw. Babcia is one of the EN57 class of electric multiple unit trains produced by Pafawag between 1961 and 1993. A total of 1,429 were manufactured, with many still in use – though none as old as EN57-038. The history of the Wrocław factory itself dates back to the 1830s (when the city was part of Germany and called Breslau), making it one of the oldest manufacturers of rolling stock in Europe. After World War Two, when Wrocław became part of Poland following border changes, the factory came under the ownership of the new communist state. In the 1990s, after the fall of communism, it was privatised, being acquired in 1997 by German company ADtranz, which was in 2001 itself taken over by Canada’s Bombardier Transportation, which was then acquired in 2021 by France’s Alstom. Train travel has been booming in Poland in recent years. In the first half of 2026, a record 44.7 million passengers travelled with PKP Intercity, the main long-distance operator, more than 10% up on the previous year’s record and some 45% higher than three years earlier. While the country is seeking to expand its high-speed rail network and increase train speeds up to 320 km/h (199mph), there has also been a growing interest in older trains. That prompted PKP to launch a special “unhurried” service earlier this year, allowing passengers to travel along scenic routes in restored 1980s trains. World.title: Poland to begin using sewage water to cool power plants
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland will begin using reclaimed sewage water to cool power plants from the start of next year. The measures are intended to reduce the use of fresh water and make the power system more resilient to increasingly frequent droughts. The change comes after some of Poland’s power plants were partially shut down this summer amid a series of heatwaves and lack of rain that led to record-low water levels in many rivers. 💧⚡ Otwieramy sektor energetyczny na wodę odzyskaną. Od 1 stycznia 2027 r. polskie elektrownie i elektrociepłownie będą mogły wykorzystywać wodę odzyskaną ze ścieków komunalnych w systemach chłodzenia. Nowe rozwiązania przedstawiliśmy dziś wspólnie z ministrem energii… pic.twitter.com/qRDOgjcDwb — Dariusz Klimczak (@DariuszKlimczak) September 3, 2026 “This may seem to many like a minor change, but it is of fundamental importance for many power-generating units in Poland,” said energy minister Miłosz Motyka. “Thanks to this, we will be even more resilient and even better prepared for crises of all kinds.” The legislation was first proposed by a group of MPs from The Left (Lewica) and the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), two members of the current ruling coalition, in May, and was then approved by parliament in July. Last week, President Karol Nawrocki signed it into law. The law, which will come into force at the start of 2027, introduces a definition of water recovered from municipal sewage, which, in turn, will allow its use in the cooling circuits of power stations and combined heat and power plants. Power stations require large amounts of water to help cool and condense steam, which drives the turbines, back into liquid form so that it can be reheated into steam once more. Orlen Termika, a subsidiary of state energy giant Orlen, has announced that it plans to invest more than 1 billion zloty (€230 million) over the next four years to maximise the benefits of the change by connecting sewage treatment plants with three of its power and heat plants around Warsaw. According to Andrzej Gajewski, the CEO of Orlen Termika, one of the plants, Żeran, will be able to save up to 80% of previous water use. Another, Siekierki, will save up to 20%. The company also plans to install heat pumps to extract heat from sewage, which can then be used to help supply heat to residents of Warsaw before the water is then used to cool down the plants. Sewage is relatively warm, typically between 10°C and 20°C, making it a good source of recoverable heat. “From the point of view of security of supply for Warsaw’s residents and from the point of view of efficiency – that is, the price of heating – this is the best and most advantageous solution,” emphasised Gajewski. Poland’s power grid operator has, for the second time in three days and third time this summer, invoked emergency measures to ensure supply amid a heatwave. Before this summer, it had only done so twice in the eight years since such powers were introduced https://t.co/fIDR4SimgG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 6, 2026 Poland has experienced increasingly hot temperatures in recent years. This summer, the country broke its all-time record, as temperatures reached more than 40°C. That, along with low amounts of rainfall, has seen rivers reach record lows. As a result, Poland’s power grid operator has this summer been forced three times to invoke emergency measures to ensure supply. Previously, it had only done so twice in the eight years since such powers were introduced. Last month, state power supplier Enea announced that it had reduced operations at two of its coal-fired plants due to the low level of water in the Vistula. Around 1.1 gigawatts (GW) of capacity, just over 1% of Poland’s total, was taken offline. Temperatures in Poland have reached the highest level on record, with a figure of 40.3°C (104.5°F) recorded this afternoon, as the heatwave that has hit Europe this week moves eastwards https://t.co/eRhRxiuCGq — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 28, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers.
