World.title: Azerbaijan and U.S. discuss peace process and TRIPP project (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 8. On September 8, Deputy Foreign Minister Elnur Mammadov met with David Allen, the U.S. Chargé d’Affaires ad interim in Armenia, who is visiting Azerbaijan, and Amy Carlos, the U.S. Chargé d’Affaires ad interim in Azerbaijan, to discuss the peace process and the implementation of the TRIPP initiative.

This was announced in a statement by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Azerbaijan.

According to the Ministry, during the meeting, the parties discussed ongoing efforts to normalize relations between Azerbaijan and Armenia, advance the peace process, ensure long-term and sustainable peace, and strengthen stability and security in the region.

The sides also exchanged views on the outcomes of Elnur Mammadov’s visit to the United States on the occasion of the anniversary of the Washington Peace Summit and the signing of the trilateral statement. Discussions also covered ongoing efforts to implement the “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” (TRIPP), as well as the establishment of the TRIPP Development Company, which will oversee the construction of the route’s infrastructure.

In addition, the parties reviewed the bilateral agenda between Azerbaijan and the United States and prospects for further cooperation in the areas outlined in the Charter on Strategic Partnership.

World.title: Polling officials say they were ignored after offering to work at SA election
World.content:
The South Australian Electoral Commission (ECSA) did not follow up with polling officials who had indicated they wanted to work at the 2026 state election, according to multiple former officials who say they were surprised to hear booths were understaffed.

The ABC revealed on Monday that ECSA was trying to find people to manage polling booths only hours before state election day, with frantic internal messages showing staff in tears on election eve because polling booths were so disorganised.

Since publication of that story, more than half a dozen people have contacted the ABC to share their experience with ECSA.

This includes several who said they had previous election experience and were willing to work "anywhere" at the state election but did not receive any follow up from ECSA.

Chaotic SA election preparations revealed The South Australian Electoral Commission was trying to find staff to manage polling booths only hours before election day, with internal messages revealing the extreme pressure officials were under.

Among those was retired Australian Defence Force member Crispin Boxhall, who said he had worked at three previous elections, including as a polling booth manager in the Adelaide Hills at the 2025 federal election.

Mr Boxhall said he applied online to work at the state election after being approached by ECSA, and his application was accepted three months ahead of the March poll.

"Because the confirmation email said, 'thanks very much for applying, we'll be in touch with you nearer the time to discuss specifics', I left it like that and allowed a month or two to go past," he said.

Mr Boxhall said he contacted ECSA a month before the election to "remind them I was here and looking forward to being appointed to a position".

"With about 2 weeks to go, it was very getting very very close and I still hadn't heard a peep," he said.

"They hadn't even come back and said, 'hang on a minute we're having problems here', or 'you're not needed' … it just went silent.

"About two weeks out I contacted them again and said 'look, unless I hear from you, I'll take it I'm not needed'."

Do you know more about this story? Get in touch with Thomas Kelsall at thomaskelsall@proton.me

Mr Boxhall said he did not have any communication from ECSA leading up to the election or after it.

"I just thought that they must be so flat out they must already have enough staff that they're not contacting people they don't need," he said.

"It wasn't till I read your article that I realised actually it's quite likely that there's something bigger afoot here.

"It just seems that maybe they didn't have enough people, and to not contact people who not only have applied but are actually following up looking to help out I thought was bit strange."

The March 21 state election saw various issues before, during, and after polling day. (ABC News: Trent Murphy)

'I just don't understand': Ex-AEC worker surprised by no call-up

Semi-retired consultant Andrew West said he worked 10-days for the Australian Electoral Commission (AEC) counting and aggregating votes for the Indigenous Voice to Parliament referendum in 2023.

He said he had ticked a box when signing up for the AEC indicating he would be happy to work at an SA election.

"I wasn't necessarily wanting to manage a booth, but I would have happily ticked off people's names, I would have happily travelled anywhere," he said.

Mr West said upon reading the ABC's story on Monday, he was "even more amazed that someone didn't ring me at the time of the election".

"I would have stopped everything if they had of rung me the day before to go and do something," he said.

"I just don't understand why they didn't ring."

Long waits at several polling booths, like this one at Goodwood, were reported on election day. (ABC News: Evelyn Leckie)

Election review expected in two months

ECSA's handling of the election is already subject to an independent review led by former Australian Electoral Commissioner Tom Rogers.

He is examining an array of issues including technical glitches, long queues, missing ballots, payment delays and Aboriginal voters being mistakenly turned away trying to vote in the First Nations Voice election.

Mr Rogers's report is expected to be handed down in the next two months, Premier Peter Malinauskas said on Tuesday.

Former Australian electoral commissioner Tom Rogers is leading an independent review into ECSA's performance in the 2026 state election. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

"There were clearly logistical issues going on behind the scenes at the most recent state election that were avoidable," Mr Malinauskas said.

"Thankfully, there's no suggestion of any compromise to the integrity of the conduct of the election or otherwise, but there were logistical issues that had an impact on staff."

Former SA electoral commissioner Mick Sherry stepped down in June after overseeing the issue-plagued poll.

"The commissioner has resigned, I'm grateful for that," Mr Malinauskas said on Tuesday.

" We'll get a new one who I have no doubt will be dedicated to making sure that we don't see a repeat of those issues. "

The ABC has contacted Mr Sherry for comment.

Acting South Australian electoral commissioner Leah McLay says she is looking forward to any recommendations from the review. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

Acting electoral commissioner Leah McLay, who joined ECSA in January, said she was "concerned about issues relating to recruitment and training for positions at the 2026 state election, which have been raised by application and employees".

"We won't be pre-empting Mr Rogers' independent findings by commenting publicly about the issues he is investigating," she said in a statement.

"We look forward to receiving any recommendations from the external review to make improvements for future elections."

World.title: Breaking: Second child dies after crash west of Melbourne
World.content:
A second child has died in hospital following a single-vehicle crash west of Melbourne on Tuesday afternoon.

A seven-year-old girl died at the scene after a 4WD with seven children inside rolled near Parwan just before 4pm.

An 11-year-old boy was flown to hospital with critical injuries but died overnight.

The single-vehicle crash happened at Parwan, west of Melbourne on Tuesday afternoon. (ABC News)

Five other children were taken to hospital with non-life threatening injuries and the driver, a 34-year-old woman, was taken to hospital for observation.

Detectives are continuing to investigate the circumstance behind the crash, which happened near the intersection of Nerowie and Parwan-Exford roads.

Victoria Police said seven children were inside the vehicle when it rolled on Tuesday afternoon. (ABC News)

Detective Sergeant Tony Gentile from the Major Collision Investigation Unit said the woman had picked the children up from school.

"From my understanding, the scene was quite hectic, people everywhere, witnesses who witnessed it, they stopped and rendered assistance," he said.

"Obviously, with seven children, they were distressed and they were cared for by paramedics, members of the public and police.

"This is just a really sad set of circumstances, very sad. We just ask the public to drive to the conditions and be mindful of their surrounds."

Police have asked anyone who witnessed the crash or has dash cam footage to come forward.

World.title: Foreign 'AI slopaganda' network targets Australian politicians
World.content:
Dozens of Australian politicians have been deepfaked by a "foreign influence" network operating on Facebook, and researchers say there are many more just like it.

Research organisation Reset Tech has tracked more than 200 Facebook pages impersonating Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, opposition leader Angus Taylor, One Nation's Pauline Hanson, and many more political figures over the past eight months.

A report from the group has revealed the seemingly co-ordinated campaign and linked it back to an influencer business in Sri Lanka.

It found roughly 10 per cent of the network's pages have been monetised by Facebook, as part of the platform's in-house scheme to pay content creators, allowing a page's owner to profit directly.

"This isn't foreign interference as we traditionally think of it," Rys Farthing, chief research officer for Reset Tech, said.

" What we see here is foreign influence for commercial motivations. "

A screenshot from one of the pages showing AI-generated images of Anthony Albanese and Peter Dutton. (Facebook)

Researchers found most targets were impersonated in short clips on Facebook Reels, in which they were falsely shown to be saying something inflammatory.

The content often centred on anti-migrant, anti-Muslim, or nationalistic themes, and baited users into participating in polls.

Another common pattern was the use of sexualised images and videos of female politicians.

"Sometimes it is directly related to news events, but basically … it's just throwing spaghetti at the wall," Dr Farthing said.

"They work out which [posts] get them the clicks, which ones bring the money in, and then they create more like that again."

Senator Fatima Payman, who left Labor to sit on the crossbench, was among those targeted by a page called Australia Info Live.

Senator Payman, a Muslim, was falsely shown in an AI-generated clip to say: "Please don't deport me back to Afghanistan. It's not safe for me there. Vote no to support me."

The post has hundreds of likes and comments, and no apparent label to indicate it was false or AI-generated.

The AI-generated post of Fatima Payman was widely liked and commented on. (Facebook)

Crossbencher Allegra Spender has also been targeted. (Facebook)

Fellow independent senator David Pocock was targeted by a page called Australia Life & News, in a clip where he was falsely shown to say he had "joined forces" with One Nation.

Senator Pocock told the ABC he was not aware of the specific clip, although his team had been sent "a bunch of deepfakes of me over the last few months".

"I'm concerned deepfakes really undermine our democratic system," he said.

"As humans, when we see someone say something, we generally believe that it's them saying it".

Deepfake laws have now been used for the first time. What are they? As the first case under new anti-deepfake legislation goes before the courts, authorities and experts say the rise in the creation of the non-consensual sexually explicit material is concerning.

With names such as I Love Australia, Life in Australia, or Beautiful Australia, the pages are often designed for mass appeal.

Reset Tech said one of the common tactics was to lure audiences in with AI-generated images of animals, attractive women, or posts praising Australia's beauty.

Later, the page takes a political turn, although many pages are political from the outset.

"There's nothing domestic about this," Dr Farthing said.

" [This] is foreign distortion of Australian political discourse. "

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke, who has been deepfaked by the same network, said it was more important than ever that people checked their sources.

"Last election for the first time I saw photos of myself online with people I had never met," he said.

"In more recent times, I have seen videos … and interviews of some of my colleagues saying things they have never said."

Rys Farthing says propaganda networks are targeting political systems across the world. (Supplied)

Reset Tech found the same Sri Lanka-based network was also targeting France, Italy, the UK, the US, Canada and Mexico, among other locations, using the same playbook.

In total, it was believed to operate 1,864 coordinated Facebook pages globally, with mostly identical branding, and a combined follower base of 5.9 million users.

"We really wanted to highlight that this wasn't just a unique issue with one bad actor or a couple of bad actors misusing a platform system," Dr Farthing said.

Rather, she said, the research showed "AI slopaganda" networks were targeting political systems on a "massive industrial scale".

'Outrage, eyeballs and clicks': The monetisation system fuelling AI slop

Reset Tech found relatively few instances where political AI slop on Facebook had been appropriately dealt with, in accordance with the platform's own policies.

Only one in three of the posts received AI labelling, and one in 33 of the posts had been deleted, the report stated.

"We have a handful of researchers, and we were able to find this and detect all of these networks with ease," Dr Farthing said.

"If we can do it, I don't quite understand how these companies that have billion-dollar revenues can't do it."

Reset Tech said the network targeting Australia was in breach of several Facebook policies designed to target "inauthentic behaviour networks", as well as hate speech and AI deepfakes.

AI deepfake scams surge Regulators are removing record numbers of fake celebrity-endorsed investment scams, using AI images of famous faces.

Dr Farthing said ultimately, platforms were incentivising the creation of AI slop and failing to contain it.

"[The platforms] have made all of the decisions that enable their monetisation system to work, right?"

"And this is the result."

Senator Pocock said it was increasingly clear tackling the issue was not in the interests of social media companies.

"Their business model is based on outrage, on eyeballs on the screens for as long as possible, and on clicks," Senator Pocock said.

The ABC has contacted Meta, Facebook's parent company, for a response to Reset's Tech report.

World.title: Woman allegedly attacked in Brisbane emergency department
World.content:
A 73-year-old woman suffered serious injuries when she was allegedly bashed by another patient in a random attack inside the emergency department of a major public hospital in Brisbane.

It comes as medical groups continue to warn about escalating violence in overburdened emergency units across the country.

Queensland Police Service (QPS) said the woman was allegedly punched in the face "a number of times in an unprovoked attack" by a 43-year-old man shortly before 11:30pm on August 23.

The shocking event happened at the Princess Alexandra Hospital in Woolloongabba.

"The woman sustained serious facial injuries during the incident," a QPS spokesperson said in a statement.

"Medical staff disrupted the incident, and the man was arrested shortly afterwards by responding police."

The 73-year-old woman was left with serious injuries after allegedly being punched in the face multiple times. (ABC News)

Police said the man had been charged with one count of grievous bodily harm, was remanded in custody and is due to reappear in the Brisbane Magistrates Court later this month.

A spokesperson said the hospital was aware of "an alleged assault involving a patient and another unrelated patient" and support was provided to the person impacted as well as "the staff who witnessed the incident".

"The safety of our staff, patients and visitors is our number one priority, and we have zero tolerance for violence and aggressive behaviour in our hospital," the spokesperson said in a statement.

They said Metro South Health — which runs the Princess Alexandra Hospital — had taken "significant action" to address occupational violence and employed security officers who were "available 24/7 across the hospital".

"We have invested more than $37 million to increase the number of security officers, and implement additional CCTV, body-worn cameras, duress alarms, peer support programs, hospital ambassadors and de-escalation training for staff."

The woman has since been discharged from hospital.

The alleged assault took place in the PA Hospital's emergency department last month. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

Violence 'hugely common' in overcrowded hospitals

ABC News asked Metro South Health for annual figures on the number of assaults on hospital patients and staff, but none were provided.

Australasian College for Emergency Medicine (ACEM) president Peter Allely said violence was a "hugely significant" and "hugely under-reported" occurrence in emergency departments nationwide.

"It shouldn't be accepted or normalised," Dr Allely said.

" Whenever somebody gets punched on an airplane it makes national news, whenever someone gets punched in an emergency department, it's [just a normal] Friday. "

Australasian College for Emergency Medicine president Dr Peter Allely says violence and aggression from patients is "hugely common" in emergency departments. (Supplied: ACEM)

The Perth specialist said the "number one overwhelming driver" for an increase in violence and aggression was "the degree of overcrowding that our health care system faces".

He said violence was "not excusable" but it was exacerbated by the conditions in emergency units.

"This is in an environment where the lights are on 24 hours a day. There are minimal shower and toilet facilities and people may not have the ability to walk around the way that they normally would in normal aspects of life," Dr Allely said.

" It's not designed for people to be spending long lengths of time in. "

Do you know more? Have you experienced violence in a hospital? Contact health reporter Emma Pollard at pollard.emma@abc.net.au

Last year ACEM published the report Breaking Point — An Urgent Call to Action on Emergency Department Safety.

It included national survey results that found nine out of 10 respondents reported an incident, or multiple incidences, of violence by a patient or accompanying person in their ED within the past week.

Recommendations included fostering a culture of, and systems for, reporting violent incidents and bolstering well-trained, directly employed, hospital security officers for emergency departments.

Violence in EDs a 'national crisis' Long waits in overcrowded emergency departments are leaving patients frustrated and exacerbating violence towards staff, according to the peak body for emergency medicine.

Figures released in July by the Australian Institute for Health and Welfare show assaults were the second leading cause of injury hospitalisations, after falls, among health care workers in 2024-25, with the rate almost doubling since 2015-16.

Dr Allely said ACEM had not "seen a whole lot of tangible change" from governments on the challenge.

"We want a razor-sharp focus on overcrowding. That's going to have the biggest impact," he said.

The call for action was echoed by the Queensland Nurses and Midwives' Union (QNMU).

Secretary Sarah Beaman said the problem of violence and aggression in hospitals was "at crisis point".

"The impact on staff is that they're coming in with a level of fear, they just want to get in and provide care and when you're worried about whether you're going to get assaulted, that is problematic," Ms Beaman said.

Queensland Nurses and Midwives' Union secretary Sarah Beaman says creating safe workplaces is a legal obligation. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

She said 82 per cent of respondents in this year's survey of more than 8,000 QNMU members said they had experienced occupational violence within the last 12 months.

The union called for more state government investment in a de-escalation security program called the Ambassador Model and a better reporting system.

Ms Beaman said workplace safety was essential for retaining health care professionals.

"The more people that leave the professions means that safe, free, high-quality care cannot be provided," she said.

World.title: Almost one in three waiting too long for surgery under reset Tasmanian target
World.content:
A revised Tasmanian Health Department performance target will allow for up to almost one in three elective surgery patients to wait longer than they should for surgery.

There are about 9,500 people on the department's elective surgery waitlist.

Under its annual service plan — which sets out key performance indicators (KPI) for the year — the department has set the KPI for the percentage of patients waiting longer than clinically recommended for elective surgery as "not more than 30 per cent".

Put another way, the department has set a target of getting at least 70 per cent of elective-surgery patients treated within their clinically recommended time frame.

For the Australian Medical Association (AMA) Tasmania, it's a bar that has been set too low.

"No system is perfect," AMA Tasmania president Dr Meg Creely said.

" But we should always be aiming for something that is much, much better than one in three missing out. "

Dr Creely said the way the KPIs were measured across subsequent years further complicated the picture.

Meg Creely says the revised elective surgery target will create a "two-tier health system" between those who can afford private healthcare and those who can't. (ABC News: Owain Stia James)

In last year's plan, the health department's target for the amount of patients waiting longer than clinically recommended times for elective surgery was measured as a number, rather than a percentage.

That number was no more than 270 patients who should wait longer than clinically recommended for elective surgery.

"When you work it out as a percentage, it's gone from about 1.2 per cent to 30 per cent," Dr Creely said.

" That is a phenomenal difference. "

The lack of continuity between annual service plans made it difficult for health practitioners and members of the public to understand what was going on within the health service, Dr Creely said.

"It's really hard when there's different numbers that are used, where it's hidden in budget papers, hidden in annual services plans."

A Tasmanian Health Department spokesperson said the revised target reflected the increased demand for elective surgeries.

It is "a realistic and evidence-based assessment of current demand, service capacity and the health system operating environment caused by ongoing issues with bed availability due to a lack of aged care and NDIS placements for Tasmanians," the spokesperson said.

The spokesperson did not answer a question from the ABC about whether the AMA's claim that the previous target has increased from 1.2 per cent to 30 per cent was accurate.

The latest data from July shows at 59 per cent of elective surgeries were delivered on time, meaning fewer than six in 10 patients across the state received surgery within the clinically recommended time frame.

And performance has deteriorated over the past year.

In July last year, the number of elective surgeries performed within the clinically recommended time frame was 64 per cent.

Urgent surgeries delayed

In Tasmania, elective surgeries are broken down into three categories.

Category 1 is deemed "urgent", with patients needing to be treated within 30 days.

In that most urgent category, 65 per cent were admitted within the recommended time frame in July, meaning more than one in three category 1 patients waited longer than the clinically recommended time.

Under its new plan, the health department said it wanted 95 per cent of category 1 surgeries performed within the clinically recommended time frames.

Category 2 is "semi-urgent", and is designated for patients to be treated with 90 days, while category 3 is for "non-urgent" elective surgeries which should be treated within 365 days.

Under the new 2026-27 plan, the health service aims to complete more than 21,500 elective surgeries, a slight decrease of about 400 from last year.

According to the state budget, health funding will increase by 8 per cent over four years, due to extra federal funding.

However, the Tasmanian government has also tasked the health department to find $702 million in efficiency cuts over four years.

Loading...

Dr Creely said the elective surgery backlog risked entrenching a two-tier system between those who can and can't afford private health care.

"We don't think it's acceptable for patients and we don't think it's acceptable for Tasmanians," she said.

Within the new health department plan is another target: clearing its elective surgery backlog.

It lists a target of "zero" for the number of patients waiting for elective surgery prior to 30 June 2024.

World.title: Who is taking the biggest cut of the apple profits?
World.content:
The price of apples has shot up in the past year because of supply shortages, but new figures show the major supermarkets took a big chunk of the profit.

The data collated by Apple and Pear Australia Limited (APAL) reveals the price paid for apples in the shops grew at a significantly higher rate than the price that was paid to the grower.

After a tough period of drought, particularly in Victoria's Goulburn Valley, orchard consolidation and growers leaving the industry, the shortage of apples started to emerge a year ago, leading to the price uptick.

The price of apples went from an average of $4.50 per kilogram 18 months ago, peaking at an average of about $6.20 earlier this year.

It is now averaging about $5.20 a kilo.

Apples are currently averaging about $5.20 a kilo. (ABC South East SA: Elsie Adamo)

The APAL figures show the profit margin for major stores, including Woolworths, Coles and Aldi, got as high as 65 per cent in early 2026, up from the average of about 25 per cent.

"We saw an extremely large increase, a significant increase in the difference between the price of purchasing and the price of selling to the consumers," APAL general manager Jeremy Griffith said.

While the wholesale data did not detail the exact prices paid by the supermarkets to the growers, Mr Griffith said it was a good representation.

"It's a good proxy for what the market is doing," he said.

"The return for growers over the past six or seven years has been too low … so from the grower point of view, getting a better return, it's good, but we would be concerned if the supermarkets are taking an excess margin on top of that.

" Consumers want good value for apples, but we don't think they should pay an overly inflated price for them. "

Jeremy Griffith says he would be concerned if supermarkets are taking an excess margin. (ABC Rural: Justine Longmore)

'Supporting Australian growers'

The major supermarkets have defended their pricing decisions.

"Retail prices for fresh apples are strongly influenced by seasonal availability, market conditions, and supplier wholesale input costs," a Woolworths spokesperson said.

"We are proud to support Australian apple growers and bring high-quality, locally grown fruit to millions of customers.

"We work collaboratively with our suppliers to meet the needs of our customers every week of the year."

Coles also said the price of fresh produce reflected "a range of factors".

"[Those factors include] the price agreed with our suppliers, seasonal availability, weather events, quality specifications and the costs involved in getting fresh produce to customers," a spokesperson said.

"Coles is committed to providing customers with great value and high-quality fresh produce, and we are proud to provide 100 per cent Australian-grown apples."

Aldi was contacted for comment but did not respond to the ABC's questions.

APAL wants the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) to better police the relationship between major supermarkets and the farmers that supply their produce.

APAL wants the ACCC to police the relationship between supermarkets and farmers. (ABC Rural: Justine Longmore)

"If there's no significant change, it could undermine the long-term viability of the sector," Mr Griffith said.

"Every Monday night the growers are expected to put in the volume of apples or pears that they want to sell, the price that they want to sell them at."

The ACCC told the ABC that wholesale and retail prices are influenced by a range of market and supply chain factors.

"Supermarkets must at all times deal with suppliers in good faith, including when negotiating prices," a spokesperson said.

"Failure to act in good faith will make the large grocery business liable to civil penalties."

The ACCC did not say whether it would investigate the concerns of inflated prices for apples.

Mitchell McNab runs his family's orchard in Ardmona. (ABC Rural: Annie Brown)

Despite what was happening with the supermarket prices, orchardists in Victoria's Goulburn Valley said the increases were helping their bottom line.

"Hopefully we can maintain that pricing going forward and continue to have that bit of positivity over the next couple of years," Fruit Growers Victoria chair Mitch McNabb said.

Fruit Growers Victoria industry development officer Michael Crisera agreed.

Michael Crisera says there is a bit more confidence in the apple industry. (ABC Rural: Annie Brown)

"I think there's a bit of a buzz around, and I think obviously everyone's a bit happy when they've got more income, and they're a bit more profitable," Mr Crisera said.

"There's definitely a lot more confidence in the industry."

World.title: Man wanted over axe attack arrested in Victoria's east
World.content:
Police have arrested a Victorian man who had been on the run since Saturday after allegedly attacking family members with an axe.

Police allege Peter O'Ryan, 48, assaulted his brother, Paul O'Ryan, father, Keith O'Ryan, and mother, Janine O'Ryan, with the weapon before fleeing their home in Tyers on foot.

Mr O'Ryan was arrested on Tuesday night after officers were called to reports of a person acting suspiciously near the Tyers-Walhalla Road just before 9pm.

He will be interviewed in relation to the attack over the weekend.

His family remain in the Alfred Hospital where his father is in a critical but stable condition, while his brother and mother are in serious but stable conditions.

World.title: Victims of serious youth crimes to be told when offenders leave prison
World.content:
Grieving and traumatised victims will soon be warned when youth criminals convicted of murders, home invasions and carjackings are set to be released from prison.

Unlike for adult offenders, there is no formal system in Victoria that alerts people directly impacted by youth crime if the offenders are released or there is an upcoming parole hearing.

Victoria is the only state or territory that does not allow youth crime victims to register to receive that information.

Police can choose to share it with some victims at their discretion, while the Youth Parole Board responds to victims' requests on a case-by-case basis.

But youth crime victims and their families will soon be able to apply to a register, which is currently exclusively for information about adult offenders, under significant changes that come into effect from September 30.

The eligible youth crimes include murder, rape, home invasions, carjackings, serious sexual crimes and assault.

However, the reform will not be applied retrospectively, meaning those affected by recent high-profile crimes are ineligible for the notifications.

Victim's sister welcomes change

While they cannot register themselves, the opt-in system has been welcomed by the family members of those killed in some of Victoria's most high-profile youth crimes.

Natalie Gordon, whose brother Ash Gordon was stabbed to death with a hunting knife by a 16-year-old boy in a home invasion in 2024, told the ABC she had always wanted the chance to be kept informed about his killer's movements.

Natalie Gordon is the sister of Ash Gordon, a doctor who was murdered by a 16-year-old in 2024. (ABC News: Darryl Torpy)

"I don't know why it's not already an option," she said.

"Victims and victims' families aren't acknowledged, and that's probably the most heartbreaking and disappointing part of the system."

The offender, the son of a Victoria Police investigator, is serving a 17-year sentence for murdering Mr Gordon, with a non-parole period of 12 years.

Natalie Gordon says she is shocked Victoria does not already have systems in place to keep the families of victims informed. (ABC News: Darryl Torpy)

The ABC can reveal the teen is appealing his conviction and sentence.

Despite now being an adult, he still cannot be named because he was underage when he murdered Mr Gordon.

The youth justice changes will also require the Youth Parole Board to make families' concerns central to parole decisions.

Until now, only some families and victims could make submissions to the board about why they believed their attackers should be kept behind bars or released.

The changes place greater weight on the concerns of victims' families during parole decisions. (ABC News: Darryl Torpy)

Ms Gordon said she often thought about the day her brother's killer would be released, and that she knew exactly what she would say when he was up for parole.

"I can't wait to tell him that your excuses for bad behaviour are pathetic," she said.

Government vows to put victims first

Minister for Victims Support Ros Spence said the new register helped put community safety first by giving victims access to information they needed.

"Victims and survivors should never feel like an afterthought in our justice system," she said.

"Their voices matter, and we're making sure they are heard."

Jesuit Social Services chief executive Julie Edwards said the register was only one part of helping victims heal while holding young offenders responsible for their actions.

She said it was important victims were also offered a chance to face their young attackers directly under a restorative justice framework — where victims and offenders agree to meet with each other.

"We support anything that will help a victim heal, but we don't think just putting your name on a register and finding out what date someone's getting out, or what date their parole hearing is, is sufficient," Ms Edwards said.

"We would really like to enhance that opportunity for the victim and use it as an opportunity to hold the young person to account, to take responsibility, to make amends and develop a plan to make sure they don't end up hurting anyone else."

Julie Edwards says support for victims should go beyond simply informing them of certain dates. (Supplied)

The new alert system will arrive as youths convicted of some of Victoria's most violent crimes approach the end of their sentences.

They include two young men who were 16 and 17 when they were involved in the fatal 2022 group stabbing of 25-year-old Khalid Mahat, and were sentenced to between two and three years in youth detention in 2024.

A 17-year-old boy who fatally punched Jason Langhans with a screwdriver hidden in his fist after gatecrashing a birthday party in 2021 also became eligible for parole in the middle of 2025.

However, as the register will not apply to existing convictions, victims' families in those crimes will not be eligible for notification.

Changes to youth arrest procedures

The register is one of a host of changes coming into effect under the new legislation at the end of the month.

Among other changes are how police respond to youth offenders when placing them under arrest.

Internal force communications seen by the ABC show officers have been told to take the least invasive approach, instead of making an arrest, where possible.

Police will have a new framework for arresting young people. (ABC News)

Under the new framework, police can decide to take no action against a young person, issue them with a youth warning or caution or ultimately commence criminal proceedings.

They must also consider the seriousness of the offence, consider whether the youth has reoffended, and record their reasoning for the actions they take when determining whether to arrest a teenager.

A Victoria Police spokeswoman said the changes were designed to break cycles of offending in the long term and connect young people with appropriate support, but officers would not hesitate to put repeat offenders before the courts.

World.title: ASX eyes gains, Wall Street drifts lower; Oil hovers near $US100
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX eyes gains, Wall Street drifts lower; Oil hovers near $US100 Stan Choe Updated September 9, 2026 — 6:17am ,first published 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks drifted lower in their return to trading from a three-day weekend. The S&P 500 fell 0.6 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 628.2 points, or 1.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite closed 0.3 per cent lower. Wall Street has retreated after returning from a long weekend, with rising oil prices weighing on investors. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures at 6am AEST pointing to a gain of 21 points, or 0.2 per cent, at the open. The ASX shed 1 per cent on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was trading at US72.22¢. US stocks felt pressure from oil prices, after a barrel of Brent crude briefly climbed as high as $US99.46. It later gave back most of its gain and was most recently up 0.1 per cent at $US97.05. It’s nevertheless jumped from roughly $US72 since early July as increased fighting in the Middle East keeps the global flow of oil constricted.



More expensive oil has worsened worries about the high inflation weighing on people and companies across the country, which gives extra heft to a couple reports coming later this week. On Thursday, the US government will release its August report for inflation at the wholesale level, which economists expect will show an acceleration to 5.4 per cent from 4.7 per cent in July. The more closely watched report on inflation that US consumers are feeling will arrive on Friday. That update will show how much more people are paying for groceries, clothes and other costs of living, and economists expect it eased a bit to 3.3 per cent from July’s 3.4 per cent inflation rate. That, though, remains well above the 2 per cent target that the Federal Reserve has set as its goal. Related Article Opinion

Trade wars Fighting the bully: Canada throws a punch back at Trump Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist This week’s updates on inflation will be the last before the Fed meets next week to decide whether to cut, raise or hold interest rates steady. The traditional move for the Fed when inflation is high is to raise its main interest rate. That in turn would filter out into the rest of the bond market, make it more expensive for companies and people to borrow, slow the overall economy, undercut prices for investments and hopefully rein in inflation. But President Donald Trump has been lobbying for lower interest rates instead, which could give the economy — and inflation — an extra kick. The Fed’s new chairman, Kevin Warsh, has meanwhile said he wants to give financial markets fewer clues about what the Fed plans to do with interest rates in the short term.



That all has traders betting on a 60 per cent probability the Fed will raise its federal funds rate at the conclusion of its next meeting on Sept. 16, according to data from CME Group. In the bond market, the yield on the 10-year Treasury inched up to 4.79 per cent from 4.78 per cent and remains near its highest level since the autumn of 2023. Higher Treasury yields put more pressure on companies to grow their profits in order to lift their stock prices. On Wall Street, Boston Scientific fell 4.6 per cent after saying that a network outage earlier this summer caused by a cybersecurity incident means that it’s unlikely to meet forecasts it gave for sales and profit for the third quarter and for the fully of 2026. It expects to make back some of the revenue as it continues to ramp operations globally, fulfil customer orders and reduce remaining backlogs, but it doesn’t yet know the full impacts. Shares of Novartis that trade in the United States tumbled 13.9 per cent after the Swiss pharmaceutical company gave a discouraging update on a study of a therapy for people living with myotonic dystrophy type 1, a neuromuscular disease.



Qualcomm helped limit the market’s losses after rising 2.9 per cent. It announced a deal to collaborate with Amazon on large-scale AI data centres. The deal also gives Amazon the right to acquire up to 25 million of Qualcomm’s shares at $US161.26 per share. Related Article Opinion

Donald Trump The Taxman v Trump: ATO opens new front in fight with Big Tech Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer In stock markets abroad, Japan’s Nikkei 225 sank 1.7 per cent under the weight of losses for major exporters, which were hurt by more rises for the value of the Japanese yen against the US dollar. A stronger yen erodes the value of sales made in US dollars when Toyota Motor, Panasonic Holdings and other Japanese exporters have to translate them back into yen. The Bank of Japan is also scheduled to meet next week on interest rates, and speculation is climbing that it could raise rates. In China, indexes fell 0.4 per cent in Hong Kong and rose 0.2 per cent in Shanghai after the world’s second-largest economy said its exports jumped 25 per cent year-on-year in August, driven by strong demand for autos and high-tech items.



AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Three-Michelin-starred Dominique Crenn chooses Melbourne for her next restaurant
World.content:
Exclusive Eating outComing soon Three-Michelin-starred Dominique Crenn chooses Melbourne for her next restaurant The trailblazing French chef will open her first Australian venue in October. Expect cocktails, gougeres and her signature steak tartare. Dani Valent September 9, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One of the world’s most decorated chefs is opening a restaurant in Melbourne. From October, Dominique Crenn’s all-day Petit Crenn will serve pastries, coffee and French classics at InterContinental Melbourne The Rialto, in a ground-floor site that until recently housed a Haigh’s Chocolates store. “I love the city, I love Australian people, I want to be part of the community,” she told Good Food, in an exclusive interview. Dominique Crenn will open her first Australian venue in October. John Troxell Born in France, and cooking in California since 1988, Crenn is the only woman to be awarded three Michelin stars in the US, an honour she’s held since 2018. She was named “best female chef” by World’s 50 Best Restaurants in 2016 and one of the world’s 100 most influential people by Time in 2024, not only for her culinary artistry, but also for her decision to serve less red meat, as part of a push towards sustainability. The awards focus on her fine-dining restaurant Atelier Crenn in San Francisco, where the tasting menu is written as a poem, and many dishes are expressive renderings of memories of Brittany. One signature snack is a cocoa butter sphere filled with apple cider and topped with creme de cassis jelly, representing a regional aperitif.



Petit Crenn’s savoury madeleines with caviar. Verena Dohmen Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Melbourne’s 40-seat Petit Crenn is more casual, a resurrection of a concept brought to life in San Francisco, where the first Petit Crenn ran for a decade until 2024. It will offer coffee and pastries in the morning, and bistro-inspired dishes, plus cocktails, for lunch and dinner. Opening menu highlights include comte gougeres, savoury madeleines, duck rillettes with red onion jam, sardines with fennel pollen and preserved lemon, Nicoise salad and Crenn’s signature steak tartare with egg yolk jam and sauce au poivre. “It’s beautiful and fun, an homage to my heritage, the way I grew up with my mama and grandmother, the best produce, simple cooking, eating together,” Crenn says. “We live in a world where we have lost community. It’s all AI, being on the phone. We have a drink then disappear, we don’t take time to sit together.” Crenn’s fond impressions of Melbourne make it an ideal location. “There’s authenticity,” she says. “You can go up to someone, learn their story. It’s not superficial, the conversation flows.” Petit Crenn’s Nicoise salad with quail eggs. Verena Dohmen



Crenn’s influence extends beyond the kitchen and dining room. “I want people to be more connected to the ecosystem,” she says. In California, Crenn has her own organic farm. In Melbourne, she is getting to know farmers and artisans. “You have amazing produce,” she says, pointing to Great Ocean Ducks, vegetable grower Five Tales Farm, local oysters, and potter Sam Gordon. “It’s about working with the best ingredients, and from there I will do my little magic, celebrate their work. My dad used to say, ‘You kill it once, you don’t want to kill it twice.’ I’ll embrace the gift, so the farmer can be proud. It’s part of going deeper, understanding the ‘why’ behind it all.” Petit Crenn is a partnership with Salter Brothers, an investment, property and hospitality company that also owns Rick Stein’s NSW restaurants. Its Victorian portfolio includes the Intercontinental, where Salter’s culinary director, Matthew Butcher, already oversees Italian dining room Ronnie’s. Butcher has spent time with Crenn on both sides of the Pacific to plan the Melbourne opening. Steak frites at Petit Crenn. Verena Dohmen



Crenn is the first in a new wave of big-name international arrivals. Pichaya “Chef Pam” Soontornyanakij, from Michelin-starred Potong in Bangkok, and Sweden’s Bjorn Frantzen, who has a trifecta of three-star restaurants, will both open at Crown Sydney and Perth in 2027. Hong Kong’s Mott 32 is coming to Crown Melbourne. Crenn is also designing a menu for next year’s Australian Open and hopes to spend plenty of time here. “I don’t think people talk enough about Australia, the culture and people, the different origins, the richness of the country,” she says. How does she feel about opening a restaurant so far from home? “Life is about putting yourself out there, taking a risk and learning,” she says. “I’m grateful to have this experience. I want to bring a little bit of my heart, create a place I would like to go, and hopefully, it’s somewhere exciting for Melbourne.” 495 Collins Street, Melbourne, petitcrenn.com.au

World.title: ‘It was just so over the top’: Why Hazlewood isn’t expecting repeat of 2018 on South Africa return
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket ‘It was just so over the top’: Why Hazlewood isn’t expecting repeat of 2018 on South Africa return Tom Decent September 9, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australian cricket stars Josh Hazlewood and Alex Carey are confident the behaviour of South African crowds will not be an issue next month but insist they are ready for whatever is thrown their way on Australia’s first Test tour of the country since the infamous “Sandpapergate” series of 2018. The drama-plagued tour eight years ago was marred by the ball-tampering scandal involving Cameron Bancroft, who took sandpaper onto the field and admitted he had used it on the ball. The incident resulted in Bancroft, captain Steve Smith and David Warner being banned from the game. Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith face the media in Cape Town 2018. Getty Images TV cameras will follow Australia on their return to South Africa after Amazon Prime confirmed another season of The Test will document the men’s team over the next 12 months during a whirlwind international schedule. The popular documentary, which has run for three seasons, will be produced by Cricket Australia and Whooshka Media and released in 2027 after Australia’s tilt at Ashes glory in the UK next year.



It shapes as a fascinating return to the country for Pat Cummins’ men, with the first Test due to start in Durban on October 9 – and the cameras will be there to capture it all. If only, you cannot help but think, they had been inside Australia’s dressing room in Newlands in 2018. “Obviously, Cape Town is the third Test,” Hazlewood said. “We are going to be two Tests into the series and three one-dayers [down], so we’re going to be there for a while before that last frontier. The teams have changed a lot over the last eight years. It’s a long time ago. Honestly, I think it’ll be fine. Travis Head, Nathan Lyon, Alex Carey and Josh Hazlewood in Sydney ahead of their tour to South Africa. Scott Ehler/Amazon Prime “I can’t see it going like that [in 2018]. I haven’t seen a series go like that since. It was just so over the top, almost from ball one. I don’t know whether it was two teams at boiling point who had been on the road for a long time and were mentally drained and fatigued.” Hazlewood said South African crowds, along with those in New Zealand, tended to target individual players more than their counterparts elsewehere.



“Australia and India are mass crowds and mass noise. You might have a whole side in Birmingham singing a song about you or whatever,” Hazlewood said. “But I think New Zealand and South Africa are probably more one-on-one targeting. I don’t know if it’s worse or better, but it’s more individualised. It’s pretty easy to deal with.” Carey is no stranger to being heckled after his infamous stumping of Jonny Bairstow during the 2023 Ashes. Steve Smith addresses the media at Sydney Airport after arriving back from the sandpaper scandal in South Africa in 2018. Janie Barrett The Australian wicketkeeper was not on the 2018 tour – he made his Test debut against England in December 2021 – but feels well-equipped to handle whatever South African crowds throw at the team. It helps, Hazlewood pointed out with a laugh, that Carey spends most of his time safely stationed near the pitch rather than on the boundary.



“I learned not to worry about it,” Carey said. “In sport, there is always going to be a level of rivalry and someone is going to be a villain and a hero. Nation to nation, someone is going to cop it. “The boys on the boundary line cop it regularly when they head overseas. It’s part of sport I guess and [it’s about] not letting it affect us. I don’t think it really has. Josh Hazlewood during the 2018 Test series between Australia and South Africa. AP “I don’t know what South Africa is going to be like. We’ve been there twice for ODI series [since 2018]. There’s that normal level of country versus country banter. We’ll wait and see but from my point, learn to embrace it and laugh it off.” Smith, who served a 12-month ban alongside Warner for his role in the scandal, has already returned to South Africa for white-ball cricket but is preparing to play his first Test there since 2018.



Related Article Exclusive

Big Bash Renegades put up for sale as players launch fresh dispute action with Cricket Australia The 37-year-old was named on Monday in Australia’s 16-man squad. “We saw him come back at Edgbaston that time [in the 2019 Ashes] after 12 months out and get 100 in both innings, so he has that in him,” Hazlewood said. “He always wants to do well. Look out if he has that sort of feeling again. “It’s a nice time to do a doco. Hopefully we play ball for the doco and win a few games and get the right results and make it a good season. “I think [Kagiso] Rabada is a big one whether he is in or out [with his hamstring injury]. He’s a massive player for them as well, so that’ll play a part.”

World.title: ‘We’ve got work to do’: The blunt MCG warning from the AFL chairman
World.content:
In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of footy news: Magpies VFL coach Matthew Lokan will undergo anger management training

A Collingwood great will help select the new North Melbourne coach

The AFL chairman has conceded the MCG has fallen behind the world’s best stadiums

AFL matches could be shortened when Tasmania enter the competition in 2028

Chris Scott shoots down a shock retirement rumour

Western Bulldogs great Tom Liberatore has walked away after 268 games Recently retired Collingwood great Steele Sidebottom has been added to North Melbourne’s coaching selection panel. Sidebottom ended his celebrated 375-game career after the Magpies’ wildcard loss to the Western Bulldogs, but he will immediately step into his first post-playing role as the outside voice on a six-person panel. On his way: Steele Sidebottom was given a guard of honour on Friday night after playing his final game for the Magpies. AFL Photos The Roos sacked celebrated coach Alastair Clarkson last week and are now searching for his replacement.



The selection panel will be made up of Roos chief executive Jennifer Watt (chair), football general manager Todd Viney, director and former Roos captain Andrew Swallow, Roos AFW premiership coach Darren Crocker, club vice president Nick Dowling, and Sidebottom. Roos president Dr Sonja Hood is not on the panel, with prospective candidates asked to contact Watt or Viney to register interest. The club said it would not be providing a running commentary on the process until they have appointed their next coach. “The club is seeking a person with recent and relevant AFL coaching experience from successful environments who can deliver North Melbourne its next silverware in the men’s competition,” the club said in a statement. “Candidates will need a proven track record in demonstrating outstanding leadership, relationship building, communication, and education.



“Specific role information will be provided to individuals who express interest in the position and who meet the selection criteria.”

- Roy Ward Magpies VFL coach sanctioned for umpire abuse Peter Ryan Collingwood’s VFL coach Matthew Lokan will undergo anger management training as part of his sanction for abusing umpires after a round 20 VFL match against Essendon at Windy Hill. Lokan, who also works as a development coach with the AFL team, received a two-match ban (which was suspended until the end of 2027), a $4000 fine and will attend an AFL-approved anger management course at his own expense.



The alleged abuse happened on the ground after the game, which Essendon won by a point. It was considered serious enough for Magpie officials to enter the umpire’s rooms after the game to apologise. Collingwood was then sent a “please explain” after the matter was referred to the AFL Integrity Unit. The charge was proved, and the penalty accepted by the Magpies. Lokan, who was appointed VFL coach this season, said he recognised he had overstepped the mark and was prepared to do whatever the AFL required to ensure he set the right example. Collingwood VFL and development coach Matthew Lokan. AFL Photos “My behaviour was unacceptable, and I have apologised to the officials involved, as well as to the league and those at the club,” Lokan said. “I have a responsibility to always show respect to officials and will handle these situations better in future.”



Lokan joined the Magpies as their VFL coach at the start of 2026 after a career coaching in the SANFL. He played 46 matches for Collingwood between 2003 and 2005, including the Magpies’ 2003 grand final. The Magpies’ VFL team won seven matches and finished 16th in 2026. In an incident earlier in the season, Richmond VFL coach Jack Madgen was forced to explain his comments to umpires at half-time of a match against North Melbourne earlier this season. Richmond were fined $5000 and Madgen received a two-match ban which was suspended until the end 2027. The VFL and AFL are determined to set an example when it comes to interaction with umpires.



Craig Drummond with Eddie McGuire at the SportNXT conference in Melbourne. AFL chairman discusses shorter games, India, and upgrading the ’G Sam McClure AFL matches could be shortened when Tasmania enter the competition in 2028 as the league prepares for a major overhaul of its fixture. AFL chairman Craig Drummond has revealed reducing the length of games is among the options being considered as the league works through how to accommodate a 19th team without further increasing player workloads.



Drummond said players were already close to their physical limit and warned simply adding more football to the calendar was not sustainable. Related Article CBD AFL boss Craig Drummond declares zero tolerance for ‘poor behaviour’ after Sydney Swans scandal “If we want to have more games – do we need to have more games? If we want to have more games, we probably need a shorter game,” Drummond said at the SportNXT conference in Melbourne on Tuesday. “Most football people would say, and players certainly, and the PA and others would say, we’re probably just about maxed out on the number of minutes that players are playing.” Drummond said Tasmania’s arrival meant the existing fixture could not simply continue in its current form.



“We can’t have the current number of rounds [games per side] of 23. We need to have either 24, or something different.” The AFL is already consulting clubs about its options, with Drummond foreshadowing “meaningful change” to scheduling. The rethink comes amid record interest in the competition. The AFL attracted 7.8 million fans during the home-and-away season, while Drummond said many venues were now reaching capacity. That growth is also driving plans to modernise the MCG, with Drummond conceding the home of football had fallen behind the world’s best stadiums. “The spiritual home of our game is the MCG, and we need to continue, like any home, continue to renovate, rebuild and reimagine,” he said.



Drummond pointed to new American venues including SoFi Stadium as the benchmark, saying they were “so far and above what we’ve got” in functionality for supporters, broadcasters and players. “We’ve got work to do.” The AFL chairman also outlined an aggressive push into India, with the league approving increased investment aimed at growing participation from just over 10,000 players to more than 100,000. The strategy is partly designed to strengthen Australian football’s connection with the rapidly growing Indian-Australian community, which Drummond put at 1.3 million people. Drummond said there’s “work to do” to bring the MCG up standard in matching the world’s best stadia. AFL Photos



The AFL has already experimented with Hindi-language broadcasts, while chief executive Andrew Dillon has travelled to India as part of the league’s push. “Ideally, what we want to see is young Indian boys and girls playing our game, both at grassroots but also at the elite level,” Drummond said. “We need to have role models.” Drummond said growing football among Australians born overseas, as well as expansion in Queensland, western Sydney and Tasmania, would be central to his tenure as chairman. “We can’t feel fat and happy with where the game’s at today,” he said.



“Despite the fact that it is in great shape … we’ve got to grow it.” Chris Scott shoots down a shock retirement rumour Peter Ryan Geelong coach Chris Scott has confirmed he expects to be coaching at the Cats until at least the end of his current contract, which expires in 2029, after being questioned about his future at his weekly media conference. The question no one had on their mind arose after 3AW’s Rumour File aired a call on Tuesday morning speculating that the dual premiership coach would retire when the Cats’ current finals campaign ends.



Chris Scott’s Cats have won yet another final as they hunt for a flag Getty Images Scott was surprised at the inquiry but made it clear he had no intention of walking away as the Cats are on the cusp of securing Port Adelaide’s Zak Butters and the Giants’ Toby Greene in the upcoming trade period. “I expect to see out my contract,” Scott said. Scott has been open in recent seasons about the demands of the job but has also been keen to emphasise that the good outweighs the bad. He once again relayed his broad view of what life was like for senior coaches in the current environment but said any pitfalls were the “price of admission”.



“I love parts of [the job] and I despise parts of it,” Scott said. “The price of admission in the AFL is that some parts are going to be bloody hard, and some bits you are not going to be in love with, and some bits you just have to endure, to be frank.” Scott has coached the Cats since 2011, winning two premierships and leading them into 14 of the past 16 finals series. He began his coaching career as an assistant at Fremantle, the club his team will play in a semi-final on Friday night at Perth’s Optus Stadium. Gryan Miers is playing with a partial ACL tear Getty Images



The Cats will consider recalling Sam De Koning for the final, but Scott indicated midfielder James Worpel could be unavailable for the rest of the season with a troublesome hamstring. Related Article AFL briefing

AFL 2026 Cats’ players press AFLPA to assist Kolodjashnij return; Kangas veteran says, ‘we loved Clarko’ Meanwhile, small forward Gryan Miers is continuing his remarkable run as he plays with a partial ACL tear. He said it took time before he decided to continue after initially booking in with a surgeon to have a reconstruction. “I’m willing to fail with the opportunity to succeed,” Miers said on Monday. “So I’m really happy with the route I’ve taken: that if it goes wrong, and it still might, but that could be for different reasons, that could be because we just lose, I play bad, or another injury – that I’m OK with that because I think I’ve made the right decision.”



He said there were no plans for him to have a reconstruction at season’s end.

- Peter Ryan ‘Libba’ calls it a day Scott Spits Decorated Western Bulldogs star Tom Liberatore has announced his AFL retirement after 16 seasons and 268 matches – including the 2016 premiership. A key member of the club’s famous drought-breaking, flag-winning side, the now-34-year-old is hanging up the boots after 11 games in his final season.



Tom Liberatore (left) and teammate Cody Weightman during the Bulldogs’ round-22 clash with the Kangaroos. AFL Photos Liberatore has a long history with concussion – suffering his latest in round six this year against Geelong. He didn’t play again until round 15 against the Saints – given he was also battling a knee injury. His final game was the round 23 draw against the Blues. Liberatore and his father Tony became only the second father-son pairing to play 250 games for the same club – along with Essendon greats Ken and Dustin Fletcher. “This club and its community have been such a huge part of my life,” Tom said in a statement on Tuesday. “I’m so fortunate to have lived out my dream for 16 years, from watching my old man play for the club, to being part of a premiership that meant so much to all of our fans and to the western suburbs, it’s been a real privilege.



“I still love being here and competing each week, but it’s time for me to step aside, spend more time with my family and friends and support this great club from the stands. “I’ve built lifelong friendships with many teammates through the years, that’s what means the most to me. Tom and Tony Liberatore share a moment after the 2016 premiership. Getty Images “I want to take the opportunity to thank everyone at the club: players, coaches and staff for the amount of effort and time they’ve dedicated to me over the years.” Liberatore became just the 15th Bulldog to reach the 250-game milestone, and was last year named as one of the 25 Greatest Bulldogs.



Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge lauded the contribution Liberatore has made throughout his time at “the Kennel”. “Tom has been the spiritual catalyst within our playing ranks for such a long period of time,” Beveridge said. “Through the challenges he has faced, he has had a fierce will and desire to claw his way back. ‘Libba’ has always set about influencing everyone he comes in contact with in his own unique, caring and quirky characteristic way. “Always a fierce competitor, he has been inspirational with his tenacity and confrontational brand ensuring his teammates always walk a little taller and feel a little more self-assured.



“I am extremely grateful to have coached Tom and I know all of our people see it as a great privilege to have shared Tom’s AFL football experience with him.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: ASX eyes gains, Wall Street drifts lower; Oil hovers near $US100
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX eyes gains, Wall Street drifts lower; Oil hovers near $US100 Stan Choe Updated September 9, 2026 — 6:17am ,first published 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks drifted lower in their return to trading from a three-day weekend. The S&P 500 fell 0.6 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 628.2 points, or 1.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite closed 0.3 per cent lower. Wall Street has retreated after returning from a long weekend, with rising oil prices weighing on investors. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures at 6am AEST pointing to a gain of 21 points, or 0.2 per cent, at the open. The ASX shed 1 per cent on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was trading at US72.22¢. US stocks felt pressure from oil prices, after a barrel of Brent crude briefly climbed as high as $US99.46. It later gave back most of its gain and was most recently up 0.1 per cent at $US97.05. It’s nevertheless jumped from roughly $US72 since early July as increased fighting in the Middle East keeps the global flow of oil constricted.



More expensive oil has worsened worries about the high inflation weighing on people and companies across the country, which gives extra heft to a couple reports coming later this week. On Thursday, the US government will release its August report for inflation at the wholesale level, which economists expect will show an acceleration to 5.4 per cent from 4.7 per cent in July. The more closely watched report on inflation that US consumers are feeling will arrive on Friday. That update will show how much more people are paying for groceries, clothes and other costs of living, and economists expect it eased a bit to 3.3 per cent from July’s 3.4 per cent inflation rate. That, though, remains well above the 2 per cent target that the Federal Reserve has set as its goal. Related Article Opinion

Trade wars Fighting the bully: Canada throws a punch back at Trump Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist This week’s updates on inflation will be the last before the Fed meets next week to decide whether to cut, raise or hold interest rates steady. The traditional move for the Fed when inflation is high is to raise its main interest rate. That in turn would filter out into the rest of the bond market, make it more expensive for companies and people to borrow, slow the overall economy, undercut prices for investments and hopefully rein in inflation. But President Donald Trump has been lobbying for lower interest rates instead, which could give the economy — and inflation — an extra kick. The Fed’s new chairman, Kevin Warsh, has meanwhile said he wants to give financial markets fewer clues about what the Fed plans to do with interest rates in the short term.



That all has traders betting on a 60 per cent probability the Fed will raise its federal funds rate at the conclusion of its next meeting on Sept. 16, according to data from CME Group. In the bond market, the yield on the 10-year Treasury inched up to 4.79 per cent from 4.78 per cent and remains near its highest level since the autumn of 2023. Higher Treasury yields put more pressure on companies to grow their profits in order to lift their stock prices. On Wall Street, Boston Scientific fell 4.6 per cent after saying that a network outage earlier this summer caused by a cybersecurity incident means that it’s unlikely to meet forecasts it gave for sales and profit for the third quarter and for the fully of 2026. It expects to make back some of the revenue as it continues to ramp operations globally, fulfil customer orders and reduce remaining backlogs, but it doesn’t yet know the full impacts. Shares of Novartis that trade in the United States tumbled 13.9 per cent after the Swiss pharmaceutical company gave a discouraging update on a study of a therapy for people living with myotonic dystrophy type 1, a neuromuscular disease.



Qualcomm helped limit the market’s losses after rising 2.9 per cent. It announced a deal to collaborate with Amazon on large-scale AI data centres. The deal also gives Amazon the right to acquire up to 25 million of Qualcomm’s shares at $US161.26 per share. Related Article Opinion

Donald Trump The Taxman v Trump: ATO opens new front in fight with Big Tech Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer In stock markets abroad, Japan’s Nikkei 225 sank 1.7 per cent under the weight of losses for major exporters, which were hurt by more rises for the value of the Japanese yen against the US dollar. A stronger yen erodes the value of sales made in US dollars when Toyota Motor, Panasonic Holdings and other Japanese exporters have to translate them back into yen. The Bank of Japan is also scheduled to meet next week on interest rates, and speculation is climbing that it could raise rates. In China, indexes fell 0.4 per cent in Hong Kong and rose 0.2 per cent in Shanghai after the world’s second-largest economy said its exports jumped 25 per cent year-on-year in August, driven by strong demand for autos and high-tech items.



AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.
