World.title: Three-Michelin-starred Dominique Crenn chooses Melbourne for her next restaurant
World.content:
Exclusive Eating outComing soon Three-Michelin-starred Dominique Crenn chooses Melbourne for her next restaurant The trailblazing French chef will open her first Australian venue in October. Expect cocktails, gougeres and her signature steak tartare. Dani Valent September 9, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One of the world’s most decorated chefs is opening a restaurant in Melbourne. From October, Dominique Crenn’s all-day Petit Crenn will serve pastries, coffee and French classics at InterContinental Melbourne The Rialto, in a ground-floor site that until recently housed a Haigh’s Chocolates store. “I love the city, I love Australian people, I want to be part of the community,” she told Good Food, in an exclusive interview. Dominique Crenn will open her first Australian venue in October. John Troxell Born in France, and cooking in California since 1988, Crenn is the only woman to be awarded three Michelin stars in the US, an honour she’s held since 2018. She was named “best female chef” by World’s 50 Best Restaurants in 2016 and one of the world’s 100 most influential people by Time in 2024, not only for her culinary artistry, but also for her decision to serve less red meat, as part of a push towards sustainability. The awards focus on her fine-dining restaurant Atelier Crenn in San Francisco, where the tasting menu is written as a poem, and many dishes are expressive renderings of memories of Brittany. One signature snack is a cocoa butter sphere filled with apple cider and topped with creme de cassis jelly, representing a regional aperitif.



Petit Crenn’s savoury madeleines with caviar. Verena Dohmen Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Melbourne’s 40-seat Petit Crenn is more casual, a resurrection of a concept brought to life in San Francisco, where the first Petit Crenn ran for a decade until 2024. It will offer coffee and pastries in the morning, and bistro-inspired dishes, plus cocktails, for lunch and dinner. Opening menu highlights include comte gougeres, savoury madeleines, duck rillettes with red onion jam, sardines with fennel pollen and preserved lemon, Nicoise salad and Crenn’s signature steak tartare with egg yolk jam and sauce au poivre. “It’s beautiful and fun, an homage to my heritage, the way I grew up with my mama and grandmother, the best produce, simple cooking, eating together,” Crenn says. “We live in a world where we have lost community. It’s all AI, being on the phone. We have a drink then disappear, we don’t take time to sit together.” Crenn’s fond impressions of Melbourne make it an ideal location. “There’s authenticity,” she says. “You can go up to someone, learn their story. It’s not superficial, the conversation flows.” Petit Crenn’s Nicoise salad with quail eggs. Verena Dohmen



Crenn’s influence extends beyond the kitchen and dining room. “I want people to be more connected to the ecosystem,” she says. In California, Crenn has her own organic farm. In Melbourne, she is getting to know farmers and artisans. “You have amazing produce,” she says, pointing to Great Ocean Ducks, vegetable grower Five Tales Farm, local oysters, and potter Sam Gordon. “It’s about working with the best ingredients, and from there I will do my little magic, celebrate their work. My dad used to say, ‘You kill it once, you don’t want to kill it twice.’ I’ll embrace the gift, so the farmer can be proud. It’s part of going deeper, understanding the ‘why’ behind it all.” Petit Crenn is a partnership with Salter Brothers, an investment, property and hospitality company that also owns Rick Stein’s NSW restaurants. Its Victorian portfolio includes the Intercontinental, where Salter’s culinary director, Matthew Butcher, already oversees Italian dining room Ronnie’s. Butcher has spent time with Crenn on both sides of the Pacific to plan the Melbourne opening. Steak frites at Petit Crenn. Verena Dohmen



Crenn is the first in a new wave of big-name international arrivals. Pichaya “Chef Pam” Soontornyanakij, from Michelin-starred Potong in Bangkok, and Sweden’s Bjorn Frantzen, who has a trifecta of three-star restaurants, will both open at Crown Sydney and Perth in 2027. Hong Kong’s Mott 32 is coming to Crown Melbourne. Crenn is also designing a menu for next year’s Australian Open and hopes to spend plenty of time here. “I don’t think people talk enough about Australia, the culture and people, the different origins, the richness of the country,” she says. How does she feel about opening a restaurant so far from home? “Life is about putting yourself out there, taking a risk and learning,” she says. “I’m grateful to have this experience. I want to bring a little bit of my heart, create a place I would like to go, and hopefully, it’s somewhere exciting for Melbourne.” 495 Collins Street, Melbourne, petitcrenn.com.au

World.title: ‘It was just so over the top’: Why Hazlewood isn’t expecting repeat of 2018 on South Africa return
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket ‘It was just so over the top’: Why Hazlewood isn’t expecting repeat of 2018 on South Africa return Tom Decent September 9, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australian cricket stars Josh Hazlewood and Alex Carey are confident the behaviour of South African crowds will not be an issue next month but insist they are ready for whatever is thrown their way on Australia’s first Test tour of the country since the infamous “Sandpapergate” series of 2018. The drama-plagued tour eight years ago was marred by the ball-tampering scandal involving Cameron Bancroft, who took sandpaper onto the field and admitted he had used it on the ball. The incident resulted in Bancroft, captain Steve Smith and David Warner being banned from the game. Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith face the media in Cape Town 2018. Getty Images TV cameras will follow Australia on their return to South Africa after Amazon Prime confirmed another season of The Test will document the men’s team over the next 12 months during a whirlwind international schedule. The popular documentary, which has run for three seasons, will be produced by Cricket Australia and Whooshka Media and released in 2027 after Australia’s tilt at Ashes glory in the UK next year.



It shapes as a fascinating return to the country for Pat Cummins’ men, with the first Test due to start in Durban on October 9 – and the cameras will be there to capture it all. If only, you cannot help but think, they had been inside Australia’s dressing room in Newlands in 2018. “Obviously, Cape Town is the third Test,” Hazlewood said. “We are going to be two Tests into the series and three one-dayers [down], so we’re going to be there for a while before that last frontier. The teams have changed a lot over the last eight years. It’s a long time ago. Honestly, I think it’ll be fine. Travis Head, Nathan Lyon, Alex Carey and Josh Hazlewood in Sydney ahead of their tour to South Africa. Scott Ehler/Amazon Prime “I can’t see it going like that [in 2018]. I haven’t seen a series go like that since. It was just so over the top, almost from ball one. I don’t know whether it was two teams at boiling point who had been on the road for a long time and were mentally drained and fatigued.” Hazlewood said South African crowds, along with those in New Zealand, tended to target individual players more than their counterparts elsewehere.



“Australia and India are mass crowds and mass noise. You might have a whole side in Birmingham singing a song about you or whatever,” Hazlewood said. “But I think New Zealand and South Africa are probably more one-on-one targeting. I don’t know if it’s worse or better, but it’s more individualised. It’s pretty easy to deal with.” Carey is no stranger to being heckled after his infamous stumping of Jonny Bairstow during the 2023 Ashes. Steve Smith addresses the media at Sydney Airport after arriving back from the sandpaper scandal in South Africa in 2018. Janie Barrett The Australian wicketkeeper was not on the 2018 tour – he made his Test debut against England in December 2021 – but feels well-equipped to handle whatever South African crowds throw at the team. It helps, Hazlewood pointed out with a laugh, that Carey spends most of his time safely stationed near the pitch rather than on the boundary.



“I learned not to worry about it,” Carey said. “In sport, there is always going to be a level of rivalry and someone is going to be a villain and a hero. Nation to nation, someone is going to cop it. “The boys on the boundary line cop it regularly when they head overseas. It’s part of sport I guess and [it’s about] not letting it affect us. I don’t think it really has. Josh Hazlewood during the 2018 Test series between Australia and South Africa. AP “I don’t know what South Africa is going to be like. We’ve been there twice for ODI series [since 2018]. There’s that normal level of country versus country banter. We’ll wait and see but from my point, learn to embrace it and laugh it off.” Smith, who served a 12-month ban alongside Warner for his role in the scandal, has already returned to South Africa for white-ball cricket but is preparing to play his first Test there since 2018.



Related Article Exclusive

Big Bash Renegades put up for sale as players launch fresh dispute action with Cricket Australia The 37-year-old was named on Monday in Australia’s 16-man squad. “We saw him come back at Edgbaston that time [in the 2019 Ashes] after 12 months out and get 100 in both innings, so he has that in him,” Hazlewood said. “He always wants to do well. Look out if he has that sort of feeling again. “It’s a nice time to do a doco. Hopefully we play ball for the doco and win a few games and get the right results and make it a good season. “I think [Kagiso] Rabada is a big one whether he is in or out [with his hamstring injury]. He’s a massive player for them as well, so that’ll play a part.”

World.title: ‘We’ve got work to do’: The blunt MCG warning from the AFL chairman
World.content:
In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of footy news: Magpies VFL coach Matthew Lokan will undergo anger management training

A Collingwood great will help select the new North Melbourne coach

The AFL chairman has conceded the MCG has fallen behind the world’s best stadiums

AFL matches could be shortened when Tasmania enter the competition in 2028

Chris Scott shoots down a shock retirement rumour

Western Bulldogs great Tom Liberatore has walked away after 268 games Recently retired Collingwood great Steele Sidebottom has been added to North Melbourne’s coaching selection panel. Sidebottom ended his celebrated 375-game career after the Magpies’ wildcard loss to the Western Bulldogs, but he will immediately step into his first post-playing role as the outside voice on a six-person panel. On his way: Steele Sidebottom was given a guard of honour on Friday night after playing his final game for the Magpies. AFL Photos The Roos sacked celebrated coach Alastair Clarkson last week and are now searching for his replacement.



The selection panel will be made up of Roos chief executive Jennifer Watt (chair), football general manager Todd Viney, director and former Roos captain Andrew Swallow, Roos AFW premiership coach Darren Crocker, club vice president Nick Dowling, and Sidebottom. Roos president Dr Sonja Hood is not on the panel, with prospective candidates asked to contact Watt or Viney to register interest. The club said it would not be providing a running commentary on the process until they have appointed their next coach. “The club is seeking a person with recent and relevant AFL coaching experience from successful environments who can deliver North Melbourne its next silverware in the men’s competition,” the club said in a statement. “Candidates will need a proven track record in demonstrating outstanding leadership, relationship building, communication, and education.



“Specific role information will be provided to individuals who express interest in the position and who meet the selection criteria.”

- Roy Ward Magpies VFL coach sanctioned for umpire abuse Peter Ryan Collingwood’s VFL coach Matthew Lokan will undergo anger management training as part of his sanction for abusing umpires after a round 20 VFL match against Essendon at Windy Hill. Lokan, who also works as a development coach with the AFL team, received a two-match ban (which was suspended until the end of 2027), a $4000 fine and will attend an AFL-approved anger management course at his own expense.



The alleged abuse happened on the ground after the game, which Essendon won by a point. It was considered serious enough for Magpie officials to enter the umpire’s rooms after the game to apologise. Collingwood was then sent a “please explain” after the matter was referred to the AFL Integrity Unit. The charge was proved, and the penalty accepted by the Magpies. Lokan, who was appointed VFL coach this season, said he recognised he had overstepped the mark and was prepared to do whatever the AFL required to ensure he set the right example. Collingwood VFL and development coach Matthew Lokan. AFL Photos “My behaviour was unacceptable, and I have apologised to the officials involved, as well as to the league and those at the club,” Lokan said. “I have a responsibility to always show respect to officials and will handle these situations better in future.”



Lokan joined the Magpies as their VFL coach at the start of 2026 after a career coaching in the SANFL. He played 46 matches for Collingwood between 2003 and 2005, including the Magpies’ 2003 grand final. The Magpies’ VFL team won seven matches and finished 16th in 2026. In an incident earlier in the season, Richmond VFL coach Jack Madgen was forced to explain his comments to umpires at half-time of a match against North Melbourne earlier this season. Richmond were fined $5000 and Madgen received a two-match ban which was suspended until the end 2027. The VFL and AFL are determined to set an example when it comes to interaction with umpires.



Craig Drummond with Eddie McGuire at the SportNXT conference in Melbourne. AFL chairman discusses shorter games, India, and upgrading the ’G Sam McClure AFL matches could be shortened when Tasmania enter the competition in 2028 as the league prepares for a major overhaul of its fixture. AFL chairman Craig Drummond has revealed reducing the length of games is among the options being considered as the league works through how to accommodate a 19th team without further increasing player workloads.



Drummond said players were already close to their physical limit and warned simply adding more football to the calendar was not sustainable. Related Article CBD AFL boss Craig Drummond declares zero tolerance for ‘poor behaviour’ after Sydney Swans scandal “If we want to have more games – do we need to have more games? If we want to have more games, we probably need a shorter game,” Drummond said at the SportNXT conference in Melbourne on Tuesday. “Most football people would say, and players certainly, and the PA and others would say, we’re probably just about maxed out on the number of minutes that players are playing.” Drummond said Tasmania’s arrival meant the existing fixture could not simply continue in its current form.



“We can’t have the current number of rounds [games per side] of 23. We need to have either 24, or something different.” The AFL is already consulting clubs about its options, with Drummond foreshadowing “meaningful change” to scheduling. The rethink comes amid record interest in the competition. The AFL attracted 7.8 million fans during the home-and-away season, while Drummond said many venues were now reaching capacity. That growth is also driving plans to modernise the MCG, with Drummond conceding the home of football had fallen behind the world’s best stadiums. “The spiritual home of our game is the MCG, and we need to continue, like any home, continue to renovate, rebuild and reimagine,” he said.



Drummond pointed to new American venues including SoFi Stadium as the benchmark, saying they were “so far and above what we’ve got” in functionality for supporters, broadcasters and players. “We’ve got work to do.” The AFL chairman also outlined an aggressive push into India, with the league approving increased investment aimed at growing participation from just over 10,000 players to more than 100,000. The strategy is partly designed to strengthen Australian football’s connection with the rapidly growing Indian-Australian community, which Drummond put at 1.3 million people. Drummond said there’s “work to do” to bring the MCG up standard in matching the world’s best stadia. AFL Photos



The AFL has already experimented with Hindi-language broadcasts, while chief executive Andrew Dillon has travelled to India as part of the league’s push. “Ideally, what we want to see is young Indian boys and girls playing our game, both at grassroots but also at the elite level,” Drummond said. “We need to have role models.” Drummond said growing football among Australians born overseas, as well as expansion in Queensland, western Sydney and Tasmania, would be central to his tenure as chairman. “We can’t feel fat and happy with where the game’s at today,” he said.



“Despite the fact that it is in great shape … we’ve got to grow it.” Chris Scott shoots down a shock retirement rumour Peter Ryan Geelong coach Chris Scott has confirmed he expects to be coaching at the Cats until at least the end of his current contract, which expires in 2029, after being questioned about his future at his weekly media conference. The question no one had on their mind arose after 3AW’s Rumour File aired a call on Tuesday morning speculating that the dual premiership coach would retire when the Cats’ current finals campaign ends.



Chris Scott’s Cats have won yet another final as they hunt for a flag Getty Images Scott was surprised at the inquiry but made it clear he had no intention of walking away as the Cats are on the cusp of securing Port Adelaide’s Zak Butters and the Giants’ Toby Greene in the upcoming trade period. “I expect to see out my contract,” Scott said. Scott has been open in recent seasons about the demands of the job but has also been keen to emphasise that the good outweighs the bad. He once again relayed his broad view of what life was like for senior coaches in the current environment but said any pitfalls were the “price of admission”.



“I love parts of [the job] and I despise parts of it,” Scott said. “The price of admission in the AFL is that some parts are going to be bloody hard, and some bits you are not going to be in love with, and some bits you just have to endure, to be frank.” Scott has coached the Cats since 2011, winning two premierships and leading them into 14 of the past 16 finals series. He began his coaching career as an assistant at Fremantle, the club his team will play in a semi-final on Friday night at Perth’s Optus Stadium. Gryan Miers is playing with a partial ACL tear Getty Images



The Cats will consider recalling Sam De Koning for the final, but Scott indicated midfielder James Worpel could be unavailable for the rest of the season with a troublesome hamstring. Related Article AFL briefing

AFL 2026 Cats’ players press AFLPA to assist Kolodjashnij return; Kangas veteran says, ‘we loved Clarko’ Meanwhile, small forward Gryan Miers is continuing his remarkable run as he plays with a partial ACL tear. He said it took time before he decided to continue after initially booking in with a surgeon to have a reconstruction. “I’m willing to fail with the opportunity to succeed,” Miers said on Monday. “So I’m really happy with the route I’ve taken: that if it goes wrong, and it still might, but that could be for different reasons, that could be because we just lose, I play bad, or another injury – that I’m OK with that because I think I’ve made the right decision.”



He said there were no plans for him to have a reconstruction at season’s end.

- Peter Ryan ‘Libba’ calls it a day Scott Spits Decorated Western Bulldogs star Tom Liberatore has announced his AFL retirement after 16 seasons and 268 matches – including the 2016 premiership. A key member of the club’s famous drought-breaking, flag-winning side, the now-34-year-old is hanging up the boots after 11 games in his final season.



Tom Liberatore (left) and teammate Cody Weightman during the Bulldogs’ round-22 clash with the Kangaroos. AFL Photos Liberatore has a long history with concussion – suffering his latest in round six this year against Geelong. He didn’t play again until round 15 against the Saints – given he was also battling a knee injury. His final game was the round 23 draw against the Blues. Liberatore and his father Tony became only the second father-son pairing to play 250 games for the same club – along with Essendon greats Ken and Dustin Fletcher. “This club and its community have been such a huge part of my life,” Tom said in a statement on Tuesday. “I’m so fortunate to have lived out my dream for 16 years, from watching my old man play for the club, to being part of a premiership that meant so much to all of our fans and to the western suburbs, it’s been a real privilege.



“I still love being here and competing each week, but it’s time for me to step aside, spend more time with my family and friends and support this great club from the stands. “I’ve built lifelong friendships with many teammates through the years, that’s what means the most to me. Tom and Tony Liberatore share a moment after the 2016 premiership. Getty Images “I want to take the opportunity to thank everyone at the club: players, coaches and staff for the amount of effort and time they’ve dedicated to me over the years.” Liberatore became just the 15th Bulldog to reach the 250-game milestone, and was last year named as one of the 25 Greatest Bulldogs.



Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge lauded the contribution Liberatore has made throughout his time at “the Kennel”. “Tom has been the spiritual catalyst within our playing ranks for such a long period of time,” Beveridge said. “Through the challenges he has faced, he has had a fierce will and desire to claw his way back. ‘Libba’ has always set about influencing everyone he comes in contact with in his own unique, caring and quirky characteristic way. “Always a fierce competitor, he has been inspirational with his tenacity and confrontational brand ensuring his teammates always walk a little taller and feel a little more self-assured.



“I am extremely grateful to have coached Tom and I know all of our people see it as a great privilege to have shared Tom’s AFL football experience with him.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: 'Such a relief': Mayor backs National's bed tax replacement
World.content:
National announces new alternative to bed tax Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Rotorua's mayor says it's a "welcome surprise" councils will take charge of how they spend new International Visitor Levy funding if National is re-elected.

National's alternative to a bed tax announced by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, Tourism Minister Louise Upston, and Finance Minister Nicola Willis would redistribute the International Visitor Levy tourists pay at the border.

Instead of the $100 levy going into government baselines, they announced $100 million a year would go to the Department of Conservation, $50m to tourism projects, and the rest to councils.

Each council's share would depend on the number of overseas tourists who stayed in its area.

This would also be topped up with more than $105m taken from future operating allowances.

The new policy is a replacement for a bed tax which National had originally agreed to consider but has now ruled out.

Louise Upston, Christopher Luxon and Nicola Willis at the announcement in Auckland. RNZ/Nick Monro

Auckland mayor Wayne Brown said it was a step in the right direction but would still leave his council millions of dollars short compared with the take from a bed tax.

Rotorua mayor Tania Tapsell, a former National candidate, said it was "such a relief" to hear of the new policy.

"We do need significant investment in our regions and actually this has come as a welcome surprise because we've actually got what we wanted as councils.

"We said we want to make the decisions for our communities and that's exactly what's going to happen - a significant amount of money guaranteed over the next few years."

It was crucial councils decided how the money would be spent. The South Island would focus on infrastructure, Auckland on attracting events and Rotorua would be looking at destination marketing, Tapsell said.

She believed Queenstown which would get more than $80m over the next four years to help with its infrastructure spending.

Rotorua which hosts around 1 million foreign tourists a year would get around $20m over four years.

Tapsell said the region would have got more with a bed tax, however, it was still a significant amount of money.

Using the visitor levy was preferable to avoid New Zealanders having to pay any levy, she said.

"This is quality over quantity."

The new money would also lift a burden from ratepayers. Rotorua with a population of 78,000 hosted 2 million visitors annually.

"This is going to help us without hurting the pockets of those domestic visitors."

A good first step

Hotel operator responds to visitor levy funding announcement Morning Report Download MP3 5m

Sudima NZ operating officer Les Morgan also praised the levy announcement which he said was a good first step.

He said a lot of work had been done on the bed tax and it was disappointing to have it "tossed aside".

However, the levy was the second most favoured option.

The raising of the levy from $35 to $100 had so far had little impact and showed visitors were prepared to pay it, Morgan said.

He was among those concerned that while it was positive that councils would receive the levy funding, it was not "fresh investment".

It was redistributing existing money.

With the government aiming for 4.7 million visitors by 2034, there remained "a huge funding gap" to pay for the infrastructure upgrades that would be needed.

World.title: Government to implement findings from mental health hotline review
World.content:
Matt Doocey responds to report into mental health services Morning Report Download MP3 7m

The government has accepted all the recommendations from a report into the telehealth service for mental health.

The review found too many people who tried to call for help didn't get through.

"Too many people approaching these services do not get their calls answered, a proportion of whom may be experiencing acute distress," the independent report said.

It also found the telehealth services weren't adequately integrated with the wider mental health and addiction system.

"I was very disappointed with that finding", Minister for Mental Health Matt Doocey told Morning Report.

"It beggars belief there was a high volume of calls not being answered.

"I'd like to put a target in to say that all calls are connected within, say, five to ten minutes. "

Doocey said the government was "acting swiftly to implement the findings of the review".

"The review provides reassurance that core safety systems are in place, including triage, risk assessment, escalation processes, and clinical governance," he said.

"But it also makes clear there is more work to do. Too many people are not getting through quickly enough, and we do not always have enough visibility of what happens after someone is referred or escalated to another service."

He outlined three initiatives intended to address the report's findings.

First was to expand peer support via the 1737 hotline, which previously operated between 2pm and 10pm, to 9am to midnight.

It would also commission a pilot to attempt proactive follow-up calls to people who had contacted 1737 in distress.

The third initiative would set up a 24/7 suicide prevention crisis line within the telehealth system.

"We are clear, and there are no exceptions to the rule; when someone reaches out for help, they should be able to access the support they need without waiting too long," Doocey said.

Where to get help:

Need to Talk? Free call or text 1737 any time to speak to a trained counsellor, for any reason.

Lifeline: 0800 543 354 or text HELP to 4357.

Suicide Crisis Helpline: 0508 828 865 / 0508 TAUTOKO. This is a service for people who may be thinking about suicide, or those who are concerned about family or friends.

Depression Helpline: 0800 111 757 or text 4202.

Samaritans: 0800 726 666.

Youthline: 0800 376 633 or text 234 or email talk@youthline.co.nz.

What's Up: 0800 WHATSUP / 0800 9428 787. This is free counselling for 5 to 19-year-olds.

Asian Family Services: 0800 862 342 or text 832. Languages spoken: Mandarin, Cantonese, Korean, Vietnamese, Thai, Japanese, Hindi, Gujarati, Marathi, and English.
